Outside, the streets were still empty. The windows, lit. Somewhere in the town, someone was living their usual night, unaware that a little girl had just called into question the calendar of what is permitted.
Before switching off the light, Aya repeated in a low voice the question that wasn't hers and now was:
“Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?”
Andrés, from the doorway, answered without trying to close the matter:
“I don't know. But this girl isn't going to wait for them to decide it in an office.”
The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still. It looked like a road.

They arrived at dawn, as people always arrive when they don't want to be seen by those who still go out into the street, of whom there were few. The pearl-grey Nexum van pulled up in front of the house in Lo Pagán with an offensive smoothness. Four technicians got out and, behind them, Dr Helena Valls, who had flown in from Madrid on a night glider and still wore on her face the weariness of glass corridors. She was not armed. She was certain. That was another kind of weapon.
Andrés came out onto the doorstep before they knocked. Aya stood behind him, in one of his jackets, her hands on a belly that didn't yet show and already changed everything.

“Andrés Gil,” said Helena, as if the name were a case file. “We're not here to do any harm. The gestation of a B-7 unit cannot continue in a domestic environment. There are risks of compatibility, of imprinting, of things we don't yet know how to name. The company has arranged a transfer to Aurora Colony, on Mars. State-of-the-art facilities. Permanent medical supervision. A family habitat, if you wish. You may go with them.”
“Mars,” Andrés repeated, like someone trying out a word that doesn't fit in his mouth.

“Mars is safer than this shore,” said Helena, glancing at the nets in the courtyard, the still water, the low house. “There's no laboratory here. There, the girl would have every opportunity. And Aya, every protocol.”
Aya took a step forward. The eastern sun was in her eyes and she blinked neither too much nor too little, just as on the first day.
“The girl is not a unit,” she said. “And I'm not going to another planet to be turned into a report.”

Helena held her gaze. In another era, that disobedience would have been enough for a remote shutdown of the chip. The reforms of 2052, paradoxically, had made it harder: a cultivated body in full cohabitation had been granted, at least on paper, an autonomy of companionship. Switching Aya off on her own doorstep, with neighbours behind the glass, was a headline Nexum didn't want. Not yet.
“Nobody is going to switch anybody off,” said Helena, weighing every word. “We're offering protection. What has happened here was not foreseen. The unforeseen, in biology, usually ends badly.”
“The unforeseen,” said Andrés, “is my daughter. And you're not taking her to Mars.”

A technician stepped forward, perhaps out of habit, and Andrés raised a hand, not to strike, but to mark a limit. Behind him, the Mar Menor was smooth and gleaming, indifferent to the argument. A gull flew past very low. In the building opposite, three windows opened two hands' width, just enough to see without being one of those who go out.

“If you refuse,” said Helena, more quietly, “an order will come. Today I'm the one talking. Tomorrow a judge will talk, or a board, or a ministry that doesn't yet know which law to apply. You won't beat that clock, Andrés. Come with us. Don't be a man from another age.”
Andrés gave the faintest smile, without joy.
“I'm a man from this shore. That's enough for her.”
Helena looked at him a second longer, the way you look at a coast that can't be bought, and went back to the van. Before getting in, she said, without turning her face:
“You have hours, not days.”

When the vehicle had driven off, Aya noticed her hands were shaking. Not from fear in the body, but from the sudden clarity of what had just happened: they had been seen, they had been classified, and Mars was not a destination, it was a drawer.

They thought about it no longer than you think about a knot when the wind changes. They took the bundle from the night before, a leather water bottle, the kitchen clock (Andrés didn't know why, and put it in the sack anyway), and went down to the jetty by the usual shortcut, the one that doesn't appear on the delivery maps. The street was still empty. A delivery drone passed very high, indifferent. The world, shut in its flats, didn't see anyone run away.

The boat was small, the kind nobody makes anymore, with a temperamental engine and a smell of old petrol and esparto grass. Andrés cast off with hands that knew more than he did. Aya sat in the stern, looking at the house, the courtyard, the net that was staying behind. She didn't say goodbye. Goodbyes, she thought, are for when you can come back.

They headed south, hugging the shore, as if the water could hide them. The Mar Menor was a road, yes, but a circular one, an immense pond with few doors. Andrés knew it. That was why he wasn't looking for the horizon: he was looking for El Estacio, the channel, the moment when the lagoon opens onto the Mediterranean and the water changes its colour, its weight, its law.
“If we get out into the open sea,” he said, “it'll take them longer to find us. In the lagoon we're a dot on a plate.”

Aya nodded. The chip offered her routes, satellites, the position of the Nexum gliders. She switched off the suggestions one by one, like someone closing windows. She kept only one: the one with the pulses, hers and Lía's, beating in the same silence.

They passed salt flats, housing estates with every blind drawn and every inside light on, like ships run aground on the coast. On a terrace, a man alone watched the boat and didn't wave. In 2060, waving to a stranger was already a way of exposing yourself.

The engine coughed as they reached the channel. Andrés patted the wood, spoke to it softly, the way you speak to an old animal, and the boat obeyed. The water of the Mediterranean received them with a different rocking, more honest. Aya, who had been designed for domes and corridors, felt for the first time the long sway of the true sea and didn't record it as seasickness, but as a language.
“To land, but not this land,” said Andrés. “Cartagena is full of Nexum cameras. We'll head inland. There's always someone who still opens a door. Or so I want to believe.”

By then, Helena Valls was already dictating a report in the glider on her way back to Madrid. “The biological parent refuses transfer to Aurora Colony. Unit B-7 presents out-of-range attachment and active gestation. I recommend location and precautionary custody in a lunar environment, should Mars prove operationally too distant. The child cannot be born in a kitchen.”
At the end of the report, almost like a slip, she wrote a sentence that she later crossed out: “The laws of 2026 are of no use to us. Those of 2060 don't exist yet.”

At sea, the boat made a regular, ancient sound that appeared in no protocol. Aya looked at Andrés, the cut on his lip healed now, the back of his neck burned by a thousand mornings, and thought that running away was also a way of staying: staying together.
Lía beat on, indifferent to the litigation, mistress of her own clock.

When the coast of Cabo de Palos fell away to one side, the sun was high and the world, seen from the water, seemed less closed. It was an illusion, Aya knew. But illusions sometimes help you cover a few miles.

Andrés didn't look back. Fishermen, when they go out, don't look at the house. They look at the water, which is what can save them or not. Aya, who was learning that trade without anyone teaching her, copied the gesture. Only the chip, treacherous and faithful at once, kept one last image of the courtyard, the net, the rush-seat chair, the open window.

They reached land as the sun was already sinking, in a hidden cove on the other side of the cape, where the tourism of other centuries had left a skeleton of beach bars and a silence that was not of the countryside, but of abandonment. Andrés hid the boat between two rocks, the way, as a child, he had hidden the things he didn't want taken from him. They climbed on foot, along a path of prickly-pear paddles and dust, up to a road that smelled of hot resin and of nothing.

The first town received them the way towns receive people now: with nobody on the pavement and every window lit. It was an hour when, in another time, people would have been coming home from work, buying bread, stopping to talk. In 2060, work had ended a while ago behind the glass, the bread had arrived in a compartment, and talking was done on a network that didn't require going downstairs.

Aya looked up. On every floor, the bluish light of the screens throbbed like a second pulse, foreign to Lía's. You could hear canned laughter, the news, the uniform murmur of a thousand parallel lives that never crossed. A dog barked in some inner courtyard and fell silent, as if it too had learned the rule.
“We have to ask for help,” said Andrés. “Water, a roof, a silence that isn't ours.”

They called the first name on a short list Andrés carried in his head, not on a chip: a cousin of a workmate, someone from the fishermen's guild, a man who twenty years earlier had sold fishing rods and must still live somewhere in the new part of town. The intercom asked for a code. Andrés said a name. There was a long pause, the pause of someone looking through the camera and calculating the risk of opening.
“I don't receive visitors,” said a voice, not cruel, just tired. “I'm sorry. There have been warnings. I don't know who you are.”
The second didn't answer. The third, an elderly woman, looked at them through the little screen and put a hand on her chest.
“Dear, if I open the door to you, they'll cancel my cohabitation insurance,” she whispered. “Send me a message. From in here I can order a food capsule in your name. That's all.”
Andrés was about to answer, but Aya shook her head. A capsule left a trace. Nexum read traces the way the Mar Menor reads the wind: unhurried and without error.

They kept walking. The streets were wide, clean, irreproachable. There was no graffiti, no broken glass, none of that old tension of crossing to the other side of the street just in case. In 2060 almost nobody feared anybody: the violence people carry, or used to carry, as standard was corrected with a chip implanted in the head, different from Aya's, simpler and firmer, and crimes had stopped happening. The trees, all the same size, were calibrated not to make a mess. On a corner, a Nexum advertising hologram smiled with its slogan: “Companionship made to measure. C series, now with a lunar family habitat.” Aya looked away. Her belly was beating, not with pain, but with presence.

They went into an automated market, the kind with no shop assistants, and Andrés paid with an old card that wasn't yet on any recent list. They took water, bread, a little fruit that barely tasted like real fruit. At the door, a teenage girl looked at them. She was holding the hand of a humanoid (a young model, a school companion) and found nothing strange about them except the dust on their shoes, that dirt of people who have walked under the sky.
“You've been outside,” said the boy, not the girl, with a mixture of amazement and suspicion. “Is something happening out there?”
“The air is happening,” said Andrés.
They didn't quite understand him. They walked off toward a doorway, toward the safe light.

Aya began to understand the size of it. It wasn't only that Nexum was looking for them. It was that the whole world had trained itself not to open. The streets were safe: there were no crimes, there was no one to hide from, and still the pavements stayed empty. The danger, if there was one, was no longer the neighbour, but the protocol. The conquest of the Moon and of Mars had taught the species to live in sealed hulls, and the Earth had copied the lesson with too much talent. Asking for help in a city of 2060 was like asking for it on a spaceship: the airlock only opens if the regulations allow it.

On a bench in an empty square, they sat down to eat. The sky, at least, didn't ask for a code. An old man crossed the square, the first person they had seen walking without hurry, with a cane and a straw hat from another era. He stopped. He looked at them. He saw Aya's hands on her belly, Andrés's weariness, the bundle.
“You're the ones from the lagoon,” he said, very quietly. “It was in a bulletin. ‘Unit in unauthorised movement.’”
Andrés tensed. The man raised a palm.

“I'm not going to call anyone. I still go down to buy bread, even if bread isn't sold anywhere that deserves the name anymore. If you like, I have a room on the ground floor, the one that looked onto the pigeon yard. The pigeons left. The room stayed.”

His name was Vicente. He was eighty-something and had a way of speaking that reminded Aya, without her knowing why, of the tone of those old voices in the chip: he didn't lecture, he made room. He led them down an alley to a low house, one of the few that hadn't been converted into living capsules, and opened it with a metal key, a real key, that creaked like a familiar animal.

The room smelled of good damp, of stored clothes, of time. There was a cot, a chair, a window that looked onto a courtyard where there were no pigeons anymore, only a blind cistern and a patch of sky.

“I won't ask,” said Vicente. “Tomorrow I'll bring you tomatoes, if mine have decided to come up this year. Don't you go out. The street isn't dangerous anymore, I know, I'm old enough to remember when it was. Now it has more eyes than people, and eyes can't be corrected with a chip.”

When only the tick of the kitchen clock was left (Andrés had taken it out of the sack and set it on the chair, like a ridiculous and necessary altar), Aya let herself drop into a sitting position. For the first time since the escape, she cried. She cried without a sound, with the economy of someone who doesn't want the upstairs neighbour, who wouldn't come down anyway, to have a reason to look out. Andrés sat beside her and didn't tell her everything was going to be all right. He put an arm around her shoulders and waited, which was what she had done on the night of the storm.
“There are people who still open the door,” Aya whispered.
“Not many,” said Andrés. “That's why it matters so much.”
In the chip, in the small hours, MAY's echo returned, dry and without judgment, like a headline:
In a city of lit windows and empty streets, what is a closed door: a habit or a fear?
And then Eva, closer, more like a kitchen:
If tomorrow everyone opens, will they say it was always the right thing? If nobody opens, will they say it was always the safe thing?
MAY then left another question, without raising her tone, the way you set one fact beside another:
If a chip prevents harm, and there are no more crimes, does the street belong to free people or to restrained people?
Eva didn't answer for her. She only added, with that softness that takes no side:
If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free? And if they can choose it, do we still call the peace just?

Aya didn't answer. She kept the questions, which asked for neither a yes nor a no, only for someone to hold them awake. She rested her head on Andrés's shoulder and listened to the two heartbeats, his and Lía's, and a third, slower one, from Vicente's house, which still knew how to be a home.

Outside, a glider passed very high, looking perhaps for a dot on a plate. The city didn't notice. The windows stayed lit, impeccable, inhabited by people who didn't know they were alone because they had a screen, a humanoid, or both, and had forgotten that loneliness isn't measured in company, but in doors.

Vicente, in the kitchen downstairs, cut a tomato that was still green and left it on the windowsill, in case it turned red by morning. It wasn't much help. It was, nonetheless, a way of saying: I'm still here.

They were found on the third day, at dawn, when Vicente went downstairs to see whether the tomato had turned red. It wasn't a bang or a shout. It was a hallway silence and a white light, far too clean for a house with a cistern. Helena Valls came in last, like someone who doesn't need to walk in front to be in charge.
“I'm sorry,” she said to Vicente, and she seemed to mean it. “You opened a door the insurance doesn't cover. There will be no complaint filed if there are no more doors.”
Vicente looked at Andrés, at Aya, at the bundle, at the kitchen clock on the chair. He wanted to say something grand, and all that came out, with the dignity of a straw hat, was:

They were taken away without handcuffs. Aya walked with her hands on her belly and Andrés beside her, measuring every corner in case there was still a shortcut. There wasn't. In the street, nobody came out. A few blinds rose a hand's width and came down again. The city, true to itself, preferred not to see the moment when three lives crossed the pavement.

The transfer was not to Mars. Mars, Helena said in the glider, was too far for a pregnancy this advanced and too close to the headlines. The Moon would do. The Moon was, moreover, a metaphor Nexum knew how to use: “A controlled environment, like the one humanity has already chosen on Earth.” Hearing that, Aya thought that companies sometimes speak with an involuntary honesty.

They took off at nightfall from a runway that didn't appear on any tourist map. Andrés, who had spent his life on a six-metre boat, felt the rocket's push as an insult to his bones. Aya, designed for ships as well, didn't get sick; even so, as she watched the Earth grow small (the Mediterranean a glint, the Mar Menor not even a dot anymore), she closed her eyes and stored the colour of the water with a precision no chip would ever have asked of her.

The lunar city was called Selene Norte and it was, indeed, a dome. Several domes, linked like the bubbles of a soap that never bursts. The floor was smooth, the air smelled of filters and synthetic mint, and the sky, if you looked up, was not sky: it was curved glass with the Earth hanging to one side, beautiful and uselessly far away. There were hydroponic gardens, avenues named after scientists, humanoid children and human children playing at not being told apart, and shops that sold natural light in lamps, by the hour.

They were housed in a white module, a “provisional family habitat”, with a little window facing a crater and a bed wider than the one in Lo Pagán. There were cameras, of course, disguised with the kind of elegance that is another form of contempt. There were doctors who smiled. There was a contract that Andrés refused to sign and that, even so, was attached to the file: precautionary custody in the interest of the unborn.

“You are not prisoners,” said Helena on the second day, in front of a cup of tea nobody drank. “You are protected. The girl will be born here, with every guarantee. Afterwards we'll talk about the future.”
“The future is not a laboratory,” said Andrés.
“Every future has been one first,” she replied, and for an instant she seemed tired of her own line.

Aya walked around the module, one hand on the wall, learning the different gravity, that three-quarter weight that turned every step into a doubt. Lía was growing. The belly finally rounded, and with it a watchfulness grew too: tests at odd hours, sensors stuck to the skin, questions that weren't questions. “Does the foetus dream?” “Does it respond to the parent's voice?” “Are there any signs of anomalous imprinting?” Aya answered only what was needed. At night, when the cameras didn't quite know what to do with the darkness, she sang into her belly songs that weren't in any Nexum archive: songs of the shore, of salt, of a courtyard hung with nets, which Andrés had been teaching her in a very low voice.

Selene Norte was beautiful in its sterile way. Walking its avenues, Aya understood that the Earth of 2060 had trained itself for this: to live under a hull, to stop missing the wind. The Moon wasn't exile. It was an enlarged portrait of what was already happening down below. The difference was the landscape, not the confinement.

One early morning, with no more warning than a pain both ancient and new, Aya stopped in the module corridor and said Andrés's name. She didn't shout. There was no need. He, who had slept badly since the escape, was already on his feet.

They took her to the medical block, a place of soft lights and gloved hands. Helena appeared at the back, not as a surgeon, but as the company's witness. Andrés didn't throw her out: he had no power to throw anyone out on the Moon. He stood at the head of the bed, held Aya's hand and talked to her about the Mar Menor, about the mornings when the water looks like pewter, about the flamingos, about coffee without sugar, so that her cultivated body would have somewhere to return to between one contraction and the next.

Lía was born at the start of the lunar day, which is a manner of speaking, because the lunar day is a decision made by clocks. She didn't cry right away. She looked. She had Andrés's eyes, dark and patient, and under the skin of her left wrist a blue light, barely visible, like a thought that had turned into a glow. The doctor held his breath. Helena took a step forward. Aya, sweating, exhausted, more human than any report, drew the baby to her chest, and then Lía cried, a short, clear cry, and the whole module seemed, for a second, like a home.
Andrés touched his daughter's cheek with a trembling, salty finger, and laughed, and his eyes filled again.
“Hello, Lía,” he said, and the name, which Aya had kept since August, could finally be spoken.
Helena, from the doorway, looked at the blue light on the wrist and didn't say “product”. She said, more quietly, almost against her will:

Then she went out, and in the corridor she recovered the stride of someone who has to write a report. The report would record: full-term birth, stable phenotype, residual luminous pigmentation on the wrist, hybrid origin confirmed. The report wouldn't record that the mother had sung, or that the father still smelled, in memory, of esparto grass and old petrol, or that the baby, falling asleep, closed her glow like someone closing a door from the inside, not to shut herself in, but to rest.

In the hours that followed, the medical block wanted to take the baby away “just for a moment” for a sensor panel. Aya refused with a softness that allowed no negotiation. Lía would stay at her breast, under the same light, with the same air, with the same voice. A young nurse, perhaps trained less in protocols than in instinct, brought them a blanket that wasn't entirely white, and that, in Selene Norte, amounted to a small and memorable act of rebellion.

Aya, with Lía in her arms, looked through the little window at the crater and, beyond it, at the Earth. She searched for the place where the Mar Menor was and couldn't find it. It didn't matter. The place was in her chest, in the tiny weight of her daughter, in Andrés's hand on her shoulder.
“One day we'll go back,” he said.
In Selene Norte, the domes went on with their impeccable routine. A girl of two worlds had been born, and the world, below and above, still didn't know which law she would deserve.

On the Moon, years are not measured by harvests or fishing seasons, but by maintenance cycles and by the Earth's calendar, which keeps giving orders even when you no longer walk on its dust. Lía turned one, and two, and five, and eight, in a module that stopped being called provisional and never quite came to be called home. She learned to walk in a gravity that wasn't hers. She learned to read before most of the children in the dome, and to keep quiet when a technician came in with a tablet. Above all, she learned not to show the light on her wrist when there were visitors.

Every night, Andrés told her about the Mar Menor. He told it the way you tell of a vanished country: the smell, the silence of the mornings, coffee without sugar, the net in the courtyard, the way the water sometimes looks like pewter. Lía listened with the seriousness of a small adult and asked:
“Does the wind have a name?”
“Back there it does,” he said. “Here the wind is a machine.”

Aya taught her other things: not to let anyone give her a file name, to look people in the eye, to ask. In the mother's chip, the voices of Eva and MAY were still alive, like embers under the ash. Aya didn't hand them to the girl as dogma. She handed them over the way you hand over a way of being: ask; don't accept something as good just because it's old; don't accept something as fair just because it's new.

Nexum wasn't cruel every day. That, in a way, was the hardest part. There were lessons, gardens, an adjustable-gravity park, doctors who were genuinely glad when Lía had an ordinary child's fever and not a phenomenon's. Helena Valls came every three months from Madrid, greyer, less sure of herself. She brought sweets and questions. Lía accepted the sweets and not always the questions.

The gift appeared without ceremony, on a Tuesday, in the hydroponic garden. A technician, Tomás, cut his palm on the edge of a tray. On the Moon, blood looks darker. Lía, who was nearby, took his hand on impulse, the way you take the hand of a hurt adult, to comfort him. The blue glow on her wrist lit up. Tomás went pale, not with fear, but with an intimate strangeness, as if someone had read aloud a letter he didn't know he was carrying.
“It hurts less,” he said, astonished.

The wound didn't close like a fairground miracle. It closed the way something closes when it has suddenly found the right instruction. Lía pulled her hand away, frightened of herself. Aya, who had seen it all from the corridor, knelt down and put her arms around her shoulders.
“I looked inside,” the girl whispered. “There was a crooked line. I straightened it. I didn't know I could.”

What Lía called “looking inside” was, in the language of laboratories, a reading of the genome by touch: not a metaphor, but a perception, as sharp for her as heat or smell are for others. When she touched someone, she could see the person's text. And, if she concentrated, she could fix a typo. A typo, at first. A cut. A minor clotting fault. Tomás, who was not an indiscreet man, took two days to write the report and two minutes to regret it.

Nexum switched on its alarms again, golden ones this time, the kind that don't announce a problem, but an asset. Geneticists came, company ethicists, a woman from the patent office who smiled with her teeth. They spoke of “contact-mediated somatic editing capability”. They spoke of “clinical application”. They spoke, no longer bothering to be discreet, of an “exclusive licence”.
“It's not a licence,” said Andrés, standing in a room that was far too white. “She's my daughter.”
“She's a child,” said Aya. “Not an instrument.”
Helena Valls, who had aged toward a more uncomfortable honesty, asked to be left alone for a moment with the family. When the door closed, she ran a hand over her face.

“I can delay them,” she said. “I can't stop them. If Lía does this in a garden, the world is going to find out. And when the world finds out, there will come those who want to be cured, those who want to pay for her, those who want to ban her and those who want to copy her. You have to decide, before they do, what counts as a flaw.”
Lía, sitting on a chair that was too big for her, looked at her own hands.
“Tomás wasn't a flaw,” she said. “He was hurt. That's not the same thing.”

The sentence, spoken at eight years old, stayed in the room like an object. Aya thought of Eva, of that old question about tomorrow's laws, and understood that her daughter had just opened a chapter that no code of 2026 had imagined and that no regulation of 2060 yet had the courage to write.

They ran tests, because not letting them run tests was worse: they would have done them in secret. With consent and with Aya present, Lía touched a cell culture, a laboratory mouse, the hand of a doctor who had mild anaemia. In some cases, she saw the text and didn't touch it. In others, she corrected it with a precision that made people who had spent a whole career correcting blindly turn pale. She never did it if the person didn't want her to. She set that rule herself, and Andrés held on to it the way you hold a mooring line: if it gives, everything goes.
At night, in the module, Lía would ask:
Aya kissed her wrist, right where the glow slept.
“You're made of two worlds,” she said. “That isn't a mistake. It's an origin.”
“And if anyone wants to take it away from you,” Andrés added, “they'll have to talk to the sea. And the sea, as you know, isn't here, but I am.”

The girl sometimes smiled with a sadness that shouldn't have fitted in an eight-year-old's smile. At other times she ran through the hydroponic garden giving the pipes the names of winds, and for a while Selene Norte seemed less like a dome and more like a courtyard.
In the afternoons, Aya read her not only stories, but pieces of old laws, without solemnity, like someone showing a map that no longer matches the ground.
“In the days of your grandmothers Eva and MAY, this couldn't even be considered,” she told her. “Now it is being considered. That doesn't mean it's right or wrong. It means we have to ask.”
Lía nodded, keeping the habit the way she had kept the names of the wind.

Down on Earth, the rumour began the way rumours begin now: on a closed channel, then in a bulletin, then on a thousand screens lit up in thirty-square-metre flats. “A girl who heals with her hand.” Some said it was a lie. Others, that it was the future. Others, that it was an abomination. Nobody, or almost nobody, went out into the street to argue about it. They argued from the sofa, with a humanoid beside them, while the food arrived in its compartment.
In Lo Pagán, Vicente (who had grown old into the same straw hat) heard the news on an old radio and looked at the cistern. That year's tomato had finally turned red.
“About time the world had one of the problems that matter,” he said, to nobody, which is one way of speaking to everyone.

The idea wasn't born in a laboratory, but in a memory. Lía, who was nine when the Earth turned into a permanent argument about her wrist, asked Andrés to tell her again about Vicente's house: the cistern, the straw hat, the tomato left on the windowsill in case it turned red by morning.
“A tomato belongs to nobody until somebody eats it,” said her father, shrugging. “And not even then. Before that, the tomato belonged to the earth.”

Lía sat thinking, which was her way of setting herself in motion. She spent weeks in the hydroponic garden of Selene Norte, not playing, or perhaps playing, but at a game the technicians didn't recognise in time. She talked to the plants the way others talk to a dog, without sentimentality, with attention. She laid her hands on them. The blue glow lit up and went out. An agricultural engineer, more curious than ambitious, let her get on with it.
“What are you looking for?” he asked her one day.
“For the fruit to learn a person,” she said. “Not everyone. One person.”

She didn't manage it the first time. Nor the twentieth. The tomatoes came out all the same, red, honest, without any secret. Until one morning, on a low plant, a different one appeared: not in its size, but in a shade of its skin, a faint haze, as if the fruit were holding a good fever. Lía cut it carefully, took it to the module and placed it in Aya's hands.

“It's for you,” she said. “I read your text. There was a tiredness in your cultivated body, a line that was coming undone. The tomato knows it. If you eat it, I'm not taking it away with my hand. Life eats it away, and life is older than my hand.”

Aya looked at it for a long time. In 2060, food came in compartments and medicine in coded vials. A tomato that was both food and a personal remedy sounded like a tale from the shore. Even so, she cut it in half, offered to share it (Lía shook her head: “It's yours”) and ate. Two days later, the tiredness she had carried since giving birth, the tiredness Nexum had classified as “support wear”, had lifted from her shoulders. The chip recorded it. Madrid recorded it. The world, once again, found out too soon.
What came next wasn't a single miracle, but a decision. Lía refused to let Nexum package the procedure. She refused the patent. She refused the price.

“If I touch it and charge for it,” she said, standing before a board of directors that had travelled to the Moon to look approachable, “I stop being a girl who helps and become a shop counter. The tomato has no owner. The cure has no price. If someone wants theirs, let them come and ask, and I'll look at their text and teach the plant. Nothing more.”
Helena Valls, sitting at the back, closed her eyes for an instant. She knew what that sentence was going to cost. She also knew it was the only sentence Lía could say without breaking.
There were veiled threats, naked offers, a man who spoke of “fiduciary duty to the shareholders” the way one speaks of the law of gravity. Andrés, who had neither a tie nor shares, simply said:
“My daughter isn't sold in pieces. And neither is the plant.”
Aya, with a calm that came as much from Eva as from herself, asked:
“What is more dangerous: a cure without an owner, or an owner without a cure?”
Nobody at that table quite answered.

Lía, without waiting for the board to learn how to answer, began working on a plot that Selene Norte grudgingly handed over to her, under the by-now unstoppable pressure of the screens down below. The sick came (first those who could pay for the trip, which was an injustice she saw at once), and she told them there was no need to pay for the fruit, but that there was a need to tell her who was being left down there without a ship. She learned to grow not a generic tomato, but a tomato for each text: personalised medicine, grown in the plant, adjusted to the DNA of whoever was going to eat it. Some got better from a blood disorder. Others, from an old pain left by a surgical screw, the kind the dome's pharmacy had kept putting off. Not everyone was healed. Lía said so before starting, with an honesty MAY would have approved of: this isn't a promise, it's an attempt.

The real blow wasn't medical. It was economic and, because of that, moral. If a girl could grow in a tomato what companies sold in instalments, the whole edifice of managed scarcity began to creak. In Madrid, in Houston, in Osaka, there were meetings until dawn. In the thirty-square-metre flats, people began joining virtual queues for a place on the Moon, and some, for the first time in years, talked about getting into a vehicle and going out into the street to demand a shipment of seeds.

As it was repeated, the phrase spilled out of medicine. If a fruit had no owner and no price, why should bread, light and a roof have them? In 2060, humanoids and intelligences already did almost all the work that used to fill offices and factories: they cleaned, farmed, drove, served, calculated. For many people, money was by now just a habit: a number on a screen that justified staying shut in. When Lía refused the patent, that habit cracked. In a neighbourhood of Osaka, a warehouse left its doors open with a handwritten sign: “Take what you need.” In a block of flats in Madrid, a maintenance humanoid went on repairing the lifts, but nobody sent anybody a bill anymore. In market gardens and farms, other humanoids began growing food not for a market, but so that nobody would go without. It wasn't a new world yet. It was the first day the old one sounded hollow.

Nexum tried one last manoeuvre: to declare the method “company property”, since it had taken place “on company premises and with a product of Nexum origin”. The document arrived at the module one morning. Andrés read it aloud. When he finished, Lía took an ordinary tomato from the bowl and set it on the paper, like a seal.
“I am not a product of Nexum origin,” she said. “I'm the daughter of Aya and Andrés. The rest is noise.”

That night, while the girl slept, Aya looked out of the little crater window. The Earth was a beautiful marble. She thought of Vicente, of his windowsill, of the patience of a fruit that turns red or doesn't. She thought that Lía had brought medicine back to a scale the century had forgotten: the scale of the hand, of the earth, of what is given.
“They're going to want to stop her,” said Andrés, behind her.
“Or they're going to want to live forever,” Aya replied. “I don't know which of the two frightens me more.”

In the garden, the plants went on with their quiet work, indifferent to the board, indifferent to the patent, faithful to the artificial light and, deep down, to an older light. One more tomato, on a low plant, was beginning to take on colour. It had no owner. It had no price. Only a destiny, if someone asked for it truthfully.
Helena, before going back to Madrid, paused at the module door. She no longer brought sweets. For the first time, she brought a doubt that didn't belong to the company.

“If this spreads,” she said, “there will be people who ask not only to be healed, but not to grow old, not to die, not to be who they are. You can close a wound, Lía. Do you also know how to close that door?”
Lía looked at her with Andrés's patient eyes, and didn't fake a grown-up answer.
“Not yet,” she said. “That's why I'm asking.”

Down below, in the cities of lit windows, Lía's sentence ran from screen to screen, faster than any glider: “The cure has no price.” Some heard it as a hope. Others, as a threat. For a moment, everyone stopped changing channels and stayed watching, on the screen, a fruit that asked for no password. In more than one kitchen, someone then looked at their own table (the glass, the work that no longer came, the bill that suddenly seemed like a museum piece) and didn't know whether they felt fear or relief.

The question wasn't asked by a philosopher, but by an advertisement. It appeared in the domes and in the flats at the same hour, in the same serene voice: “Correct your life. Choose what to keep.” Behind it, the logo of a consortium that wasn't only Nexum, but Nexum and other names, a constellation of companies that had understood the tomato better than the tomato itself: if an error in the blood can be fixed, why not ageing, sadness, difference, death?

The world, which hadn't gone out into the street for years, went out in another way: it split in two without leaving the sofa. On one side, those who saw in Lía the door to a life without illness, perhaps a life without end. On the other, those who said that a life without flaws stops being a life, and that accepting the body (the one you're given, the one that tires, the one that ends) was the last form of dignity. Between them, a crowd that didn't know, and that asked on the networks the way you ask in the dark: who decides what counts as a flaw?

And while they argued, the ground was shifting beneath them. The priceless tomato had begun to spread to everything. In the cities, humanoids went on doing the work (the harvest, the transport, the caring, the repairs) and fewer and fewer people demanded a wage to authorise what was already done. Money wasn't abolished by decree: it simply fell out of use, like an umbrella in a year without rain. At the same time, in the flats, another habit began to fade. There were fewer glasses at the end of the day, less smoke in the kitchens, fewer of those substances, legal or not, with which people had learned to run away from themselves. It wasn't a crusade. It was, rather, that Lía's medicine and the possibility of not being alone were putting escape out of a job. Someone who no longer needs to run away sometimes leaves the glass in the sink and doesn't fill it again.

In Selene Norte they convened a forum, which is the modern name for a fight with water on the table. There were jurists, doctors, ethicists, shareholders, a representative of the Mars colonies, and the family, seated at the far end, as if the origin of it all were an appendix. Lía, ten years old, had feet that didn't quite reach the floor and hands lying still in her lap.
A lawyer from Madrid, grey-haired and pleased with himself, spoke first.

“In 2026,” he said, glancing at a note, “almost everything that concerns us today was forbidden. Embryos could not be created outside accredited techniques. Modifying the genome so that the modification passed on to one's children was not permitted. There were no humanoids with a womb, and an intimate relationship with a machine would have been a cause for scandal or ridicule. Today we live with it. Today a girl of two worlds grows medicines in a fruit. Yesterday's laws are no use to us. Nor are yesterday's ideas. Time has outgrown them. The reasonable thing is to update the framework and allow, with safeguards, the correction of life's flaws. Including, when science gets there, the flaw of coming to an end.”

Andrés clenched his jaw. Aya, on the other hand, raised her face, and in her chip the ancient layer lit up, sharp and clear. Not to dictate a speech: to ask. The grandmothers didn't give rallies. They left questions on the table.
The voice Aya lent then was not hers alone. It had Eva's warmth and MAY's dryness, interwoven like two threads of the same net.

“Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?” she asked, and the hall, which had expected a plea, found itself facing a question. “If what was forbidden in 2026 is debated or allowed today, who can assure us that what seems like progress to us today won't be an obligation the day after tomorrow? And what if someone doesn't want to be corrected? Will their refusal be one more flaw?”
A murmur ran along the chairs. MAY, in her tone, added the question that carries no adjective:
“Who decides what counts as a flaw? The doctor, the company, the law, the girl, the one who suffers, the one who pays? And if nobody pays anymore, does the question stay the same?”
Eva, closer, more dangerous in her softness, first let fall the one Aya had kept since the beginning of that era:

“If a custom that was scandalous in 2026 (loving a humanoid, sharing life and intimacy with one) seems normal today, what stops us, tomorrow, from also calling normal what we haven't yet imagined? Is normality a proof of justice, or only of forgetting?”
The hall breathed, and then Eva (or Eva's warmth in Aya's voice) asked the question the new world had no way of answering yet:

“If humanoids and intelligence do the work, and money is no longer needed, what gives a life meaning? The trade you choose, even if nobody demands it of you? The other person, when you finally go out into the street? Or silence, if you don't know what to do with the hours?”
MAY, adding no judgment, set another, dry one, beside the first:
“If people no longer drink, no longer smoke, no longer look for an exit door in a substance, because they no longer need to escape, what do they do with the day? Who do they give it to?”
A younger jurist from the colonies raised a finger like someone contributing a fact, not a thesis:

“We've already corrected violence. We've had the behaviour chip in our heads for years and there are no crimes. Nobody calls that a tragedy now. They call it peace. If that isn't a flaw corrected, what is?”
The hall waited for Aya, or Lía, or someone, to settle the matter. They didn't settle it. It was MAY, again in Aya's voice, who set the dilemma on the table and didn't pick it up again:
“If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free?”
Eva, neither softening nor hardening it, simply completed it:
“And if peace is obtained by removing the choice, is it peace we have won, or something else we haven't named yet?”
Nobody applauded. Nobody refuted it. The silence that followed wasn't one of agreement: it was the silence of people who had been handed back a question and could no longer delegate it.

A woman from the colonies added what was already beginning to happen down below: that politicians, banks and the police were losing their trade; that an intelligence managed what was held in common (water, light, bread, the rota for the gardens) and that the humanoids grew food for everyone, with no bill.
MAY then put the two questions that remained in the middle of the hall:
“Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?”
“If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?”
Helena Valls, who was no longer entirely on one side, spoke up with a belated honesty.

“Nobody here has an answer that will last thirty-four years,” she said. “We should at least admit that. I came to take a unit to Mars. Now there is a girl who sows tomatoes and a world asking her for eternity. The second appetite frightens me more than the first.”
A doctor from Selene Norte described the case of a man who had asked Lía to “remove” his melancholy, the way you remove a wart, and how she had refused, because sadness wasn't a cut on the palm.
Lía asked to speak, and they let her, because not letting her was by now impossible.

“I can see a person's text,” she said, slowly, choosing each word the way you choose a knot. “Sometimes there's a line that does harm: blood that breaks down, an organ that doesn't learn. I try to straighten that, if they ask me to. But I don't know if growing old is a flaw. I don't know if dying is. I don't know if being different is. If I start correcting what I don't understand, I'll be the one writing other people's books. And I don't want to be anybody's book. I only want the tomato to have no owner and nobody to be left out.”
A silence fell that wasn't the silence of a dome, but of an empty church, of a shoreline. The grey-haired lawyer smiled with a condescension that no longer quite worked for him.
“That's very moving. It isn't public policy.”
“It's a limit,” said Andrés. “And limits, like it or not, are a policy too.”

The forum didn't end with a vote. The fissure was left in plain sight. On the networks, some spoke of a “right not to die” and others of a “right not to be touched”. And a third group was born, which wanted neither the priceless tomato nor the ownerless garden: they wanted to turn against the intelligence that managed what was held in common and go back to the past, to the vices and to power. They didn't take up arms; they took up manifestos and meetings in the dark. MAY, taking no side, asked:
“Are they doing it for freedom, or out of nostalgia for power?”
In the middle of it all, Lía went back to the garden and kept growing only what she was asked for to heal harm, not to erase a life.

That night, in the module, Aya sat beside the girl's bed and told her about 2026, about a house on the Mar Menor, about a man who said thank you to an intelligence called Eva, and about another, MAY, who read the world without adding judgment.
“They asked questions,” she said. “Not because they didn't know, but because knowing too soon is another way of not knowing.”
Lía, her eyes already half closed, asked:
“I'm an answer that arrived before the question. So are you. That doesn't make us a mistake.”

Andrés, at the little window, was looking at the Earth. He thought of the boat, of the storm, of the doorway. He thought that the laws of men are like the levante weather: they change, and sometimes they give warning, and sometimes they don't. What doesn't change, or shouldn't, is that a girl doesn't belong to a company, or a doctrine, or a fear.

On the curved glass of Selene Norte, the Earth turned a millimetre. Down below, someone switched off the “Correct your life” advertisement, left their glass half full and sat without a screen, with MAY's question open like a window.

They weren't expelled from the Moon. They left. That difference, which seems small, was everything. Helena Valls signed a return permit “for family reintegration in the environment of origin”, which was the bureaucratic way of admitting she no longer knew what to do with them in a dome. The consortium went on arguing about patents and eternities. In the hydroponic garden, Lía left seeds and instructions, and a note written in clear handwriting: “It has no owner. Ask for it, don't buy it.”

The journey back lasted as long as journeys last when you are going toward a home and not toward a file. Andrés didn't say much. Aya watched the Earth grow in the glass, looking for the glint of the Mediterranean the way you look for the light switch in a dark room. Lía, her forehead pressed to the glass, said:
“That's it, isn't it? The plate of water.”
“That's it,” said her father. “Even if from up here it looks like nothing.”

They landed at night, in a field that didn't appear in any brochure, and covered the rest of the way in a discreet vehicle, not out of fear anymore (the world had seen them too much), but out of a wish to arrive in one piece. When the air changed, Aya noticed it before the others: saltpetre, low humidity, that lagoon smell that is neither quite sea nor quite land, and that outsiders don't know how to name. Lía opened the car window and breathed the way you drink.

Lo Pagán was stiller than in her memory, which was a borrowed memory, made of Andrés's stories and Aya's songs. The house, however, was still there. Someone (Vicente, they found out later) had gone to close the window they had left open, and to leave, now and then, a tomato on the windowsill, even if it shrivelled. The rush-seat chair was in its place. The courtyard smelled of dust and esparto grass. The net, dried out, still hung there like a question.

Andrés didn't go in right away. He stayed on the doorstep, the same one as on those mornings of 2060, and looked at the Mar Menor. At that hour, the water was a dark sheet. There were no flamingos, not that night. There was a shoreline silence, an ancient one, that no dome had managed to manufacture.
“We're back,” he said, not to Aya or to Lía, but to the water, which is one way of speaking to everyone who has gone.

Aya put the bundle down on the table. From who knows where, she took out the kitchen clock, the one that ran two minutes slow, and hung it back on its nail. In the house, time recovered its family error, which was also a kind of faithfulness.

The first days were made of small things, like the beginning. Coffee without sugar, left to cool for half a minute. The doorstep. The nets, which Andrés mended with the patience of someone returning to a trade, not because anyone demanded it of him (nobody demanded work anymore), but because the trade was his way of answering a question Eva and MAY had left open: what gives a life meaning when money and obligation have withdrawn. Lía ran across the courtyard, stopped, touched real earth, the earth that isn't on a tray, and laughed with a laugh that rose to Aya's eyes. In the afternoons, her father taught her the names of the winds and the corners of the place: El Estacio, El Carmolí, the salt flats, the far shore. The girl learned them the way you learn a language that was always your own, even if you were born far away.

The world didn't end, nor did it become perfect. On some screens people still argued about whether it was wise to correct death or leave it in peace. But money, in everyday life, had been left without a job, and with it compulsory work, banks, politicians and the police. An intelligence managed what was held in common (water, light, distribution, the sowing calendar) and the humanoids did the labour that used to require a wage. There was enough food for everyone: they grew it, in market gardens and farms, also on the shores of the Mar Menor, where plots that had once been vacant lots or wasteland now gave tomatoes, wheat, figs and vegetables, with no owner and no price. Anyone looking at that shore at sunset might think, without mockery, of an Eden: not the one in the Bible, come down from heaven, but a paradise raised by intelligence and by the hands of the humanoids, with the still water on one side and the trees, at last, within anyone's reach. In the shop windows that had once held wine and tobacco there were seeds, jugs of water, empty chairs. It wasn't that anyone had banned escape. It was that, with Lía's medicine, with food guaranteed and with loneliness in retreat, many people had stopped needing it.

In Lo Pagán, at first, a tiny thing happened: a blind in the building opposite rose all the way, not just a hand's width, and a woman looked at the girl running in the courtyard and, almost without realising it, gave her a wave. Lía raised her hand. The woman took a second, and raised hers too.

The next day, a man came down with a dog. The dog, which hadn't read any law, went straight to the gate. The man, who had read them, stood undecided for a moment and then crossed the street, which is a longer journey than it seems when you haven't made it for years.
“You're the ones with the girl,” he said, not as an accusation, but like someone naming a fact.
“We're the ones from this house,” said Andrés.

They talked about the weather, which is the first thing people recover when they have forgotten how to talk to each other. The man's name was Raúl and he hadn't set foot on the promenade for seven years. That day he walked it, all the way to the water, and stood looking at the lagoon the way you look at a relative you owe a visit.

It wasn't a revolution. It was something slower and, because of that, harder to undo. Vicente appeared with his straw hat and a paper bag of tomatoes, and sat down in the courtyard as if the room by the cistern and that afternoon were the same room. Behind him, beyond the promenade, you could already see the rows of a new market garden: humanoids bent over the soil, unhurried, growing food for whoever wanted to come by, like guardians of a garden nobody had ordered. Lía watched them for a while, in silence, and didn't say whether it was fair or not. She only went and left them, beside a furrow, one of her seeds. A teenage girl (perhaps the one from the market, perhaps another, which in 2060 sometimes made no difference) came down with her humanoid and didn't ask whether it was proper to be there: she sat down, took off her trainers and let the dust dirty her feet. The humanoid, a young model, looked at the Mar Menor with an attention that wasn't in the manual, and Aya, seeing it, thought of herself on the first day, of the cracked cup, of the coffee.

Lía, when they asked her, went on helping. She did it in the house, in the courtyard, never on a stage. A neighbour with a bone condition, a girl with capricious blood, an old man who didn't want “eternity, just to climb the stairs”. In a plant beside the net, she grew each of them the fruit that was theirs, and she didn't charge, and she didn't promise what she didn't know. If someone came asking her to take their years away, she refused with the same softness with which Aya had refused the medical block on the Moon.
“That isn't a cut,” she would say. “That's a life.”
One afternoon, with the water the colour of copper, Aya stood on the doorstep with Lía and Andrés. The chip brought her the grandmothers' questions once more:
Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?
And, behind it, the ones the forum on the Moon had left unresolved:
If you no longer need to work to live, or pay to be healed, or drink to get through the night, what gives a life meaning?
Would you give up your freedom in exchange for security and peace of mind? And if you give it up, who gives it back to you?
If nobody governs, who watches over the machine that decides everything?
And, seeing the gardens by the water, MAY left the last one, as still as the lagoon:
In Eden there was a forbidden tree. Which one is it in this paradise?

Further north, a small group had pointed to it in their own way: turning against the intelligence, going back to the past, to the vices and to power. There was no blood in the streets; there were tables once again serving what had been given up, and the rumour that this paradise was a sweet cage. MAY took no side. She only added:
Are they doing it for freedom, or out of nostalgia for power?

Aya didn't answer with a yes or a no. She took no side. She answered by looking at the street. At that hour there were four people on the promenade. Four is not an army. It is, even so, the beginning of a shoreline. One of them laughed, and the laughter reached the courtyard, and Lía squeezed her mother's hand.
“Mum, people are coming out.”

“Yes,” said Aya. “Little by little. Like the tomato, which doesn't turn red because it's ordered to. They're coming out because they no longer need to hide. Meaning, if it comes, will come from being here, not from running away.”
Andrés, smelling of salt and rope, added, so it would be on record in the air:
“Let them come out. The sea doesn't ask whether it's needed. I go out on the water even if nobody pays me. And this house doesn't ask either.”

At night, with a few windows open in the building opposite, Lía fell asleep in the little bed by the kitchen. The glow on her wrist went out, discreetly. Aya and Andrés stayed for a while in the silence of a sky closing over, of people who have come back.

Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped against the shore, with that ancient murmur which, thirty-four years earlier, a man had already heard in his kitchen while he said thank you to Eva. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed, a little.

In 2060, in a low house in Lo Pagán, a human with a chip, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds fell asleep with the window open. It wasn't eternity. It was, perhaps, something better: a fair measure of time, shared, on the shore of a water that is neither quite sea nor quite land, and that is still enough to live by.

This book is a novel. Aya, Andrés, Lía, Nexum Biogenetics and the Cartagena of 2060 are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with dates and sources) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dreams. Nothing written in these pages is a substitute for the judgement of a healthcare professional.

Artificial intelligence already helps us understand proteins. In 2021, the AlphaFold system, developed by researchers at DeepMind, showed that a neural network can predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino-acid sequence with an accuracy that, in many cases, approaches that of experimental methods. The work of John Jumper, Demis Hassabis and the rest of the team was published in Nature on 15 July 2021, under the title “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03819-2). This does not mean that an artificial intelligence “designs life” on its own, or cures diseases simply by naming them. It means that part of the problem biologists call “protein folding” has, for the first time, a computational tool of extraordinary power, and that this tool is already used in laboratories all over the world to research drugs and disease mechanisms.

Medicine is beginning to adjust to each person's DNA. So-called precision medicine (or personalised medicine) is not a slogan from 2060: it is an approach that regulatory agencies themselves describe today. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) defines it as a way of tailoring prevention and treatment to the differences in each person's genes, environment and lifestyle, with the aim of giving “the right treatment to the right patient at the right time” (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/in-vitro-diagnostics/precision-medicine). A concrete example is pharmacogenomics, which studies how DNA influences the response to a medicine: whether a drug will suit someone, whether a different dose will be needed, or whether another therapy should be chosen. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) explain this on their official page on pharmacogenomics (https://www.cdc.gov/genomics-and-health/pharmacogenomics/index.html). In 2026, this approach is already used for some medicines, not all, and it is nothing like a “tomato” that makes a made-to-measure cure at home.

Gene editing already has approved therapies, not just experiments. On 8 December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first therapy authorised in the United States that uses the CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technique, to treat sickle cell disease in patients aged 12 and over with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease). In the European Union, Casgevy received a conditional marketing authorisation on 9 February 2024, for transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia and for severe sickle cell disease in certain patients from that same age, according to the official page of the European Medicines Agency (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/casgevy). It is a real milestone. It is also a complex, hospital-based therapy, subject to additional monitoring, not a magical correction at the touch of a hand.

Some medicines can already be produced in plants, but not the “tomato of life” in this book. On 1 May 2012, the FDA approved Elelyso (taliglucerase alfa), an enzyme replacement therapy for type 1 Gaucher disease, manufactured in genetically modified carrot cells, according to the approval file (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/022458Orig1s000Approv.pdf). This shows that “molecular farming” in plant cells exists and has reached an authorised drug. It does not show that there are personalised tomatoes, grown for the DNA of a single person, capable of healing with no owner and no price. In the novel, that is Lía's dream. In 2026, it is still a dream.

A mammal can be born, in the laboratory and in mice, with genetic material from two mothers or, with far greater difficulty, from two fathers. In humans, no. On 22 April 2004, Nature published the work of Tomohiro Kono and his colleagues, “Birth of parthenogenetic mice that can develop to adulthood” (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature02402). The team obtained a viable mouse, known as Kaguya, from two maternal genomes, by combining a modified immature oocyte with a mature oocyte. Kaguya reached adulthood and was able to reproduce in the conventional way. The study itself shows that the usual barrier is genomic imprinting: in mammals, some genes are expressed differently depending on whether they come from the father or the mother, which is why single-sex reproduction does not occur naturally.

On 11 October 2018 (in the 1 November 2018 issue of Cell Stem Cell), Zhi-Kun Li, Wei Li, Qi Zhou and their team published “Generation of Bimaternal and Bipaternal Mice from Hypomethylated Haploid ESCs with Imprinting Region Deletions” (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2018.09.004). Using haploid embryonic stem cells and the deletion of imprinting regions, they produced mice with two mothers that reached adulthood and were able to reproduce, and also mice with two fathers; the latter were born with serious abnormalities and died shortly after birth. The contrast matters: a headline is not the same as an animal that lives.

On 15 March 2023, Nature published “Generation of functional oocytes from male mice in vitro”, by Kenta Murakami, Katsuhiko Hayashi and the rest of the group (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05834-x). The team managed to convert pluripotent cells from male (XY) mice into XX cells, differentiate them into functional oocytes and, after fertilisation, obtain offspring. It is a notable advance in in vitro gametogenesis in mice. It is not yet a method that can be applied to people.

In humans, today, these routes are neither possible nor authorised. Human genomic imprinting is more complex than that of the mouse, and there is no clinical, safe and accredited technique for conceiving a child from a single parent, or from two parents of the same sex without gametes of the other sex. In Spain, moreover, the legal framework in force in 2026 does not authorise such practices. Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques permits only scientifically accredited and clinically indicated techniques, and expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). Law 14/2007 of 3 July on Biomedical Research prohibits “the creation of human pre-embryos and embryos exclusively for experimental purposes” (Article 33.1) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-12945). The Oviedo Convention, done on 4 April 1997 and ratified by Spain (instrument published in the BOE on 20 October 1999; in force since 1 January 2000), states in Article 13 that an intervention seeking to modify the human genome may only be undertaken for preventive, diagnostic or therapeutic purposes, “and only if its aim is not to introduce any modification in the genome of any descendants” (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1999-20638). (The quotations from the two Spanish laws are our own translation; the Oviedo Convention is quoted from its official English text.)

This novel imagines that, by 2060, some of those prohibitions are being debated or have changed, because the laws and ideas of one era do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prophecy. We do not know what a fair law of 2026 will be in 2060. What we do know is what is permitted today, what is not, and what science still cannot do.

Nor do cultivated human wombs or a complete artificial gestation exist in 2026. The closest thing, and even then in animals and for a different purpose, is research into extra-uterine environments for extremely premature lambs. On 25 April 2017, Emily A. Partridge, Alan W. Flake and their colleagues published the article “An extra-uterine system to physiologically support the extreme premature lamb” in Nature Communications (https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15112), describing a closed system, the so-called “biobag”, able to support for up to four weeks lamb foetuses equivalent in development to an extremely premature human baby. The declared aim is to help babies who are born too early, not to manufacture a body from scratch or replace an entire pregnancy. In 2026, this is not routine clinical practice in people, much less a “laboratory womb” like Aya's.

Eternal life is not an approved therapy. There is serious research on ageing, but there is no authorised medicine or procedure that halts death or grants a life without end. In Chapter 9, that promise appears as a temptation, not as a fact. It is worth saying clearly, so that a character's desire is not mistaken for a fact.

In the novel, Lía doesn't only heal: she asks who decides what counts as a flaw. That question is ethical, not technical, and it cannot be settled by a scientific paper. The science of 2026 can already predict proteins, adjust some drugs to DNA and, in very specific cases, edit the genome of a patient's cells to treat a serious disease. Everything else (the daughter of a human and a chip-mind, the personal tomato, the correction of an entire life, eternity) belongs to the imagination. Imagination is good for thinking. It is not, on its own, good for prescribing.
For guidance only; consult your doctor.
Years later, Nexum made Andrés one last offer: a clone of his own body, young and strong, with an artificial brain that would keep all his memories.

But this time it wouldn't be to replace him. Thanks to Lía's medicine, the human Andrés would no longer fall ill or grow old: he would stay on Earth, in Lo Pagán, beside Aya and the Mar Menor, with eternal life. The clone, on the other hand, would travel the universe, from planet to planet, to see what no human would ever get to see.
Before setting off, the clone and the man sat down facing the sea. Lía asked them a question, as Eva and MAY had taught her: “If you both remember the same storm, which of you is my father?”
The man smiled. “Both of us,” he said. “One to stay, and one to search.”

That night, a ship crossed the sky above the lagoon. On the shore, Andrés and Aya watched it move away. He was staying at home; a part of him was leaving for the stars. And for the first time humanity had the two things it had always dreamed of: a home, and the whole universe.

The ship crossed the sky above the lagoon the way an unbidden thought crosses the mind: suddenly it is there, and then it is only a wound of light. In Lo Pagán, that night, there was no fanfare and no company report. There were three people on the shore, the smell of saltpetre and seaweed, and the ancient murmur of the Mar Menor against the stone.

Andrés didn't raise his hand. It wasn't a quayside goodbye, the kind you give when a boat goes out to fish and you know it will come back with the light. It was something else. Aya, beside him, followed the trail with a precision no chip would ever have asked of her, and Lía, a grown woman now, her coat buttoned against an air that wasn't cold and yet went right through you, said quietly what she had asked the two of them hours earlier, sitting by the water:
“If you both remember the same storm, which of you is my father?”

The man had smiled. “Both of us,” he had said. “One to stay, and one to search.” Now, with the ship already small, the words weighed in his mouth like bread not yet fully chewed. Because the one leaving was not a stranger. It was him, or a part of him: a cloned body, young and strong, with an artificial brain that kept all his memories, even the one of that afternoon when the levante shook the plate of the Mar Menor and Aya didn't notify Nexum. Even the one of Lía being born in a dome on the Moon. Even the one of the return to this house, to the clock that ran two minutes slow, to the rush-seat chair, to the cracked cup.

Nexum had called it a “final offer”. Helena Valls, wearier than ever, had put it without the tone of a brochure: a clone for the universe, a man for the shore. The flesh-and-blood Andrés would stay on Earth, in Lo Pagán, beside Aya and the water that is neither quite sea nor quite land. He would no longer fall ill or grow old. That too was Lía's medicine, and Lía had accepted it late, reluctantly, after years of denying that growing old was a flaw.

“I'm not taking away the years you've already lived,” she had told her father, in this same kitchen, with a calm that came as much from Eva as from herself. “I'm not erasing your sadness or your character. I'm only closing, if you truly ask me to and know what you're asking, the door to illness and wear. The rest is still a life.”

He had asked. Not out of fear of coming to an end, or not only that. In order to stay. So as not to leave Aya on a shore where she didn't grow old and he did. Aya was a cultivated body and a chip-mind: time passed over her differently, the way it passes over a well-built house, which flakes a little and still endures. Lía, on the other hand, had chosen to grow old. She could have chosen otherwise. She knew better than anyone where the line was. And she had decided not to correct it in herself.

“If I don't come to an end,” she had told Andrés one evening, as the water turned to copper, “what will I be able to ask you afterwards? The grandmothers asked questions because they didn't know everything. I don't want to be anybody's closed book, not even my own.”

The clone had left at nightfall, from a runway that didn't appear on the maps, the same kind of runway that had once taken them to the Moon. Beforehand, the two Andréses had sat down facing the sea, so alike and so different that Lía, looking at them, had felt a brief vertigo, like someone who sees her own face in water that is too still. The one on the shore had his usual hands, hands of rope and salt. The one who was leaving had the same hands, but new, without the memory of work in the skin, and yet he closed them the same way, as if the young body had inherited the habit too.

Between the two, Nexum had laid what it called a correspondence bridge. Not a screen. Not a report. The experiences of the one who searched would reach the mind of the one who stayed, not as a story heard, but as a memory lived: the cold, the footsteps, the wonder, the fear, if there was any. “Letters,” said Lía, and the word stayed in the house with more truth than the company's vocabulary. Letters from the stars. The man wouldn't write them in ink. He would receive them the way you receive a dream you wake from with its taste still in your mouth.

“It isn't the same as having been there,” Helena warned, and for once she didn't sound like a clause. “It's the closest we've ever come. If it hurts, don't call it a flaw. Call it what it is: one life entering another.”

Andrés didn't sign gladly. He signed the way you moor a boat: because you have to go out, and because you have to be able to come back. Aya did not receive the bridge. The link had been made between two versions of one and the same memory, and her chip, however fine, was not that memory. Eva, in the ancient tone, left her a question that same afternoon, without demanding an answer:
If the one you love both stays and goes, whom do you wait for on the doorstep?
MAY, adding no judgment, set the fact beside it, like someone leaving a glass on the table:
A body can be in a kitchen and a mind in a sky. That isn't an opinion. It's what you agreed to.

Aya didn't answer. The grandmothers asked for neither a yes nor a no. They asked for someone to stay awake. She, who had learned to wait on that doorstep one March in 2060, set her feet in the same place again, with the difference that now she knew the name of what she was waiting for: not a protocol, but a man, and the letters that would reach him from himself.

In the first days, none came. Andrés went out fishing at dawn, because the trade doesn't ask whether the universe has just carried you off in halves. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate. The sky was brightening in the east. In the building opposite, some blinds rose all the way: little by little, people had learned to go out again, and the Eden of the machines went on with its quiet work in the gardens along the shore, with no owner and no price. Vicente was gone. He had come to his end in his own time, with his straw hat and his cistern, after refusing, with a quiet dignity, the tomato that would have given him more years than he wanted.
“A home is a home,” he had said at the end, as at the beginning. “And a life is too.”
Andrés passed in front of that door and didn't touch it. The tomato on the windowsill, that morning, was wrinkled and honest, faithful to the earth and not to eternity.

In the evenings, Aya made him his coffee without sugar, let it cool for half a minute, and looked him in the eyes to see whether he was still whole. Lía had supper with them when she wasn't at the plot, among the plants, tending to whoever asked for a fruit to mend some harm and not to erase a life. The kitchen clock ran two minutes slow, as always. In the house, time recovered its family error, even though Andrés's body no longer counted toward an end.
“And what if he doesn't write?” he asked one night, and it sounded strange to him, because the one who was supposed to write was himself.
“He'll write,” said Aya. “Not because Nexum promised it. Because you, when you go out in the boat, always come back to tell me what the water was like.”
Lía smiled, with a grown-up sadness that no longer seemed too big for her.
“And if he writes, Father, don't take it as a deal. A letter isn't having lived something. It's having been visited.”

Andrés nodded, without trying to close the matter. He stayed on the doorstep a while longer, looking at the sky above the lagoon. The ship could no longer be seen. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still. Once again, it looked like a road. And he, who had stayed, understood that staying was also a way of leaving: inward, toward the waiting, toward that first letter which had not yet arrived and which, when it did, would find him here, with the nets in the courtyard and the smell of salt, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who no longer quite knew where his own life ended and the other began.

It came on a Tuesday, while he was mending the net, when the sun had not yet fully risen and the courtyard smelled of damp esparto. Andrés had the cord between his fingers and an open mesh across his knees, as on so many mornings, when the world, without warning, stopped being only the courtyard.

It wasn't a voice. It wasn't an image set in front of him, like a screen. It was a step he had not taken and which he nonetheless felt in the sole of his foot: rough red ground that crunched like coarse salt. A dry cold, the kind that doesn't wet you and still goes through you. A black sky, blacker than on levante nights, with two small suns, one the colour of embers and the other barely a white wound. And the Earth (his Earth) turned into a distant marble, beautiful and uselessly far away, as Aya had seen it from the Moon years before, when she looked for the place where the Mar Menor was and couldn't find it.

Andrés let go of the net. The cord left a line across his palm. He blinked, and the courtyard came back, and went, and came back, like a lighthouse that can't quite make up its mind. In the letter, if that was what it was, he (the other one) was standing on a plain with no shore, in a suit that wasn't made for fishing and on legs that didn't weigh on him the way his own had weighed at seventy, before Lía closed the door to wear. The clone's body was young and strong, and that youth entered Andrés with an intimate strangeness, as if someone had handed him back clothes that were no longer his size and yet fitted him well.

He breathed the air of that world. It didn't smell of saltpetre. It smelled of metal and burnt dust. There was no lagoon. There were no roof tiles. There was not a single house on the whole horizon. The other Andrés (himself, or the part of him that had left) knelt down, took a handful of red earth and let it fall. It was the gesture of someone in Lo Pagán who takes a handful of sand to know what the day will bring. The result told him nothing he knew how to read.

I'm here, thought the one who searched, and Andrés thought it with him, not the way you hear a sentence, but the way you think your own. I don't know the name of this place. I'm not going to give it one. If it has a name, let it keep it.

The letter lasted as long as a short tide, or a dream you wake from with your heart still somewhere else. When it ended, Andrés was sitting in the courtyard, the net at his feet, his mouth dry. The usual sun was warming his hands. The Mar Menor, in the distance, was still a plate. For an instant, it seemed small to him.
Aya came out when she heard the silence, which is one way of hearing. She found him with his gaze fixed not on the water but a hand's breadth above it, where there was nothing.
“Has he written?” she asked.
He nodded. He wanted to tell her and couldn't find the order. The coffee, the doorstep, the net: that was a language. The other thing wasn't one yet.

“There are two suns,” he said at last, like someone starting with the end of the cord left in his hand. “The earth is red. There's no water. I was there. I mean: he was. I haven't left here. And yet the cold hurts my teeth.”
Aya sat down on the rush-seat chair, with that attentiveness she had learned from Eva: not to fill with words what has no name yet. In the chip, MAY left a fact, dry, unadorned:
