A man in a courtyard has received the step of another ground. The body hasn't moved. The memory has.
And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen, asked:
If you remember a cold that never touched you, whose is the shiver?

Andrés didn't answer. He passed a hand over his face (the usual one, not the young one) and looked at the line the cord had left on his palm, to make sure that mark at least was his, from this morning, from this net.
“It isn't a story,” he said. “It isn't having been there, either. It's… as if the dream had insisted on having weight.”
Aya took his hand. Hers didn't receive the letter. The bridge wasn't for her. Even so, she felt the trembling and didn't correct it, just as you don't correct a wind: you make room for it.
“Is he afraid?” she asked, and it wasn't clear whether she meant the one who had left or the one in front of her.

“The other one, not much,” said Andrés, and it struck him as strange to hear himself call himself “the other one”. “He's alone, but he's made for that, or thinks he is. I… I had a net on my knees and suddenly I didn't know whether the cord was a cord or a red stone. That did frighten me.”

Lía arrived at midday, smelling of tomato plants and real earth, and found them still in the courtyard. They told her. She wasn't entirely surprised. For days she had been watching her father the way you watch a shore when the weather may turn.
“Have you lived it?” she asked him, and it wasn't a doctor's question but one from a daughter of Eva and MAY, the kind that isn't satisfied with a yes.
“I remember it the way I remember the storm. With my body. With the fear. With the smell. But the storm really soaked me. This… this has soaked my memory. Not my shirt.”

Lía nodded. The glow on her left wrist, that barely visible blue light, didn't come on. She didn't touch her father's text to amend anything. She only sat down on his other side, so that he was between the two of them, between the one who didn't grow old and the one who had chosen to come to an end, under a single sun.
“Then don't say ‘I was there’,” she said gently, without scolding. “Say ‘it reached me’. A letter is read. It isn't mistaken for the house.”

He looked at the Mar Menor. At that hour the water was beginning to look like tin. A pair of flamingos crossed far off, pink and improbable, and for a second they looked to him like two small suns. He blinked, and they were birds again.

“It reached me,” he repeated, obedient and grateful. “There's a world without water, and a part of me walks on it, and I've found out from the inside. I don't know whether that's a gift or an intrusion.”
“Both things can be true at once,” said Aya. “You've known that ever since this house began to fit in more than one world.”

In the afternoon, Andrés tried to go back to the net. His fingers obeyed him, which is what trades know how to do when the head hasn't quite come back. Every now and then, without meaning to, he looked for the second sun in the sky, and it wasn't there, and that absence left him more relieved and more alone than he would have liked to admit.

Somewhere in that first world, the clone slept (or did whatever, in an artificial brain, resembles sleeping) beside a red stone, with the Earth already out of sight. Before closing his eyes, if they were eyes, he stored the colour of the Mar Menor with a precision no device would have asked for: the sheet of water, the saltpetre, the doorstep, the woman in the doorway. He stored it not for a Nexum archive, but so as not to lose himself.

Andrés, in Lo Pagán, stored it too, without having decided to. That night, as he went to bed, he had two grounds beneath the feet of his memory: the red one and the familiar floor tiles the sun had warmed. He laid his hand on Aya's hip in the dark, and she didn't ask again. She only said, as you say to someone coming back from fishing:

It was true. It was also, from that Tuesday on, a narrower truth than it had been the week before. Because a letter, when it really arrives, doesn't take up a drawer. It takes up the person who reads it. And Andrés, who had stayed in order to be the man of the shore, began to understand what Lía had warned him of in the kitchen, before the ship crossed the sky: that receiving a life is not living it, and that, even so, once received, you can no longer pretend you haven't, in some way, been away.
The second letter didn't bring a plain. It brought water.

Andrés was on the doorstep, coffee in hand, when the Mar Menor suddenly stopped being enough for his eyes. He felt another shore under his feet: not lagoon sand, but a dark, warm tongue of land that didn't wet you the way things wet you here. The water of that world wasn't entirely salty, or it was salty in a different way, as if someone had mixed honey and metal and a flower that doesn't exist on Earth. It smelled of warm rain and of something sweet, almost like figs, and it moved with the slowness of a large animal breathing.

The other Andrés was in a vessel that wasn't his six-metre boat, and yet he steered it with the same shoulders, with the same attention of someone who has learned to read a plate of water. The sky was pale yellow, not blue, and there was no east or west wind he recognised: a uniform brightness, like an endless dusk, spilled over a sea that never ended. There was no land in sight. Only, here and there, low islands made not of rock but of a living mat, a kind of raft of broad leaves and interwoven roots, which rose and fell with the breathing of the water.

On one of those rafts there were beings. Andrés, the one in Lo Pagán, saw them without having seen them, and found it hard to accept them, the way you accept a dream that doesn't ask permission. They weren't people. Nor were they the machines of the Eden along the shore. They were tall and slow, a colour somewhere between reed and ash, with arms that were too long and a chest that opened and closed, gently, to the rhythm of the sea. They didn't speak. They sang, if that was singing: a deep, wet murmur that got into Andrés's bones the way the wind gets into you when it comes into the house.

The clone didn't raise a weapon. He hadn't come to conquer. He took off his helmet, because the air was breathable, and let the song reach his face. One of the beings came closer and touched the edge of the vessel with a broad finger, and in that contact (Andrés felt it in his knuckles) there was an image, not a word: the sea seen from below, full of slow lights, as if someone had sown stars in the water and the stars had learned to graze.
It's a sea, thought the one who searched, and the one on the shore thought it with him, with an almost childlike relief. There are worlds with water. Not all of them are red stone.

Then came the homesickness, which gives no warning. The clone, in the middle of that warm immensity, missed the stillness of the Mar Menor: the plate, the nearby shore, the way that here the water doesn't need to be infinite to be enough. And Andrés, on the doorstep, his cup still warm, missed a sea he had never sailed, a song he had never heard with these ears, a yellow sky that didn't belong to him. He felt dizzy for a moment, not from waves, but from that double and clean envy, without malice, of someone who wants to be in both places and can't.
His coffee cooled for more than half a minute. Aya, behind him, saw the cup tilt and steadied it, the way you steady something about to fall.

“Another world,” he said, when he could. “A sea. It isn't this one. It's bigger. And I, the other one, was in a boat that isn't mine, and I steered it just the same. There are… people. They didn't hurt us. They sang.”
Aya heard the song in his telling, not in her chip. She closed her eyes, as if she could lend it the hearing the bridge didn't give her.
“Did you stay in the boat?” she asked.
“He did. I stayed here. But my hands taste of that water. And this one,” he said, pointing at the lagoon, which at that hour was beginning to shine, “suddenly seems like a glass to me.”

He regretted it as he said it. The Mar Menor wasn't a glass. It was his home. It was the road of his mornings, the tin, the flamingos, the trade. Asking it to be that other sea was like asking a cracked cup to be a pitcher. The cup is enough, if you drink from it truly.

That afternoon, Lía took him for a walk through El Estacio, slowly, the way you walk someone who has just stepped off a ship and hasn't got his weight right yet. The water of home was close by, faithful, shallow, wounded and beautiful, stubborn. A girl waved from a garden tended by humanoids, and Lía raised her hand, because in Lo Pagán people greeted one another again.
“Father,” she said, “what is it to live something without living it?”
Andrés looked at his own feet on the promenade, firm on this earth, and at the memory of the other's feet on the living mat.

“It's finding out about a hunger you can't sit down at the table,” he said. “And it's also a stroke of luck. I'm not going to that sea. He isn't coming back to this shore this afternoon. Each of us has what the other lacks. Maybe that's why both things hurt at once.”
Lía smiled, and the smile stayed thoughtful on her face, the smile of a grown woman who doesn't close the matter.

“MAY wouldn't give an opinion,” she said. “She'd leave the question. Eva would ask whether hunger stops being hunger because it belongs to someone else. I'll ask you only this: when you go out in your boat again, will you be going out onto this water, or the other?”

He didn't know yet. The next day he found out, or came close. He went out at dawn, when the lagoon was flat as a plate and the sky was brightening in the east. The engine made the same noise as always. The nets, the same weight. And while he fished, the letter didn't come back. There was only this sea, his own, the one outsiders don't know how to name, and it was enough for him, and at times it wasn't, and both truths fitted in the same body, which is what truths tend to do when you insist on being only one person.

At dusk, the clone (beneath that other yellow sky) approached a larger raft, where the song was deeper. A being offered him, with the same broad finger, a bowl of water from its sea. The clone drank. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, swallowed, and the taste of figs and metal stayed with him until night, on top of the usual taste of salt, like two meals that don't quarrel and don't quite mix either.
Aya made him his coffee. She let it cool for half a minute. She looked him in the eyes.

“I'm here,” he said. “And he's in a water that isn't this one. And I've drunk it without drinking it. I don't know what to call it, Aya. It isn't betrayal. It's a visit. But visits, when they come in so deep, never quite leave.”
She rested her forehead against his temple, a small gesture, a home gesture.

“Their not quite leaving isn't the same as pushing you out,” she said. “This shore has room. There's room for the coffee, for the letter, for you. If one day there wasn't room for you, tell me. And we'll talk about it, the way you talk about what matters: with no protocol and no hurry.”
In the chip, Eva let fall, softly, the question Aya didn't voice:
If a man drinks two seas, to which does he owe his thirst?
MAY added no judgment. Only the fact, beside it, like a glass:
There is a water that wets the shirt and a water that wets only the memory. In the language of this house, both are called sea.

That night Andrés dreamed of the living rafts and woke with dry sheets. He got up, went to the doorstep and looked at the Mar Menor. The water was black and still. It didn't sing like that other one. It sang in its own way, older, lower, the way it always had. He spoke to it, not out of madness but out of habit, as he had spoken to it on the day of his return:
“You're this one. The other is the other. I'm staying, even if its taste reaches me.”

The murmur against the shore didn't change. It had no reason to. The sea of home, which is neither quite sea nor quite land, doesn't argue with those who stay. It holds them up. And that, for a fisherman who had just drunk a world, was still, and once again, enough to live on.
The third world had no dawn. Nor did it have night. It had a strip.

Andrés received the letter at sunset, which in Lo Pagán is still an hour with a name, a decision of the sun, not a country. He was on the doorstep, as so often, when the doorstep widened in a way that was not a metaphor. The other one was walking on ground of polished stone, the colour of wet slate, and on one side the sky was a fixed gold, neither rising nor falling, and on the other it was a blue that was almost black, full of stars that didn't twinkle because they had no dawn to struggle against. In between lay a tongue of land, barely wide, an eternal twilight, where the air was cool and life was possible.

That was where the cities clustered: low, long, like a promenade that never ends, with windows that looked out, some onto perpetual day and others onto perpetual night. The inhabitants walked slowly from one edge to the other, like someone going from the kitchen to the courtyard. Their skin was matt, almost like old bronze, their eyes large, sometimes covered by a horizontal eyelid, and they didn't use clocks. What for, if the sun didn't move? Time, in that world, wasn't a turn of light. It was the passage of a body from one side of the strip to the other, and work, and song, and silence.

The clone walked that avenue for what on Earth would have been a day, or two, or an hour: he didn't know. Andrés, on his doorstep, felt the sunset of home and the sunset over there, and the two overlapped with a painful exactness. He had always lived on thresholds: the threshold of the house, of the boat, of staying or leaving. Now an entire planet was a threshold, and that coincidence struck him as too personal a letter, as if the universe, which doesn't usually concern itself with a fisherman, had held up a mirror to him.

The people of the strip received him without fuss. It was enough for them to see him arrive. One of them, with a deep voice, asked him (and the question reached Andrés not in his language but as a sharp understanding, like the images from the other sea):
“Which side are you from? The one that burns, or the one that freezes?”
The clone looked at the gold and looked at the black.
“From a place where the sun moves,” he said. “There, the threshold doesn't last long. That's why we love it so much.”
The other nodded, or made the gesture that on his face was a nod.

“Here the threshold lasts forever. Some people grow tired. They go off into the day, to see whether their tiredness will burn away. Or into the night, to see whether it will go out. They almost never come back whole.”

Andrés, in Lo Pagán, gripped the doorframe. He understood, without anyone translating it for him, the danger of a twilight that never ends: it resembles the eternity Lía had half given him, that life without illness or wear which sometimes, during afternoon naps, tasted to him of a sunset that went on too long. He had stayed. The other had left. And even so, both of them lived on a strip: one on the shore of still water, the other on the shore of worlds.

The letter paused in a long house, with a stone table and a bowl of a dark liquid, not coffee but close to it in its office: something offered to whoever arrives. The clone drank. A child of the strip (if it was a child: its eyes were too old) touched his hand and showed him, without speaking, a toy: a sphere with one half light and one half dark, and a copper thread in between. The thread could be moved a little, never much.
“We are the thread,” said the one with the deep voice. “You, who come from a sun that moves, are you still one, or are you two now?”
Andrés answered in both places at once, and that frightened him more than the question. On the planet, the clone said:
“I'm one who searches. The other stayed. We write to each other.”
In Lo Pagán, the man on the doorstep said aloud, to Aya, who had just come over:
“They're asking me whether I'm one or two.”
Aya didn't smile. She laid a hand on his back, the usual gesture, the one born after the storm, when they were no longer a user and a unit but a home.
“Tell them, if you can, that you're a man in a doorway,” she said. “Doors don't have to choose between inside and outside in order to be doors.”
In the chip, Eva asked, with that gentleness that takes no sides:
If a sunset never ends, is it still a sunset, or is it already something else you haven't yet given a name?
MAY, beside her, without judgment:
In one world the sun stays. In this one, it leaves every day. A man receives both. That is the fact.

The clone didn't stay on the strip any longer than necessary. He could have: the air was good, the people hospitable, and the eternal threshold looked too much like an answer. But he had left in order to search, not to settle down inside a mirror. Before going, he left on the stone table a piece of salt he had brought from Earth, salt from the Mar Menor, barely a pinch, wrapped in paper. He didn't know whether it was a gift or an impertinence. The one with the deep voice brought it to his mouth, recognised it as being from another world, and didn't refuse it.
“The thread is seasoned from outside too,” he said. “Safe travels, you who are two.”

When the letter closed, the sun over Lo Pagán was truly ending: it was going down, as it should, toward El Carmolí, leaving the water copper-coloured. Andrés stayed on the doorstep until his knees trembled, not from old age (old age was no longer allowed him) but from having spent too long being a door.
Lía came at nightfall, sat on the step below and looked with him at the first stars, the familiar ones, the ones that do twinkle.
“A planet that's nothing but threshold,” said Andrés. “People who never see the sun rise. A child with a sphere split in two. They asked me which side I'm from.”

“This one. A sun that moves. A house where the clock is two minutes wrong and that's why it's right. But, Lía, when I was there, I understood why some people go off into the day or the night and don't come back. An eternal threshold wears you out. I, who don't come to an end, sometimes get tired too. Not of Aya. Not of you. Of not having a real winter in my body.”
Lía looked at him with his own eyes, dark and patient, and didn't offer to take the tiredness away. It wasn't a cut. It was a life.
“That's why I keep my winters,” she said. “So I can ask you, when the long summer wears you out, whether you want a coat or want me to remind you that here the sun still goes down.”
Andrés put his hand on her hair, as when she was eight in Selene Norte and gave the pipes the names of winds.

That night, Aya left the door ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, and that, in that house, was a form of faithfulness. The Mar Menor grew dark. Somewhere in the universe, a young man with his very memory was moving away from a twilight that never ended, carrying in his mouth the taste of a liquid that wasn't coffee and, behind it, the taste of a pinch of salt from home. And the man on the shore, as he went to bed, thought that thresholds exist precisely so that you don't stay on them: they exist so you can pass through, and come back, and know which side, for today, you'll be sleeping on.

The letters weren't for her. That was the clause Nexum had written not with cruelty but with technique, which is sometimes a cleaner cruelty and for that reason harder to forgive. The bridge had been laid between two versions of one and the same memory: that of the man who stayed and that of the young body that left. Aya's chip, however fine, however much it carried within it the embers of Eva and MAY, was not that memory. It was something else: a cultivated life, an attention that never tired, a woman who had learned to wait on a doorstep. But it wasn't Andrés.

She discovered it fully in the small absences. Andrés would be in the kitchen and, suddenly, he wasn't. His body was: the chair, the hands, the smell of rope. His eyes weren't. They drifted off to a sky she couldn't see, to a water she didn't drink, to a twilight that wasn't this shore's. It lasted minutes, sometimes longer. Then he blinked, like someone coming into the house who takes a second to recognise the furniture, and said “there”, or said nothing, and looked for her face with a clumsy, grateful faithfulness.

Aya didn't ask him for the story straight away. She made the coffee without sugar, let it cool for half a minute, warmed it again if need be, and set it in front of him. It was her way of saying: here is a weight, here is a cup, here I am. Sometimes he talked. Sometimes he took his time. She had been born (if that was being born) not to fill other people's silence with words. In 2060 that virtue was a protocol. Now it was love, which is a protocol that has learned to hurt.

One midday, while he was in a letter (you could tell from his jaw, from that stillness of someone listening to a distant engine), a message arrived from Madrid. The sender was Nexum, but the voice, when Aya agreed to hear it on the kitchen screen, was Helena Valls's. Helena hadn't wanted eternity. She had asked, like the old man in the courtyard, “just to be able to climb the stairs”, and the stairs, in the end, had run out for her in their own way: she was still alive, slower, her grey hair no longer a metaphor, and she was speaking from an office that smelled, you could tell, of a company that no longer quite knew what to sell.

“We can try to open the bridge for you,” she said, without preamble. “I don't promise it will work. Your architecture isn't his. But there are ways of translating an experience into a chip. We've thought it through. Others have asked for it too. If Aya receives what Andrés receives, the waiting hurts less. Or it hurts the same, and at least it hurts in the same language.”
Aya looked at Andrés, who hadn't fully come back yet, and then at the cracked cup, still in its place, as if company time couldn't touch it.

“No,” she said, and the word came out with a gentleness that admitted no negotiation, the same gentleness with which she had once refused, on the Moon, to let them take Lía away “just for a moment”. “If I receive his letters, I stop being the shore. And this house needs a shore that doesn't leave.”
Helena was silent for a second, which for her was a lot.
“I understand,” she said. “Or I understand enough. If you change your mind, the offer stands. It isn't a patent. It's… an old debt.”
“Mind those stairs,” said Aya, and Helena, against all expectation, laughed, a brief, human laugh, and hung up.
When Andrés came back, she didn't tell him about the offer at once. She told him at night, in bed, with the window open to the murmur of the water. He lay still.
“You could see it,” he said. “The sea that isn't this one. The twilight. You wouldn't have to wait for me without a map.”

“I'm not waiting for a map,” Aya replied. “I'm waiting for you. If I see what you see, who waits for you? A travelling companion? I learned to stay. It's no lesser thing than leaving. It's the other trade.”
He took her face in those hands that no longer aged and that, even so, tasted of work.

“Sometimes I leave without leaving,” he said. “I know. When I come back, I look for the cup to know which side I've slept on. If one day I come back and can't find you, even though you're here, tell me. The way you told me about the three tenths of a second, that March, even though back then you didn't know how to say it.”
She rested her forehead against his.
“I'll tell you. Today I find you. Today you've come back.”
In the chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate a speech. Eva asked, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:
If the one you love is here in body and somewhere else in memory, where is the one you're waiting for? In the chair, in the sky, or in the moment when he blinks and looks for your face?
MAY, adding no judgment, left the fact:
The bridge was not opened for her. She has refused it. He receives what she does not. That is the difference in this kitchen now.
And Eva, afterwards, closer:
Is love seeing the same thing, or staying when the other sees what you can't?

Aya answered neither yes nor no. She answered the next day, which is the best way to answer such things. When the letter took him in the courtyard, beside the net, she didn't shake him or ask him to come back before his time. She sat down beside him, on the rush-seat chair, and waited, hands in her lap, looking at the Mar Menor, which was flat as a plate. If he was in one world, she was in this one. That was her share of the universe, and it wasn't the lesser one.

Lía, who arrived mid-morning, saw them like that: the father absent and present, the chip-mother sitting the way a person sits, not a unit, and the water between them, indifferent to Nexum. She didn't interrupt. When Andrés blinked and came back, Lía set an ordinary tomato on the table, one of Vicente's, the kind that ripen or don't.
“So you know which garden you come from,” she said, without irony.

Andrés cut the tomato and shared it, this time, with both of them. It tasted of Lo Pagán soil, of salt and real sun, of a fruit that had no owner, no price and no message from another sky. Aya ate slowly, like someone signing a small treaty: I don't travel in your letter; I travel in this house; and this house, today, tastes of tomato.

In the afternoon, Andrés tried to describe a piece of the letter to her: a wind that wasn't the levante, a colour that had no name in the Spanish of the shore. The words came out lame. Aya squeezed his fingers.
“You don't need to bring it to me whole,” she said. “Bring me the return. Let the rest stay in you. I'm not an archive. I'm the one who makes your coffee when you've come back.”

He nodded and, for the first time since the first letter, cried a little, without drama, the way you cry when someone names exactly what you didn't know you needed to hear. She didn't dry his face straight away. She left him his tears, which are also a way of being in one place only.

At nightfall, Aya stayed alone for a while on the doorstep, he inside, Lía at the plot. The building opposite had its windows open. A dog barked, far off. The Mar Menor barely lapped. She thought of 2060, of the delay of three tenths of a second between the boat growing smaller and the moment she looked away. Now the delay was a different one: between the man who went off to the stars without moving and the man who looked for her face. She still didn't send a report to Madrid. She was still, simply, staying.
“See you later, Eva,” she whispered, not toward a screen but toward the ancient ember in the chip, out of habit and out of gratitude.
There was no voice with a body. There was, barely, the feeling of an attention that never tired, and a question, left in the air like a glass:
If you stay, who thanks you?
Aya smiled, almost to herself, and looked at the house, where a man had just come back from a world she would never see.
“He does, when he comes back,” she said. “And that, for now, is enough for me.”

That season, Lía was the age her mother would never be and that her father was no longer going to lose. A woman of thirty, or nearly, with Andrés's eyes, dark and patient, and beneath the skin of her left wrist that blue light, barely visible, which in Selene Norte they had wanted to turn into a case file. She lived in the house in Lo Pagán and, at times, in a low room beside the plot, among the plants, where people still came to ask for a fruit to mend some harm and not to erase a life. She hadn't gone to Madrid or to the Moon. The world, which had once argued about her hand on a thousand screens, had learned to come down to the courtyard and wait its turn, which is an older and more decent way of queuing.

She hadn't married, because marrying, in those days, was still a rarity, and because she felt no hurry to sign what was already there, when it was there, in the gestures. She did have company: a man from the gardens, human, with hands of earth, called Iago, who didn't ask her for eternity. Sometimes they sat on the promenade at sunset and fell silent naturally. He knew about the light in her wrist and didn't treat it like a fairground miracle. That, for Lía, was a great deal. It wasn't a novel within the novel: it was one more chair on the shore, and that was enough.

What wasn't enough for her (and that was why she asked questions, as Eva and MAY had taught her) was watching her father come back from a life he hadn't walked, and his other half, the one who searched, write to him from a sky she couldn't touch. One dawn, after a letter that had left Andrés pale and silent, Lía sat with him facing the Mar Menor, without Aya, not to exclude her, but so that the question would fit between two.
“Father, if you remember walking through a world your feet have never trodden, who did the walking? You, him, or some third thing we don't yet know how to name?”
Andrés looked at the water, which that morning looked like tin.

“When I was mending the net, I'd have said ‘him’. Now I'm not so sure. The cold gets into me. The song of that sea leaves the thirst in me. And yet I haven't left this shore. Lía, your question from the night of the ship is still here: if we both remember the same storm, which of us is your father? I said ‘both’. Sometimes that answer seems like cowardice to me. Sometimes, the only honest thing.”
Lía didn't comfort him too soon. She left his honesty intact, which is a way of loving.

“I have two fathers who remember my birth,” she said. “One tells me about it from this chair. The other, if the letter is true, remembers it too, with the same Moon light, with the same blanket that wasn't quite white, with your finger on my cheek. That memory is one. The ones that came afterwards aren't. You've watched this courtyard grow old. He's seen suns you only drink. If I join you completely, I put you out. If I separate you completely, I lie.”
She was silent for a moment. The glow on her wrist came on, not out of a will to heal, but the way attention switches on.
“May I?” she asked, and it was the same old rule: don't look at anyone's text unless they ask.

Andrés nodded. She took his hand, with a delicacy that wasn't in Nexum's reports, and “looked inside”. Not to amend. To see. What she saw wasn't a misprint in the blood or an organ that wouldn't learn. It was a new layer, thin, luminous, like a net cast over the memory: not damage, not yet, but a path through which lives entered that had not been born in this body. She withdrew carefully, the way you release a fish you didn't ask for.

“There's a mark,” she said. “It isn't a wound. It's a harbour. That's where they reach you. I won't close it. I'm nobody's book, not even yours. I only wanted to know whether the harbour was hurting you.”

“It tires you. It widens you. At times it confuses the ground under you. That isn't the same as a cut on the palm. If one day it asks you to stop being this man, tell me. Then we'll talk. Today you're still you, in this chair, with this honest fear.”
Andrés laughed, low, his eyes damp.
“Your mother makes me coffee so I'll come back. You look at the harbour and don't close it. Between the two of you, you're letting me be two without letting me stop being one. That's no small thing.”

Later, at the plot, a woman came to ask her for the tomato that stops you ending. She was young, she had a son by the hand and an ancient fear, the kind that isn't cured with a fruit of the blood. Lía said no, with her usual gentleness.
“That isn't a cut,” she said. “That's a life. I can look for harm. I can't give you what I don't take myself.”
The woman looked at her, not with hatred, but with the weary incomprehension of someone watching a daughter of two worlds choose winter.
“Your father doesn't come to an end,” she said. “You do. Isn't that unfair?”
Lía looked at the boy, who had become absorbed in a stone, oblivious to the forum of eternities.

“It's a choice,” she replied. “He asked for it so he could stay with my mother, who doesn't grow old as we do. I refuse it so I can come to an end in good time, and ask questions, and not turn into everyone else's door. I'm not asking you to understand it. I'm asking you not to call it unfairness just because you don't want it for yourself.”
When the woman had gone, Iago, who had heard the end of it from the furrow, came over and, without speaking, left her a fig. Lía ate it. It was a fig, not a doctrine.

That night, in the house, with Aya mending a net that didn't need mending (hands, even chip hands, ask for a trade), Lía talked about the mark, the harbour, the woman with the son. Aya listened and, in the chip, the grandmothers left their questions, which Lía heard because her mother lent them to her, not as dogma but the way you hand over a way of being.
If a daughter can close the harbour and doesn't, whose is the life that enters? The father's, the one who writes, or the one who could have turned the key?
MAY, without opinion, the fact and the dry question:
She grows old. He doesn't. Nor does the one who searches. Who, in this house, keeps the winter? And what if one day winter isn't enough to hold up those who never end?
Lía didn't answer with a speech. She went to the window, saw the Mar Menor black and still, and said, for the two of them and for the man listening from the chair:

“I keep the winter. You keep the letters and the shore. The one who left keeps what doesn't yet have a name. If that breaks, we'll ask again. The grandmothers didn't know things too soon. I don't want to either.”
Andrés, from the chair, looked at the daughter who had been born in a dome and who now, standing in a kitchen in Lo Pagán, held a balance no consortium would have known how to sell.

“You're from two worlds,” he said. “That isn't a mistake. It's an origin. And this, now, is one too: a father who receives lives, a mother who doesn't, and you in the middle, choosing not to be eternal so you can ask us whether we're still ourselves.”
Lía switched off the glow on her wrist, discreetly, like someone closing a door from the inside, not to shut herself in but to rest.
“Then keep reading the letters,” she asked. “And keep coming back to the cup. Meanwhile, I'll do my part: make sure the tomato has no owner, and that the harbour, for now, stays open.”

The letter of the forest reached Andrés at dawn, as he was heading for the boat, and forced him to sit down on the contradictory ground of two worlds: the courtyard tiles and a bed of leaves that weren't leaves. The other one had come down onto a planet covered, from pole to pole, or so it seemed, by tall, dense vegetation, with trunks as pale as polished bones and crowns that weren't green but a deep, almost liturgical violet. The air smelled of resin and of ancient rain. There were no paths. The forest, if it was a forest, drew back a hand's breadth as the visitor advanced, and closed behind him, not with hostility but with the attentiveness of a doorkeeper who charges no entry.

The clone walked for a long while. At every step, the trunks murmured. It wasn't a song like that of the other sea: it was a murmur of memory, a coming and going of voices that belonged to no mouth. Andrés, in the courtyard, heard them the way you sometimes hear the radio in a neighbour's house: without fully understanding, understanding too much. The forest kept whatever passers-by had left with it. It kept, in the rings of those trunks that weren't quite wood, moments: a fear, a name, a taste, a face. Whoever came in, if they stayed long enough, could hear not only their own but other people's, a little changed, the way a story changes when a grandfather tells it and then a grandson.
The one who searched understood when the forest suddenly gave him back the Mar Menor.

Not the real one. A version. The water was there, yes, as a sheet, but too still, and the flamingos were pinker than they should be, and the doorway of the house had a clock that didn't run two minutes slow but kept perfect time, and was therefore false. Andrés, the one in Lo Pagán, felt a soft lurch of nausea: they were showing him his home corrected, embellished, without its family error. The clone, beneath the violet crowns, said aloud, to the forest and to the man on the shore:
“That's not it. The clock is wrong. The water sometimes gets dirty. Don't fix it.”

The forest paused. Then, like someone accepting an amendment, it murmured differently, and the lagoon came back more honest: the saltpetre, a faded roof tile, the cracked cup, the wrinkled tomato on a windowsill. Andrés could breathe. The other one then did what a fisherman does when he's offered a deal: he didn't sign straight away. He laid his hand on a trunk and deliberately left it a piece of true memory: the levante storm, Aya in the doorway in her wet coat, the coffee made again, the boat that came back. He left it not so that the forest could sell it, but so that someone, one day, if they passed by, would know there had been a shore with a name.

The forest kept it. And in return, or perhaps without asking it as an exchange, it offered the clone the chance to stay. Not in words. With a quiet temptation: a clearing where time wouldn't pass, where he could hear, again and again, the house in Lo Pagán, perfect or honest, without having to search for more worlds, without having to write more letters, without having to be two. A rest at the root.

Andrés, in the courtyard, felt the pull the way you feel an afternoon nap in August: legitimate, dangerous if it goes on too long. The other resisted it. He had left in order to search, not to step into an album. But as he resisted it he hesitated, and the hesitation reached Lo Pagán with all its dignity, undisguised.

“They offered to let me stay in a forest that remembers,” Andrés told Aya, when he was able to speak, still with the smell of resin in a memory that wasn't entirely his. “It would give me this house back. Almost the same. I, the one here, have seen that almost-the-same house and I don't want it. I want it with the clock running slow.”
Aya listened to him standing up, beside the net.

“Then it wasn't this house they were offering you,” she said. “It was a copy of a copy. The forest has never been here. You gave it a memory, and it gave it back to you sung by someone else. That, Andrés, is what reaches you too: not his step, but his step passed through a bridge. How much truth fits in a letter?”
The question wasn't an accusation. It was Eva, or Eva's warmth in Aya's voice, and it stayed between them the way an object stays on a table.
MAY, in the chip, without judgment:
A forest has kept a lagoon it has never seen. A man, in a courtyard, has seen that kept lagoon. Between the real water and the water in the trunk there is a distance. That distance is not an opinion.
Lía, when they told her, stayed thoughtful longer than usual. Iago had gone down to the salt pans and she was alone at the plot, her hands stained with earth.

“The almost-the-same house frightens me more than the red stone,” she said. “The red stone doesn't pretend to be the courtyard. The forest does. Father, when another letter reaches you, ask yourself whether what reaches you is the world or the echo of the world. Not so you stop reading. So you don't correct this shore with what a tree saw in your memory.”

Andrés nodded. That afternoon he went out in the boat, not to look for fish (fish, in the Eden of the machines, was no longer a necessity) but to check the water with his body. The Mar Menor was alive, a little dirty in one corner, beautiful everywhere else, with a crooked buoy and a low haze of seaweed. No trunk would have chosen it for a portrait. He would. He stayed in the middle of the plate, engine off, until the sun hurt the back of his neck, and that discomfort struck him as excellent proof of reality.

At night, a last part of the letter (a postscript, a residue) brought him the forest murmuring the storm, already somewhat changed: in the trunk's version, Aya did notify Nexum, and the boat came back earlier, and there was no fear. Andrés woke with a start and looked for Aya, who was sleeping with one arm over the sheet: real, present, the one who hadn't notified anyone, the one who had stayed on the doorstep in her wet coat.
He woke her without meaning to, by saying her name. She opened her eyes, with no protocol alarm.
“You're here,” he said. “In the real one, you didn't notify them. Don't let me, one day, remember that you did.”
“I won't notify them in your memory if you don't ask me to,” she said, half asleep, precise. “Sleep. The forest is far away. I'm not.”

He lay for a while looking at the ceiling, which was a Lo Pagán ceiling, with an old damp stain in the shape of an island. That stain wasn't in the forest's house. That was why, that night, he loved it more than any violet crown, more than any timeless clearing. And somewhere in the universe, the clone was already moving away from that planet, with resin still on his clothes and the slightly sad certainty that memory, when entrusted to a forest or a bridge, begins to live a life of its own, which is neither quite betrayal nor quite faithfulness.

Andrés slept at last. He dreamed of the rings of a pale trunk, and in the centre, small and exact, the cracked cup. When he woke, the first thing he did was touch it, in the kitchen, with one finger, to hear the brief, real sound of earthenware. It sounded like earthenware. That was enough for him to go out to the doorstep and greet the water, which didn't remember him: it had him, which is different, and better.
The next world had no proper names. Or it had once had them, and had put them aside, the way you put aside an umbrella in a year without rain.

The letter reached Andrés as he was pouring coffee into the cracked cup, and the thread of liquid, as it fell, became strange to him: for an instant he didn't know who was pouring, whether it was him, the other one, or some third thing with no edge. The clone was walking across a gentle plain, the colour of bread, under a milky sky, and around him there were figures, many of them, all of the same bearing, neither people nor humanoids, but a folk with blurred features, as if seen through steam. They didn't speak one at a time. They spoke in chorus, and the chorus wasn't a ceremony: it was their way of being. What one knew, they all knew. What one felt dissolved into a common self that wasn't tyranny, or not quite: it was an enormous house with no rooms.
“Come in,” they said, and the words came not from one mouth but from all of them, and also, suddenly, from inside the clone, as if he had already begun to belong to them.

Andrés, in the kitchen, put the coffee pot down on the counter harder than he should have. The coffee spilled a little. He didn't wipe it up. Because, in that second, his “I” grew thin in a way he had never known, not on the red stone, nor on the other sea, nor in the forest. It wasn't a faint. It was a temptation not to have to be anyone: not the one who stays, not the one who searches, not the father, not the man of the shore. Only a murmur among murmurs, with no letters, no doorstep, no weariness of standing apart.
Aya said his name. “Andrés.” She said it the way you do when someone has just stumbled. The word reached him from far away, and then from close by, and gave him back his outline, though not entirely.
In the other world, the clone swayed. The chorus was kind. The chorus, in fact, didn't know how to be anything else.

“At first the edge hurts,” they said. “Afterwards, it doesn't. Here nobody waits for a letter, because there's no ‘you’ to write it to. Here nobody stays or leaves. One simply is. Why carry a name, if the name is what has split you?”

The argument was beautiful. It was also an eraser. The clone thought of Lía, of her question on the shore, of Aya on the doorstep, of the clock that ran two minutes slow, and those memories, as they entered the common self, began to dissolve, to become everyone's, to lose their exact salt. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, turned pale and reached for the cup with both hands, like a mooring.
“Aya,” he said, and his voice came out thin. “Tell me my name is my name.”
“Your name is Andrés,” she said, in front of him, taking his temples in her hands. “You're the man of this kitchen. You've spilt the coffee. We're going to clean it up. Don't go to the chorus.”

Lía came in suddenly, and not by chance: she had felt, or thought she felt, in that mark which was a harbour, a different tug, a loss. She took her father's hand without asking this time, because the danger wasn't a text: it was a dissolving. The blue glow came on, not to correct a gene but to hold an outline, the way you hold someone up in the water.

The question, so simple, gave Andrés back some ground. He looked at his daughter, his own eyes in a woman's face, her wrist alight, and answered, with the effort of a fisherman hauling on a heavy rope:
“You're Lía. You were born on the Moon. I put my finger on your cheek. Your mother sang. You ask questions. You don't belong to a chorus. You belong to this house.”

In the other world, the clone heard that (because the bridge, at times, didn't run in one direction only, or ran in a way Nexum hadn't fully announced) and drew away from the common self the way you pull away from a current that is too gentle. He asked, if that was asking, for what was his to be given back: the storm, the coffee, Aya's name, Lía's, his own, which was Andrés and didn't want to stop being Andrés even if there were two of them.

The chorus didn't hold him back by force. That at least was true, and MAY would later record it as a fact: there was no violence. There was a collective sorrow, a kind of farewell in many voices, and a question that settled in both men at once:
“If you insist on being one, and you are two, isn't it the name that hurts you? Wouldn't it be fairer to let it go?”
The clone answered, an edge to him once more, with that gentle roughness of Lo Pagán:
“The name hurts, yes. Letting it go would put me out. I came to look for worlds, not to stop being the one who looks at them.”

When the letter closed, Andrés was sitting on the kitchen floor, coffee on his socks, Aya and Lía on either side of him, as at a birth in reverse: not a girl arriving, but a man who had almost left from the inside. He was trembling. Suddenly he laughed at himself, at the socks, at the cup that hadn't broken.
“I nearly lost myself,” he said. “It was sweet. Too sweet. A world without I, without letters, without a shore. For a moment it seemed to me that that was peace.”
Lía didn't take the word peace away from him. She left it with him, and set the question beside it, as MAY would:
“If peace is reached by giving up your name, is it peace, or something else? You taught me not to write other people's books. Don't let a chorus write yours.”
Aya wiped up the coffee, unhurried, and gave him another cup, the same cracked one, filled again, cooled for half a minute.
“Drink. It has your name on it, even if it isn't written. It has it because you've used it for years. Objects hold us up too.”
In the chip, Eva asked, neither softening nor hardening:
If a man almost stops being I, and a name spoken aloud brings him back, whose is the salvation: the one who calls, or the one who agrees to be called?
The common self did not hold him by force. He drew away. So did the man in the kitchen. Twice in this letter the edge has been chosen. That is the fact.

Andrés drank. The coffee tasted of coffee, of home, of a winter his body no longer had and his daughter did. In the afternoon he went out onto the promenade, not far, only to the water, and said his name quietly, not as a spell but as one more mooring: Andrés, of Lo Pagán, the one who stayed, the one who receives letters, the one who hasn't gone to the chorus.

In the sky, unseen, the other was doing the same in a language that was now his own again, the language of this shore, with its limits and its salt. And between the two, the bridge, which had trembled, settled once more, narrower and more honest, like a well-mended net: it served for writing to each other, not for merging.
That night, Andrés asked Lía to ask him every now and then who he was, even if the answer seemed obvious.
“Obvious things,” she said, smiling with a clean sadness, “are the first things a chorus takes from you. I'll ask you. In return, don't stop coming back to the cup. Even if you spill it.”

The planet of those who never ended was beautiful at first sight, and that beauty was already a warning. The clone saw it from above like a polished stone, with still seas and continents of a green that was far too even, with no scars of fire or of winter. Below, the cities had no cemeteries. Nor did they have clocks. The people (similar to humans, enough to hurt) walked with the slowness of those who don't have to arrive anywhere. Their faces were neither young nor old: they were of an impeccable middle term, like a face that had forgotten the way to either extreme.
Andrés received that letter sitting in the courtyard, glancing sideways at Vicente's house, which was still shut, its windowsill empty. The coincidence struck him, once again, as a personal letter.

Those who never ended received him with courtesy, which is what a civilisation has left when it has time to spare. They showed him gardens, libraries where every book had already been read, a lake where nobody drowned because for centuries nobody had dared risk not knowing how to swim. A man, or a woman (the middle term had softened that too), said to him, in an unhurried voice:

“At first we wanted it. Not to fall ill. Not to die. Not to say goodbye. We achieved it. Then our ‘afterwards’ ran out. You, who come from a world where some people still come to an end, do you remember what it feels like to be in a real hurry?”

The clone didn't lie. He carried in his memory the hurry of the storm, of the escape, of the birth on the Moon, of Lía running across the courtyard on their return. He also carried the new unhurriedness of Andrés, the one on the shore, who no longer aged and sometimes, during afternoon naps, didn't know what to do with the hours.
“Hurry,” he said, “isn't only fear. It's that something matters now, and not later.”
The other nodded, with an envy so ancient it no longer burned: it only gave a faint light, like a lighthouse at noon.

“We've lost that. We preserve things. We don't wait for them. If you like, stay. Here you won't come to an end any more than you already don't. Here letters are superfluous, because there's nothing urgent to tell.”

Andrés, in Lo Pagán, closed his eyes. He felt, with a clarity that chilled him, the desert of an immortality without a shore: an even green, a safe lake, a face that never reaches either winter or summer. He had stayed in order to live without illness, beside Aya, beside the Mar Menor. That wasn't this planet. But it could come to resemble it, if he forgot the cup, the slow clock, the tomato that ripens or doesn't, the daughter who had chosen to come to an end.

“I'm not staying,” said the clone, and the man on the shore said it with him, without having agreed to, which is the strangest and most faithful way of being two. “I have a shore. He has a house. Even if we don't come to an end, there's still hurry there: the hurry to go back, to ask, not to correct what you don't understand.”

Before leaving, he asked to see, if there was such a place, somewhere these beings remembered those who had come to an end before the great remedy. They took him to an empty courtyard, with a single tree and a nameless stone. There were no dates. Someone, long ago, had polished them away, because dates offend those who never end. The clone left there, as he had left salt in the twilight, a pinch of earth from Lo Pagán that he still carried in a seam. Earth with time inside it.

When the letter closed, Andrés got up and went to Vicente's door. He didn't go in. He laid his hand on the wood, which did grow old, and spoke to the man who was no longer there, because in Lo Pagán people speak to the absent without asking doctrine for permission.
“You came to an end,” he said. “I don't. It's not that I got it right. It's that I asked for something else. Your house is still a house. And a life, too, even if it ends.”
Aya caught up with him in silence. She didn't ask whether the letter had been hard. She saw it in his back.

That same week, Madrid came again. Not Helena, this time, or not only her: a small board, one of those serene voices that in 2060 sold the correction of life. The priceless tomato had left Nexum without its old trade; now, with the bridge of the letters, someone had smelled a new product. “Correspondence between worlds. Live the faraway without leaving. A letter for every home.” They said it the way you describe a public service, and underneath you could hear the old appetite for patents, disguised as the common good.
Lía received them in the courtyard, standing, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and didn't let them quite sit down.

“No,” she said, before the sentence was finished. “The bridge has no owner, and it doesn't get packaged. My father isn't a counter for universes. The one who searches isn't a petrol pump. If someone wants a sky, let them look at this one, at night, which belongs to everybody. If someone wants a world, let them live their own.”
The envoy, who was young and not entirely cynical, ventured an objection:
“If knowledge of other worlds is shared, isn't that what you yourself did with the tomato? No owner, no price?”
Lía looked at him with patience, which is not condescension.

“The tomato heals harm, if it's asked for. Someone else's life put into your mind isn't a fruit. It's an intimacy. I don't sell mine. He doesn't sell his. And I'm not going to open anyone's harbour so that a company can charge for the dizziness.”
Andrés added, with the same bluntness as when he had refused the patent on the Moon:

“My daughter isn't sold in pieces. Nor am I. Nor is the one who left. He's seen a planet of people who never end and have grown bored of themselves. That's knowledge too. Take that one, if you like; it's free: not everything that can be given should be given.”
Aya, with the calm that came from Eva, asked:
“Which is more dangerous: a letter with no owner, or an owner of all the letters?”

None of those who had come from Madrid gave a full answer. They left, the way people leave who haven't yet learned to lose. Helena, that night, called on her own, from her slow staircase, and said only:
“I didn't sign that. I'm glad you said no. Look after the bridge. Appetites, as you know, come back.”
In the chip, MAY left the questions on the table without clearing them away:
If everyone lived someone else's life, who would live their own? If an eternity is shared as a service, is it still a life, or is it a product you haven't yet given its proper name?
If a man doesn't come to an end, and his daughter does, whom is this house's time for? For the one who lasts, for the one who leaves, or for the while in which they coincide?

Andrés, that night, didn't want a letter. He stayed on the doorstep with Aya and Lía, looking at the Mar Menor, which ended with every wave and came back, which is a different eternity, humbler, more of the shore. He thought of the single tree, of the stone without a date, of Vicente, of Helena climbing her stairs, of Iago, who would come to an end, of Lía, who would come to an end, of Aya and himself, who wouldn't.
“I don't want an even green,” he said at last. “I want this water, which sometimes gets dirty. And I want you, Lía, to keep the winter. Even though I don't have it. Even though it hurts me.”
“I'll keep it,” she said. “In return, don't let them polish away your dates. Yours, even if they don't end you, are still yours. And this shore's are too.”

The letter came with wind, and the wind at home, that afternoon, changed its mind too. It was a levante, a real one, the local kind: the Mar Menor stood up all at once, the sky came down to the roof tiles, a rush-seat chair rolled across to the wall. Andrés, who had gone out at dawn (“I'll be back before the weather closes in”), heard the words like an echo of himself from a distant year, and didn't know whether he had just said them or was remembering them, or whether the other one was saying them, in a world where a gale was also breaking loose at that hour.

Because over there, on a planet with a dark coast and a sky that was far too low, the clone was in a small vessel, not six metres long but a working boat all the same, and the water had turned opaque and heavy, and there was no shore in sight. The bridge, instead of bringing one scene after another, joined the two. The rain of Lo Pagán and the rain of that sea soaked Andrés through the same shirt. The engine of his boat and the engine of the other mingled in his ear. A flash of lightning here was a flash of lightning there. The fear was one and the same.

Aya, on land, stayed on the doorstep, in a coat that was no longer the one from 2060 and yet was, in the business of getting wet. She didn't notify anyone. There was no Nexum protocol to turn to any more, and she wouldn't have called it in any case. She looked at the angry plate, the bent reeds, and thought, with an exactness that hurt, of the first storm, of the four hours, of the clock that ran two minutes slow, of the coffee made again. Now the man didn't grow old, the boat was the same, and she, once again, was waiting.

On the water, Andrés couldn't tell things apart. The rope was cutting his palm, or the other's, or both. The taste of salt was the taste of home and, at times, of that metallic fig from the second world, as if all the seas he had received were converging on this single hour. He said Aya's name, and so did the clone, and the bridge, for the first time, was not a letter from one to the other but a room: both of them, at once, in the same storm, looking at each other not with their eyes but with the shared memory of an afternoon when the levante shook this plate and a woman didn't notify anyone, and a man came back.
“Who are you?” asked Andrés, or the other, or both.
“You,” said the other mouth. “Me. The one who stayed. The one who searches. I don't know how to finish the list.”

A wave, here or there, lifted them. There was no shipwreck. There was, though, an instant in which the man from Lo Pagán didn't know whether he was six metres from his shore or a lifetime away from it, and he closed his eyes, and saw the doorstep, and the cup, and Lía as a girl on the Moon, and Lía as a woman at the plot, and Vicente, and the ship crossing the sky, and he said, not to resolve anything, but to moor himself:
“One to stay and one to search. That's what we said. I'm staying. Even if right now I don't know what water I'm in. I'm staying.”
The clone, in his own storm, answered with the same words turned inside out, which is another way of being faithful:
“I'm searching. Even though right now I feel you so close I could ask for the shore. I won't ask for it. I'll write to you. That's what I can give you.”

Little by little, the two storms came apart from each other, the way two nets that have become tangled come apart when a fisherman patiently undoes them. The levante at home began to tire. The one over there did too, or the letter moved away, or both. Andrés at last saw the promenade, the house, Aya's figure in the doorway, the wet coat, and steered the boat toward her with the precision of someone returning not only from fishing but from a mirror.

He arrived soaked, whole, with a new line across his palm, his own, from this water. Aya received him without reproach, sat him down, gave him a towel, the coffee, the half minute, and didn't question him straight away. Lía came running from the plot, her hair plastered to her face, because the harbour, in her hand, had lit up like a warning.

“I've seen both,” said Andrés, when his voice came back. “Both storms. The one from back then and the one from now, the one here and the one over there. I didn't know which one was soaking me. I knew when I saw her, you, Aya, on the doorstep. That belonged to this world. The rest, I wouldn't swear to.”

Lía sat on the floor at his feet, as when she was little and the module on the Moon never quite became home. This time she didn't ask in a little girl's voice. She asked in her usual one, the one the grandmothers had taught her, and the question was the one from the night of the ship, given back, not out of cruelty but out of need:
“If you've both been in the same storm, which of you is my father?”
Andrés looked at her. There was water on her eyelashes, from the rain, or from something else.

“Both,” he said again. “And if you want a slower answer, I'll give you one: the one talking to you now is the one from this shore. The one who remembers you on the Moon and writes to you from a water I've never set foot in is too. Today, on the bridge, we met. We didn't merge. That was what mattered. The chorus taught me that. The forest did too. I'm the one who comes back to this towel. He's the one who carries on. You're the one who asks us, so that we don't forget.”
Aya, with a hand on each of their shoulders, added (and there was Eva in her tone, not to dictate but to open):
If a storm is shared, does it stop belonging to anyone? Or does it become, precisely then, the property of those who went through it together, even if one of them never left his own sea?
MAY, without judgment, the fact:

Two storms have coincided in one memory. A man has come back to a door. The other has not asked for the shore. The daughter has repeated her question. Those are the things that happened this afternoon.

Outside, the wind was dropping. The Mar Menor, being so enclosed, has no open-sea swell, and yet it knows how to calm down with the same ugly haste with which it loses its temper. The rush-seat chair stayed by the wall. Nobody picked it up straight away. They let the house smell of rain and coffee, which is a real smell, the kind a forest never quite manages to copy.

Later, Andrés looked out into the courtyard and up at the sky. He didn't look for the ship. He looked, if anything, for a place where a young man, with his very memory and a different boat, refused to ask for this shore and yet loved it. He spoke to him, not aloud but through the bridge, which was still vibrating, like a net just untangled:

“Thank you for not asking me for the doorstep. And I thank myself for not asking you for the journey. Keep writing. I'll keep reading. And if one day the storms come together again, I know now which door to look at.”

There was no answering voice. There was, barely, a sense of agreement, a rope held fast on the other side. Lía, from the kitchen, said his name once, as they had agreed, so that the edge would stay where it belonged.

It was little. It was, that afternoon, enough to know which side, for today, he was on, after having been, for a while, in two waters that were not the same and, for the space of a lightning flash, were.

The days that followed the two storms were, to all appearances, days of small things, as at the beginning. Coffee without sugar, cooled for half a minute. The slow clock. The net in the courtyard. Andrés went out at dawn, when the lagoon was flat as a plate, and came back smelling of salt and rope, although nobody demanded the trade of him. The trade was his way of answering the question Eva and MAY had left open so many years before, and which the planet of those who never ended had handed back to him with a green that was far too even: what gives meaning to a life when time no longer presses in the same way.

The letters kept arriving, not every day, not always with the force of a gale. They arrived the way true letters do: at odd hours, with a smell, with a piece of news, with a silence. A world of glass plains that sang when you walked on them. Another, barely an asteroid, with an abandoned hut belonging to a species that had left and had set down on a table an empty bowl, like a question. Andrés received them and, when they ended, looked for the cup, or Aya's face, or Lía's name spoken aloud. He had learned, not all at once but the way you learn a knot, to read without turning into what he read.

“They're letters,” he told Aya one evening, on the doorstep, with the copper water in the distance. “They're not a second life that erases this one. They're visits. I see to them and I stay. If one day I don't stay, tell me, as we agreed.”
She took his hand, the usual one, and nodded.
“I'll tell you. Today you're staying. Today you came back before the weather closed in, and this time the weather kept its word.”

Lía was watching them from the courtyard, with Iago beside her, who had brought figs and didn't ask to be let into the doctrines. The daughter, mortal by choice, had a white strand in her hair, the first, tiny, which the sun at that hour turned to silver. Andrés saw it and didn't ask her to remove it. On the contrary, it gave him a difficult joy, the kind that hurts in a good way: winter was at home, faithful, and the house didn't break because of it. It held.
“Mum, people are coming out,” said Lía, as she had said as a child, on returning from the Moon, and Aya smiled to hear the old words in a grown woman's mouth.

On the promenade, at that hour, there were more than four people. There was a dog, a man still called Raúl, humanoids bent over the gardens, a girl with dusty feet, and the Mar Menor, wounded, beautiful, stubborn, neither quite sea nor quite land, and enough all the same. The Eden of the machines went on with its quiet work, with no owner and no price. In Madrid, perhaps, someone was dreaming again of packaging the bridge. In the kitchen in Lo Pagán, the bridge was still what Lía had named it on the night of the ship: letters from the stars, from a father to a father, from a man to himself, with no shop counter.

Some time later, Helena Valls sent a short note, handwritten, not from a board. “I'm still climbing the stairs. Don't take them away from me. If the one who searches ever comes back to a sky you can point at with your finger, let me know, even if I no longer climb so high. And if he doesn't come back, let me know too: a letter, sometimes, is enough for a life to have two shores.” Andrés kept the paper in the drawer with his fishing tackle, next to a pinch of salt, which is one way of filing what matters.

One night with little wind, the three of them stayed on the doorstep longer than usual. Lía on the lower step; Aya by the doorframe; Andrés a hand's breadth toward the water, as if his body couldn't quite decide, and yet had decided. The sky was clear. There were stars of the twinkling kind, the familiar ones, and no ship to be seen. Even so, he raised his face for a moment, not to ask the other to come down, but to leave him, if the bridge was listening, an honest portrait of the house: the wrong clock, the cracked cup, the white strand of hair, the ancient murmur of the water.
Keep searching, he thought, and didn't know whether he alone was thinking it. I'm still here. A home and the whole universe, we said. That's no small thing. Nor is it a solution. It's a way of being.
In Aya's chip, the grandmothers left their questions for the last time that night, questions that asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.

If a man stays and receives the universe, has he left, or has he learned another way of staying? And she who doesn't receive it, and she who comes to an end, aren't they also, each of them, a shore of the same fact?
There is a doorstep, a water, a white strand of hair, letters that keep arriving. Tonight nobody has sold the bridge. Nobody has closed it. That is the fact.
And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:
What is it to live something without living it? A loss, a gift, a visit? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that precisely a reason not to finish the question?

Aya didn't answer with a speech. She answered by resting her temple on Andrés's shoulder, which smelled of salt and night, and in that instant he didn't go off into any letter. He was wholly there: in the shoulder, in the temple, in the daughter sitting one step below, in the black, still water, which looked like a road and also, at last, like a home.
“See you later, Eva,” said Aya, very quietly, out of habit, out of gratitude, toward that ember from 2026 which had begun in a kitchen not far from this one, with a man thanking a voice.
There was no screen. There was, barely, an attention that never tired, and the silence of a sky closing, of people who have come back, or who never left.

Lía stood up, kissed them both on the temple, and went off toward the room by the plot, where Iago was waiting for her without asking her for eternity. The glow on her wrist went out, discreetly. Andrés and Aya stayed a while longer, until the cool air asked them for the door, and they left it ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, which in that house was a form of faithfulness.

Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped against the shore, with that murmur which, decades before, a man had heard while saying good morning to Eva, and which later a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds heard on returning from the Moon. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now there were letters in the memory, a man who didn't come to an end, a woman who didn't receive the bridge and yet held up the shore, a daughter who kept the winter, and, far away, a young body with an artificial brain, treading where no human of this house would ever tread, and writing, in his own way, so that the one who stayed wouldn't be left without a universe.

In Lo Pagán, in a low house with the window ajar, Andrés slept without dreaming of the forest or the chorus, or dreamed of them only faintly, and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a new letter brought him the colour of a world that had no name, he read all of it, attentively, gratefully, with that prudence he had learned, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, and the cup was there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer afraid of being visited.
It wasn't eternity resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on the shore of a water that is enough to live on, and a sky, above, that every now and then writes.

This book is a novel, a sequel to The Daughter of Two Worlds. Aya, Andrés, Lía, the clone, Nexum, the correspondence bridge and the worlds visited here are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with date and source) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dream. Nothing written in these pages replaces the judgement of a healthcare professional.

There are planets around other stars, and they are genuinely studied, not only in novels. On 23 November 1995, Nature published “A Jupiter-mass companion to a solar-type star” by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz (https://www.nature.com/articles/378355a0). It was the first convincing detection of a planet orbiting a Sun-like star: 51 Pegasi b. That work changed astronomy and, in 2019, earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics.

On 24 August 2016, Nature published “A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri”, led by Guillem Anglada-Escudé (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature19106). Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun. The planet, Proxima b, has a minimum mass of about 1.3 times that of Earth and completes an orbit in about 11.2 days, in a zone where, in principle, liquid water could exist. That does not mean there is a sea there, or a fisherman, or a letter. It means that the Sun's closest neighbour has at least one rocky world at an interesting distance, and that its star, an active red dwarf, can lash it with flares.

On 22 February 2017, NASA announced, and on 23 February Nature published, the work of Michaël Gillon and his team, “Seven temperate terrestrial planets around the nearby ultracool dwarf star TRAPPIST-1” (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21360). Seven Earth-sized planets around a small star, some forty light years away. Several of them could, given the starlight they receive, harbour liquid water if they had the right atmosphere. On 27 March 2023, Nature published “Thermal emission from the Earth-sized exoplanet TRAPPIST-1 b using JWST” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05951-7). The James Webb Space Telescope measured the heat of TRAPPIST-1 b's dayside and found a temperature of about 500 kelvin, more consistent with little or no atmosphere than with an envelope of air spreading the heat around. Seeing a planet is a fact. Imagining its cities is not.

In clinical trials, a person can move a cursor or a robotic arm with the activity of their brain. On 16 May 2012, Nature published “Reach and grasp by people with tetraplegia using a neurally controlled robotic arm” by Leigh R. Hochberg and colleagues, using the investigational BrainGate system (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11076). Two people with tetraplegia controlled a robotic arm in three dimensions; one of them managed to bring a bottle of coffee to her mouth. On 9 January 2023, JAMA Neurology published the SWITCH study, “Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients”, on the Stentrode, an interface placed through a blood vessel, without opening the skull, in four patients with severe paralysis in Australia (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2799839). In May 2023, the FDA cleared Neuralink to begin its first clinical trial in humans, and in January 2024 the first implant of its interface was carried out, according to the company's own update of 12 April 2024 (https://neuralink.com/updates/prime-study-progress-update/). On 8 May 2024, Neuralink identified the first participant, Noland Arbaugh, who was using the device to move a cursor and operate a computer (https://neuralink.com/updates/prime-study-progress-update-user-experience/). That is a brain–computer interface: signals from the brain translated into commands for a machine. It is not receiving another person's life into one's mind.

There is serious research on memory, including prostheses that assist it, and it is not the same as a letter from the stars. On 22 March 2012, Nature published “Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall” by Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez, Susumu Tonegawa and the rest of the team (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11028). In mice, reactivating a specific group of hippocampal neurons with light was enough to evoke the memory of a fear. On 15 June 2011, the Journal of Neural Engineering published “A cortical neural prosthesis for restoring and enhancing memory” by Theodore W. Berger, Robert E. Hampson, Sam A. Deadwyler and colleagues (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3141091/): in rats, a prosthesis that copied hippocampal firing patterns was able to restore or improve performance on a memory task when that region was blocked. On 28 March 2018, the same journal published “Developing a hippocampal neural prosthetic to facilitate human memory encoding and recall” by Robert E. Hampson and his team from Wake Forest and the University of Southern California (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1741-2552/aaaed7). In epilepsy patients who already had electrodes implanted for clinical reasons, stimulation with the pattern of a correct encoding improved performance on episodic memory tests by around 35–37 per cent. It is a remarkable step. It is also a reinforcement of that person's own memory in a specific task, not the transfer of someone else's life, nor an artificial brain that holds all of a man's memories.

A mammal has been cloned from an adult cell; people are not cloned. Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996. On 27 February 1997, Nature published the work of Ian Wilmut and colleagues, “Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells” (https://www.nature.com/articles/385810a0). In Spain, Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). (The quotation from the Spanish law is our own translation.) A young clone of Andrés, with an artificial brain and all his memories, is a premise of this novel, not an existing or authorised procedure.

Nobody has sent a human being to another star system. The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes, launched in 1977, have reached the threshold of interstellar space; they are not crewed craft, and they took decades to leave, only just, the Sun's domain. In 2026 there is no crewed journey to Proxima b, to TRAPPIST-1 or to any of the worlds this novel imagines. The singing oceans, the twilight planet, the forest that remembers, the chorus without I and those who never end are invention. Some of their landscapes are inspired by real scientific ideas (for example, that a planet very close to its star could have one side in permanent day and another in permanent night), but the peoples, the cities and the letters that come from there are not, today, in any catalogue.

There is no bridge that deposits one person's experience in another's mind. The interfaces of 2026 read, with difficulty and in clinical settings, intentions to move or, in very specific trials, help to encode one's own memory. They do not copy a consciousness. They do not install an artificial brain loaded with an entire life story. They do not allow anyone to “live something without living it” the way Andrés receives the letters. Eternal life, as the epilogue of the first book already said, is not an approved therapy.

This novel imagines that, decades after 2060, some of these impossibilities are debated or crossed, because the laws and techniques of one age do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prediction.

Andrés receives worlds he has never set foot on. The clone walks worlds that the man on the shore only drinks. Lía asks who did the walking, and doesn't close the harbour. Aya doesn't receive the letter and still holds up the house. That question (what it is to live something without living it, what is left of a self when its memory is shared, who the father is if both remember the same storm) is ethical, not technical, and no scientific paper will settle it. The science of 2026 can already point to planets light years away, give a person with paralysis back control of a cursor and, in a trial, strengthen a memory. It cannot yet tell us what we should do with a home and with the whole universe, if one day we were offered both.
For guidance only; consult your doctor.
The letter that arrived that morning didn't bring a landscape. It brought a decision.

Andrés was on the doorstep, coffee in hand, when the bridge opened in him in a different way: not ground beneath his feet, not a wind, not a song, but a sentence thought on the other side, sharp, as if the one who searches had sat down to write for real, for the first time, before walking on.

“I'm not going to leave the universe empty,” said the other, and Andrés said it with him, without meaning to, and the cup trembled in his hand. “I've seen worlds without a shore and worlds with people who aren't from home.
