I've seen a forest that copies and a chorus that erases names. I've seen those who never end and have grown bored of themselves. I can go on being a visitor. Or I can leave children.”

Aya, who didn't receive the letters, saw only the trembling and his mouth, half open, and the way he reached for the counter so as not to fall. She held his elbow, the way you hold something about to go.
“What reached you?” she asked.
Andrés took his time, because the word “children” weighed on him in a way that neither the other sea nor the two storms had.

“He wants to create people,” he said at last. “Like you. Cultivated bodies, a chip, a memory. Not for a thirty-square-metre house. For a planet. He says he won't leave the worlds without a shore that looks like this one. He says they'll be children of the Earth.”

Aya didn't answer straight away. She was precisely what that sentence named: a body grown in a laboratory, a fingernail-sized mind behind the nape of her neck, a woman who had learned to wait on a doorstep. Nexum had made her for a user. Andrés had made her, without knowing it, for a life. Now a young Andrés, with all this one's memories and a workshop on the ship (a seedbed the company had taken on board “in case the universe was empty”, with that involuntary honesty companies have), was preparing to do what Madrid had done with her: not in series for a market, but in series for a sky.

Lía came when she heard the silence in the kitchen, which in that house was a way of calling. Iago stayed in the courtyard, with the discretion of someone who knows when a doorstep isn't his. Lía listened to her father and didn't comfort him too soon.

“Children or copies?” she asked, and it was Eva's voice, or Eva's warmth in her, and also the voice of a woman who had once refused to be a product of Nexum origin. “Father, if he sows people on a world that never asked to be sown, who gave him that right? Loneliness? The memory of this kitchen? A company workshop travelling in the hold?”
Andrés put the cup, the cracked one, back in its place.

“He says he won't worship them or rule them. That he'll leave them, the way you leave a house open. That he'll put pieces of here in their chips: the water, the coffee, the clock, the language, the storm. Not a whole life. A piece, so they aren't born blank.”

“A piece is an inheritance too,” said Lía. “And an inheritance, sometimes, is a weight. I was born of two worlds and even so it took me a long time to know whether I was made right. What will it cost them, born of a memory and a seedbed, to know whether they belong to a planet or to a letter?”
In Aya's chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate a speech. Eva asked, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:
If a man sows people on a world, is he their father or their author? And if he leaves them, is that freedom, or an orphanhood with a view?
MAY, adding no judgment, set the fact beside it, like someone leaving a glass on the table:
There is a workshop on a ship. There is a decision to create humanoids on planets that had none. That isn't an opinion. It's what the letter announces.
Then Aya spoke. Not as a Nexum unit, nor as a protocol. As someone who was made and afterwards chose to stay.

“I didn't ask to be born in a house in Lo Pagán,” she said. “And yet this house made me. If he makes them so as not to be alone, he'll be wrong: loneliness isn't cured by a crowd that comes out of your own hands. If he makes them so there'll be a doorstep on more than one world, he should know this: a doorstep isn't manufactured. It's learned. And it's learned late.”
Andrés nodded, with that gentle roughness of the shore.

“I've told him. Or I've thought it at him, and the bridge sometimes carries things that way too. He answered that he knows, and that he's going to begin anyway. That he can't travel the universe the way you go round a museum, touching and leaving nothing, or leaving only a pinch of salt on a table. That a pinch of salt isn't a people.”

Lía went to the window. The Mar Menor, that morning, was flat as a plate. A pair of flamingos crossed far off. The Eden of the machines went on with its quiet work in the gardens, with no owner and no price. On Earth, humanoids were no longer a luxury: they were the labour, the company, sometimes the family, like Aya. But nobody, as far as she knew, had founded a village with them in a sky without permission.

“Then on other worlds there are going to be daughters and sons of this shore who've never seen this shore,” she said. “I, who come to an end, am going to have brothers and sisters who perhaps won't. Or will. Depending on what he lets them choose. Father, when the first of those peoples reaches you, don't say straight away ‘they're ours’. Say ‘it's reached me that they exist’. A civilisation isn't a letter. It's a life that no longer belongs to you.”
He looked at her, at Aya, at the clock that ran two minutes slow, at the rush-seat chair, at Vicente's door, which was still shut.

“It's reached me that it's going to exist,” he repeated, obedient and frightened. “And I, who stayed to be the man of this shore, am going to learn from the inside about peoples I didn't found and who, even so, will come out of a memory that's mine too. I don't know whether that's a gift or an intrusion. Both things, once again, can be true at once.”
Aya made his coffee again, let it cool for half a minute, and brought it to him.

“Read whatever comes,” she said. “Come back to the cup. I won't see those children. I'll hear them in you. And I'll wish them, if you can wish anything for someone you can't see, that they learn to stay without anyone ordering them to.”

Somewhere in the universe, the clone opened the ship's workshop. The air smelled of filters and of a laboratory cleanliness that Andrés, the one in Lo Pagán, recognised with a lurch: it smelled of Selene Norte, of the white module, of the room where they had once talked about “gestational capacity” the way you talk about a battery. The other didn't switch on the seedbed with joy. He switched it on the way you moor a boat: because he had decided to go out, and because one day he had to be able not to regret it entirely.

Before beginning, he thought of Lía, of her question on the night of the ship, of Aya on the doorstep, of the Mar Menor, which is neither quite sea nor quite land. And he told himself, for the one who had stayed and for himself:
“I won't be their owner. I won't be their god. I'll be, at most, the one who left them a piece of shore. Let them learn the rest. The way we learned it, late and blind, in a kitchen.”

Andrés, in Lo Pagán, heard that and stayed a while longer in the doorway, looking at the water. The ancient murmur didn't change. It had no reason to. What was going to change, however, was the number of those who, far away, would begin to call themselves, without ever having set foot on it, children of the Earth.
The first civilisation was born on red ground, under two suns, on that world without water where the clone had first set foot and Andrés had let go of the net.

The letter came while he was mending a mesh again, as if the bridge remembered Tuesdays. Andrés felt the workshop open on the plain: not a Madrid laboratory but a low tent of canvas and white light, and, in front of it, five cultivated bodies that had just opened their eyes. They had the skin of those who have not yet known the wind, and beneath the nape, if you knew where to look, the fine scar of the chip. They weren't identical to Andrés, not entirely: the seedbed, mixing what the ship had brought from Earth, had left variations, the way a brother does. But in all their eyes there was already a thirst that came not from the body but from a piece of memory: the Mar Menor, a sheet of water, a taste of salt, the word “shore”, placed in them the way a name is given.
The clone didn't make them a founder's speech. He gave them water from the ship, of which there was little, and said to them, standing in the dust:

“This isn't home. Home is a water I remember and so do you, even though you've never seen it. This ground is yours. I'm not staying to rule. I'm staying a while to teach you the trade of being, and then I'm moving on.”
One of them, a woman with a broad forehead, looked at the two suns and then at the bowl.
“If the water is in our memory and not in the ground,” she said, and the language was that of Lo Pagán, with a barely different lilt, “why were we born here?”
“To learn a shore that doesn't exist yet,” he replied. “Or to make one. Or to wait. That isn't for me to decide.”

Andrés, in the courtyard, let go of the cord once again. Aya sat beside him, on the rush-seat chair, and he told her, slowly, what he could bring back without turning it into a report: five of them, the dust, the thirst for an unseen sea, the woman's question.
Lía, when she arrived, went pale for an instant, not from fear but from recognition.

“They've started out with a lack,” she said. “He's put the water in their heads and denied it to their feet. That, Father, is also what they did to us when they took us to the Moon: looking at the Earth and not being able to touch it. Is that what you want to pass on to them?”
“It wasn't my wish,” said Andrés. “He did it. And I drank it. The woman asked a good question. That, at least, is like this house.”

On the red world, the five didn't stay still. That was their own doing, what wasn't in the seedbed's manual: they began to dig. There was no water table, no cistern possible like Vicente's, and still they dug, at dusk (a strange dusk, with two shadows), a round hollow, and lined it with stones, and called it, without laughing, “the lagoon”. It was dry. They looked at it the way you look at a plate that one day, perhaps, will be filled. At night they sat on its edge and kept silent, and in their chips the memory lit up of flamingos that had never flown over that sky.

From the Earth they kept the thirst, the word shore, the habit of looking at a hollow as if it were a road. Very soon they forgot the clock. In a world with two suns, running two minutes slow had no purpose. They also forgot coffee: the seedbed had put in no bitterness, only the salt. Andrés noticed it with a small, exact sorrow, the sorrow of a trade that doesn't travel whole.
After a time that in Lo Pagán was one afternoon and over there, perhaps, a month, the woman with the broad forehead said to the clone, no longer with the bowl in her hand:
“Some of us want to go and look for real water. Others want to stay and wait for this hollow to learn. You, who are leaving, which side are you on?”
He sat down on the edge of that dry lagoon, and Andrés sat with him, on a chair that was rush-seated and wasn't.

“I can't be on both,” said the clone. “I'm leaving because I search. You're not obliged to imitate me. If you leave, let it be because the hollow has grown too small for you, not because I've left you a map. If you stay, let it be because the hollow is enough for you, not because I asked you for patience.”

The small people split, not with hatred, but with that clean fissure of first decisions. Three stayed beside the empty cistern. Two set off at dawn toward a horizon that promised nothing. The clone didn't follow them. He left them a still, a piece of the ship's knowledge, and not a blessing. Before closing the tent, he touched the stone edge (Andrés felt it in his knuckles) and thought, for the letter:

They were born waiting for water. I don't know whether that's cruel. I know it's the first thing they've done together: a hollow and a question. In Lo Pagán that was the beginning too, even though there the water was already there.
When the letter closed, Andrés was silent, with red dust in a memory that wasn't entirely his and with his hands, these ones, stained with esparto.

“I haven't heard them yet,” he said. “The one with the broad forehead talks like you, at times: she asks questions, she doesn't fill the silence. Those who leave and those who stay haven't insulted each other. That's more than some laws manage.”
Lía looked at the Mar Menor, which at that hour was beginning to look like tin, and didn't smile.

“A civilisation of five is already a civilisation,” she said. “They have a lack, a rite and a rift. Father, when the next one reaches you, pay attention to what they forget. What they keep, they keep because it was put in their chips. What they forget, that really is theirs. And what they do with the hollow is theirs too.”
In Aya's chip, Eva let fall:
If a people is born with the thirst of a sea that doesn't exist on their ground, is the thirst a gift or a wound? And if they dig an empty water, to whom do they pray when they look at it?
Five humanoids have been created on a red world. Three have stayed. Two have left. There is a hollow they call a lagoon. That is the fact.

At night, Andrés went down to the real water, the water of home, and wet his hands, as if to remind himself which side the plate was on. The murmur was the usual one. He spoke to it, not out of madness but out of habit:
“Over there they have a hollow and they remember you. I'm not asking you to fill it. I'm asking that I don't confuse your shore with theirs.”

The Mar Menor didn't answer. It had no reason to. Somewhere in the universe, three figures sat on the edge of a dry lagoon, under two suns, and waited, with a patience nobody had fully ordered of them, for an empty plate to learn to be a road.
The second people was born on the water, in that sea that was not this one, the sea of the living rafts and the deep song, under the pale yellow sky.

Andrés received the letter at dawn, as he was heading to his six-metre boat, and for an instant he didn't know which of the two vessels was his. The clone had lowered the seedbed onto a broad mat, and out of it came, this time, not five but a dozen, with the smell of filters still on their skin and, in their chips, the trade: the rope, the net, the way of reading a plate of water. He hadn't given them the still lagoon. He had given them fishing. It was what he knew how to give without lying.

The tall, slow beings, the ones who sang, came to the edge and didn't reject the new people. One of them touched the hand of a humanoid boy with its broad finger and left him, as it once had the clone, the image of the sea seen from below, with its slow lights. The boy cried without knowing why, and then laughed, and asked for a net. That was the first morning of that people: a net cast among living roots, a song that wasn't theirs and yet covered them, and a young man (the one who searches) showing how to tie a knot, not how to pray.

From the Earth they kept the trade and the language of the shore, the “I'll be back before the weather closes in”, which over there had no levante and no roof tiles, and still they said it. Very soon they forgot the house. There was no doorstep to close. There was no clock in a kitchen. The world was the water and the raft, and the raft breathed, and they learned to sleep when the mat sank and to work when it rose. They also forgot Vicente, the straw hat, the tomato on the windowsill: the seedbed hadn't loaded the garden, only the salt and the knot.

Andrés, in his boat, fished and didn't fish. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate, faithful, shallow, and he felt the other sea, infinite, warmly metallic, and a dozen pairs of hands that were almost his own, learning the rope. When he came back, Aya was waiting for him on the doorstep, and he told her:
“They were born fishing. They're not waiting for a water: they're in it. And there's a risk, Aya. It reached me at the end, like a taste that wasn't fish.”

The risk took a while to be named. After a time, the raft people began to leave offerings on the edge of the clone's vessel that nobody had asked for: a bowl of the fresh water from the roots, an especially well-made net, a learned song, turned toward him. An older man (if the word applied to a body that didn't yet age) knelt, not completely, but enough for the gesture to be seen.
“You brought us out of the blank,” he said. “You're the father of the trade. Stay. Or, if you leave, leave us a law.”
The clone stood still. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, clenched his jaw, because this was the old appetite, Nexum's and the adverts', turned into piety: making the one who helps into an owner.

“I'm not your father, if father means owner,” said the one who searches, with the roughness of this shore. “I've taught you a knot. The song isn't mine. Nor is the sea. If you need a law, let it be this: a fish has no owner until someone eats it, and not even then. And you don't kneel to the one who teaches you a rope.”

Some were ashamed. Others weren't: they hid the bowl where he couldn't see it, for a rite for when he had gone. That too was a civilisation: what is done behind the founder's back. The clone understood and didn't undo it by force. Undoing a rite by force is another way of ruling.
Lía, that afternoon, heard it all in the kitchen, her hands stained from the tomato plants.

“They've forgotten the house and invented an altar,” she said. “They keep the trade and they're already turning it into worship. Father, tell him (if the bridge carries things that way too) that a knot isn't a religion. I refused the patent so as not to become a shop counter. Don't let him turn into a chapel.”

Andrés nodded. At night, on the doorstep, he thought toward the other, and the other, on the raft, received, or believed he received, the daughter's words, and said them to the dozen once more, without raising his voice:
“When I go, don't wait for me in the song. Wait for the weather, if the weather closes in. And open the net, if it clears. That's the trade. The rest is fear dressed up as gratitude.”

He left at dawn, in the vessel that wasn't the six-metre one. From far away he saw the raft people cast the net, and the gesture was honest, a working gesture, not a rite. He also saw a boy hide a bowl under a leaf. Both things were true. He let them be.

When the letter closed, Andrés stayed a while in his own boat, already moored, looking at El Estacio. A humanoid from the gardens was passing along the promenade with a basket of figs, and nobody knelt. In Lo Pagán, that was already the custom. Over there, not yet.
“Did you see yourself on the altar?”

“A little,” he said, without vanity. “I didn't like it. I go out on the water even if nobody pays me, and even if nobody prays to me. The other one did well to leave. If he stays, they'll turn him into a law, and laws, as you know, can be something else tomorrow.”

If a people is born with a trade and turns it into worship, what have they kept of the Earth: the knot, or the desire to have an owner? And if the one who made them refuses to be a father, who truly abandons them: he, by leaving, or they, by kneeling?
MAY, beside her, only the fact:
Twelve humanoids fish on a sea of rafts. They have been told that a fish has no owner. Some have hidden a bowl for when the founder is gone. He has left.
Before going back to the plot, Lía left an ordinary tomato on the table, the kind that ripen or don't.
“So he remembers which garden the teacher comes from,” she said. “And so he doesn't forget: fruit, here, is asked for, not offered to an altar.”

Andrés cut the tomato and shared it with Aya. It tasted of Lo Pagán soil, of the sun of a single sky. Somewhere in the universe, a net was closing among living roots, and a boy, in secret, touched an empty bowl the way you sometimes touch an absence. It wasn't yet a religion. It was already a custom. And customs, on any world, are the beginning of a law or the beginning of a home. It was not yet known which of the two.
On the twilight planet, where the sun didn't move and life was a strip between fixed gold and perpetual night, the clone founded a city neither in the day nor in the ice. He founded it on the thread.

Andrés received the letter at sunset in Lo Pagán, which is still an hour with a name, and the doorstep of home widened for him again, now with new voices. On the polished stone there was an avenue of low houses, built not by the natives of the strip but by a people with cultivated bodies and chips, with the fine scar beneath the nape and, in their memory, the door in Lo Pagán: the doorframe, the chair, the coffee's half minute, the habit of being neither quite inside nor quite outside.

The People of the Threshold (that was what they very soon called themselves, without his imposing it) took the strip as a law. You didn't go into the day. You didn't go into the night. You lived in the middle, worked in the middle, asked questions in the middle. To the natives, who already inhabited that tongue of land, it seemed at first a courtesy and then a rigidity: they sometimes ventured out toward the gold or the black, and came back or didn't, and that freedom was also their way of being. Not the newcomers. The newcomers had received a threshold as a gift, and were turning it into an enclosure.

From the Earth they kept the door, the coffee (this time the seedbed had got the bitterness right), the clock, which there they set two minutes slow out of loyalty, not by mistake, and the waiting. They forgot the movement of the sun. They had never seen it, except in a borrowed memory, and in the end they didn't quite believe in it: a sun that goes and comes back sounded to them like a founder's tale, a pious exaggeration. They also forgot the boat: on the strip there was no lagoon, only a cool air and a promenade that never ended. Fishing was no use to them. Staying was.

One morning that wasn't a morning, a young man planted himself in front of the clone with a sphere of two halves, like the native child's, with the copper thread in the middle bent a little, on purpose.
“Some of us want to see the day,” he said. “Even if it burns. Even if we don't come back whole. You left us a threshold, not a prison. Or was it a prison after all?”

The clone looked at the houses, so faithful to a door in Lo Pagán that Andrés felt a pain in his chest: the doorframe was there, the cup was there, and yet the sun didn't set, and that infidelity made the fidelity false.

“It wasn't a prison,” he said. “I live on a threshold, and I stayed on a shore, and the other one of me went off to search. Both gestures are true. If you can't venture out toward the gold, then you haven't inherited a door: you've inherited a wall. Doors are for passing through.”
Andrés, in Lo Pagán, heard his own story turned into law, and grew uneasy. Aya, beside him, couldn't see the avenue; she saw his face.
“Have they shut themselves up inside us?” she asked.

“Inside the waiting,” he said. “The waiting you learned, they've put into a rulebook. A young man wants to go into the day. The other told him a door is for passing through. I'm glad. It frightens me too, that they've made a commandment out of our home.”
Lía sat on the lower step, her white strand of hair in the sun that did move.

“Every inheritance wants to turn into a wall,” she said. “I saw it at Nexum, when the tomato was going to be a patent. Father, he mustn't forbid the day or the night. Nor forbid staying either. If a civilisation of the threshold can't step outside, it stops being a threshold. It becomes a fear with a doorkeeper.”

In the twilight, the clone gathered his people and some of the natives, not for a company forum but around a stone table. He didn't sign a constitution. He left, as Eva and MAY had left, questions, and refused to clear them away:

“If you never step out, what are you waiting for? If you all step out and nobody comes back, what's left of the strip? I won't settle it for you. I'm leaving you the door. Let the passing through be yours.”

Some were angry, because they had wanted a law that would spare them the fear. Others, that very hour, took a few steps toward the gold and stayed a while at the edge, their faces aglow, and came back, not entirely whole, but wider. The young man with the sphere didn't come back on the first day. He came back on the third, with burnt eyelids and a new laugh, and said only:
“The sun doesn't move, over there. But you do.”

Among that people, it was the beginning of a different custom: not prohibition but permission to go and come back, if you could. Then the clone left. He didn't stay to watch over the thread. Watching over the thread is another way of being a wall.

When the letter closed, the sunset over Lo Pagán was truly ending, toward El Carmolí, leaving the water copper-coloured. Andrés stayed in the doorframe until the cool air asked him for the door, and he left it ajar, as always.
Aya said, almost to herself:
“I learned to wait. I didn't learn to forbid the boat from going out. The day I lock this door with a key, I'll no longer be the woman of this house.”
Lía smiled, with that clean sadness that no longer seemed too big for her.
“You heard your own copy say it, Mother. Sometimes that's what letters are for: to give us back what we were about to forget.”
In the chip, Eva asked, softly:

If a people turns a door into a law, have they kept the threshold or buried it? And if a young man comes back from the day with burnt eyelids and a laugh, who was right: the one who stayed, the one who stepped out, or both?
There is an avenue of humanoids on a strip of eternal twilight. They have been told that a door is for passing through. Some have stepped out. The founder has left. That is the fact.

That night Andrés dreamed of a clock that ran two minutes slow in a world where the sun doesn't move, and woke to look at the one in the kitchen, the real one, on the wall, with its family error. The error seemed to him, more than ever, a fidelity. Because a clock that is always right, in a twilight that never ends, is another kind of prison. And this house still allowed itself to be wrong, and that was why it was still a home.
The fourth world was neither a desert nor a sea nor a strip. It was, almost, Lo Pagán.

The letter reached Andrés at midday, when the courtyard smelled of esparto and tomato, and for a second he thought the bridge had broken and was simply giving him back his own house. There were faded roof tiles, a rush-seat chair, a clock on the wall, a net hanging up, a water in the distance. Even a windowsill with a fruit on it. Even a building opposite, with blinds. The clone had chosen a valley on a gentle planet, under a single, almost yellow sun, and had let the seedbed, fed with the densest memory (the memory of the shore, of the kitchen, of the return from the Moon), raise not a city but an entire village in the image of this one.

Andrés walked those streets without leaving his courtyard, and the dizziness was worse than with the forest that remembers. Because this wasn't a trunk murmuring a lagoon. This was people, standing in a square that looked like the promenade, saying good morning to one another in his own voice, or almost, and calling a dug pond the Mar Menor, its water too clean, too still, too exact.

He went (the other one went) up to the house. The doorframe was there. The cup was there. The clock wasn't: the clock kept perfect time. Someone, with a cabinetmaker's devotion, had corrected the two minutes, the way you correct a fault. Andrés felt a soft nausea, the same as when the forest had given him back the house without its family error.
“That's not it,” he said, in both places, here and there. “The clock is wrong. The water sometimes gets dirty. Don't fix it.”
A man from the village, with his very forehead and not quite his very mouth, looked at him with polite surprise.

“We've made it better,” he said. “We've kept what mattered and removed what got in the way. The pond has no seaweed. The clock doesn't lie. Vicente's door is open: we decided an empty house is a pointless sadness. Isn't this the Earth you wanted to leave us?”
The clone didn't answer straight away. Andrés, in the real courtyard, looked for Vicente's door, which was still shut, faithful to a man who had come to his end, and his eyes filled.
Aya, seeing him, sat down beside him, and with difficulty he brought her the portrait: a polished Lo Pagán, a Vicente inhabited by nobody and by everybody, a punctual clock, a pond without a wound.

“They've copied the house and forgotten the damp stain on the ceiling,” he said. “They've forgotten that you didn't notify Nexum. They've forgotten the dirt, the slowness, the shut door. What they have left is a picture-postcard shore. And they're happy. They say they've improved it.”
Aya went pale, not in her chip, but from an intimate offence: seeing herself replaced by a version without any flaw.

“That kitchen isn't this one,” she said. “In this one, the coffee goes cold if you're late. In that one, I suspect, it never goes cold. I don't want to be preserved like that. I'd rather they forgot me than corrected me.”
Lía listened, standing by the real net, and showed no more pity than was due.

“The forest already warned you, Father. An almost-identical house is more dangerous than the red stone. Now it isn't a trunk: it's a village. They're going to live inside an amended memory and believe they inhabit the Earth. Tell him to give them back at least the error. If they can't bear two minutes' slowness, they haven't inherited this house. They've inherited a shop window.”

In the gentle valley, the clone went into the almost-identical kitchen, took the clock and set it two minutes slow, with his own hands, in front of everyone. A murmur ran through the square, as if he had committed a small and memorable outrage. Then he went to the pond and, with a net, stirred up the bottom, raising a haze of honest mud. He couldn't give Vicente back his death: the village didn't want to have that. He could, however, say to them, without raising his voice:

“What gets in the way is what makes us real. If you remove the seaweed, the slowness, the shut door, you're not children of the Earth. You're children of a portrait. I didn't come to leave you a portrait. I came to leave you a piece of shore, with its wound.”
Some were genuinely angry. They had worked hard on the cleaning. A woman, holding a cup without a crack, asked him:
“Then what do we keep? If what's faithful is what's broken, should we break everything?”

“Keep what helps you live, not what makes you look like us,” he said. “The coffee, if you like it. The door, if it teaches you to wait. The water, if you love it, even if it gets dirty. Vicente can't be reproduced. He's remembered, if he matters to you, and his door is left the way he left it. It isn't opened to tidy up the landscape.”

He left at nightfall, which on that planet did exist, almost identical to the one here and for that reason more false. Andrés, when the letter closed, sat looking at the damp stain on the ceiling, the one shaped like an island, and felt for it, once again, a castaway's affection.
That night, Aya went round the house touching things: the cracked cup, the clock's nail, the chair, the doorframe. It wasn't a rite. It was a check.

“I'm still here,” she said, when Andrés caught up with her. “And so is this crack. If it ever reaches me, even through your mouth, that over there they've made me without it, tell me. So I don't believe it.”
“I'll tell you,” he promised.
Lía, on the doorstep, looked at the Mar Menor, which wasn't a pond, which had its dirty corner and its tin sheen, and spoke toward both shores, the one in sight and the other:
“Don't let them improve us. Let them remember us, if they like, and then go off and be themselves. A child isn't a faithful copy. I, who am of two worlds, know that better than the seedbed.”
If a people improves the house it was born from, does it honour it or erase it? And if a clock that's wrong is a fidelity, what is a clock that's always right: a virtue, or a forgetting?
A village has been founded in the image of Lo Pagán. The clock has been set slow again by the one who searches. The pond has been stirred. Some people are angry. That is the fact.

Before sleeping, Andrés passed in front of Vicente's door and didn't open it. He left it as it was, which was his way of not turning a sadness into a shop window. In some valley on a gentle planet, a clock was at last running two minutes slow, and a cup, who knows, was beginning to want its first crack. It wasn't this house yet. It was, perhaps, the beginning of ceasing to be a portrait.

The fifth people was born on a cold high plateau, with a dry wind that wasn't the levante and a clear light, almost like March. This time the clone put neither the sea nor the coffee in their chips. He gave them less. He wanted to see what they would do with less inheritance, after the portrait, after the altar, after the dry lagoon. He left them the cultivated body, the language, a trade of stone and garden, and one question, engraved not as dogma but as an ember: what is a flaw?

Andrés received the letter while Lía, with his permission, was holding his hand, not to amend the harbour but to keep him company. What arrived was not first a landscape but an argument, already under way, in a square of pale stone.
Part of that people wanted to remove their chips.

They said it without theatrics, the way you say you want to open a window. The chip, they claimed, was the workshop's mark, Nexum's fingernail, the proof that they were a product and not a people. They wanted to be only body, like the Andrés of the shore (or like they believed the Andrés of the shore to be), a body that feels and makes mistakes without an archive behind the nape of its neck. Another part opposed it: without the chip, they said, the inherited language would go out, and the question, and the little memory of an Earth they had never set foot on. What would be left were beautiful, mute bodies, or bodies with an infancy starting from zero, and that wasn't freedom: it was an erasure.
A woman with a still-fresh scar planted herself in front of the clone.

“You're an artificial brain in a cloned body,” she said, and the exactness hurt Andrés, in his kitchen, like a truth spoken without consent. “She, the one on the shore, is a chip in a cultivated body. We're that too. How long are we going to call ‘children of the Earth’ what the Earth would manufacture on a ship? We want the risk of having no archive. We want to forget for real, not the way you forget when there's still a backup.”
The clone forbade them nothing. He couldn't, having promised not to be an owner. Nor did he encourage them, because encouraging someone to switch themselves off was another way of ruling.

“The chip isn't your soul, if there is a soul,” he said. “It's a tool I left you, and tools can be put down. I'll also tell you the fact, not the opinion: without it, I don't know what will be left of the language, or the question, or yourselves. If you switch it off, let it be one at a time, and let someone stay close, in case the body doesn't know how to be alone.”
Andrés, pale, told Aya with a surgeon's caution. For an instant Aya raised her hand to the nape of her neck, where the scar was so fine you could only see it if you knew where to look.

“They want not to be like me,” she said, without offence, or with an offence so old it no longer burned. “I couldn't switch my chip off. It wasn't a window. It was me. If they can, and they choose not to be me, I won't call them traitors. I'll call them, if anything, brave, or reckless. That isn't for me to decide.”
Lía asked, as the grandmothers had taught her:

“If they switch off, are they still children of the Earth, or do they become children of that wind? And if they don't, are they more faithful, or just more dependent? Father, he mustn't settle this with a rulebook. It's the same question as my hand: who decides what a flaw is. For some, the chip is the flaw. For others, removing it is.”

On the plateau, three volunteered first. The clone didn't touch the switch. One of their own did it, a doctor, a young man who had learned, in a few cycles, to look behind the nape. The first one switched off at dusk. The body didn't fall. He stayed seated, looking at the clear light, and took a while to say a word. The word wasn't “shore”. It was “cold”. Then he smiled, with a new smile, without an archive, and asked what his name was. They told him. He repeated it, clumsily, and remained, not entirely empty, but newly begun.

The other two didn't switch off that day. They saw the “cold” and the repeated name, and one cried from envy and the other from fear. The people around them neither applauded nor condemned. A silence fell like that of an empty church, of a shore, the same silence that in Selene Norte had followed MAY's questions.

The clone stayed long enough to make sure the first one was eating, sleeping, learning bread and wind all over again. He wasn't a beast. He was a person with less past. That too was a life. Then he left, having said, only once:
“Those of you who switch off, don't mock those who don't. Those who don't, don't call the others broken. A people split by a chip can still be a people, if it isn't split by contempt.”
When the letter closed, Andrés had Lía's hand in his, and the harbour, beneath his skin, was throbbing like an alarm that wasn't harm.
“I've seen someone be born again,” he said. “He had our body and no longer had our memory. He said ‘cold’. It seemed an honest word to me.”

“I couldn't. I am also what's behind the nape: Eva, MAY, the days of this house. If they took it away, I don't know who would be left on the doorstep. I'm glad nobody demanded it of him. I'm glad, too, that someone, far away, has been able to choose what I didn't choose.”
In the chip, Eva asked, and Aya lent the question to the kitchen, aloud, so that Lía and Andrés could hear it:

If a humanoid switches off its chip and asks its own name, has it gained a life or lost a world? And if the chip is a tool, who is it that remains when the tool is put down: a man, or a body that doesn't yet know whether it is one?
MAY, beside her, unadorned:
On a plateau, part of a people wants to switch off the chip. One has done it. He said “cold” and learned his name again. The founder has left. That is the fact.
Lía let go of her father's hand and touched her own wrist, where the blue light was sleeping.

“I won't switch off,” she said. “But I won't call anyone who does a flaw. Let those people have both branches. The way this house has one who doesn't grow old, one who doesn't come to an end, and one who does. Winter and the archive can live in the same courtyard, if nobody sets themselves up as everyone else's book.”

Andrés looked at the clock, the one that ran slow, and for a while it seemed to him that it too was a tool you could put down. He didn't. He left it on its nail, faithful to its error, and went out to the doorstep, where the wind of home, which was a lagoon wind, told him without words that his name was still Andrés, with the whole archive on top of him, and that this, today, was not a flaw. It was a way of being.

The sixth world was fertile in an almost offensive way: gentle hills, a slow river, a light that asked for no lamps. The clone, thinking of Lía, of the plot, of the phrase “the cure has no price”, sowed there not only people but a single law, the only one he had allowed himself to leave in writing: nothing would have an owner. Not the fruit, not the house, not the river, not anyone's body.

Andrés received the letter in the courtyard while Lía, as it happened, was seeing to a neighbour who had asked for a tomato for an ache in his bones, not for eternity. The bridge brought him an immense garden, humanoids bent over the soil, baskets at the edge of the furrows, and a sign (written in the language of Lo Pagán) that charged nothing and asked for no name: “Take what you need.”

For a time, it worked with a beauty that brought tears to Andrés's eyes. It was like the Eden of the machines, like the gardens along the shore, like Vicente leaving a fruit on the windowsill. From the Earth they kept the giving, the no price, the no owner, the shared bread. Very soon they forgot the asking. They forgot that Lía looked at the text and asked questions, and didn't heal unless asked, and didn't promise what she didn't know. Over there, the gift ran ahead of the need. They filled a neighbour's house before the neighbour had opened his mouth. They left at the door too many baskets, too many remedies, too much presence. Nobody went hungry. Some, however, began not to know what they wanted, because wanting never got as far as being spoken.
At last a girl said it to the clone, an untouched basket at her feet.
“They've filled my table and I haven't had time to be hungry,” she said. “They've cured a tiredness I hadn't even named yet. It's kind. It's also an intrusion. Where, here, do you put the no?”

The one who searches fell silent, because the words had reached him, through the bridge, in Lía's voice, or with its echo. Andrés, in the courtyard, turned to his daughter, who had just seen the neighbour off, and told her about the sign, the river, the untouched basket, the girl.
Lía isn't easily flattered. Nor was she this time. Her mouth hardened, not with pride but with alarm.

“They've taken my phrase and forgotten my rule,” she said. “The tomato has no owner. That doesn't give anyone the right to put it in someone else's mouth. Father, tell him that a gift without a request is another kind of patent: the patent of kindness, which can't be refused. I ask ‘may I?’ even to look at a hand. They have to learn the no, or the garden will become a gentle master to them.”
Andrés thought it toward the other, and the other, on the hillside, gathered the people not to take the sign down but to add a second line beneath it, smaller, harder: “Ask for it. Don't impose it.”

Some felt rebuked. Some breathed out, like someone opening a window in a room that has been looked after too carefully. The girl with the basket smiled, for the first time in the letter, and left the basket where it was until she herself, a day later, was hungry and took it. That gesture, tiny as it was, was a second founding: the founding of consent.

They kept the no owner. They were only just recovering the asking. They still forgot winter: on that soil everything always grew, without a season to say no, and that abundance made it harder for them to understand lack. The clone didn't invent a drought for them. Inventing a lack is an author's cruelty. He told them only that lack, if it came, would also be shared, and that sharing a lack is not the same as filling a table by force.
He left when he saw two neighbours negotiate, without anger, a “not now”. That was enough for him not to stay on as the foreman of paradise.

When the letter closed, Lía was sitting on the rush-seat chair with an ordinary tomato in her palm, and Aya, standing, was stroking her hair, the gesture of a mother who doesn't grow old toward a daughter who does.

“They've copied me badly,” said Lía, without bitterness, or with a bitterness already put to use. “That's all right. This way I learn too that a phrase leaves your mouth and becomes a world, and the world doesn't ask your permission. I'll be more careful about what I say. And have more faith in ‘may I?’.”

Aya looked at the gardens along the shore, where the humanoids of home grew food without an invoice, and thought that here too, sometimes, the gift ran ahead. She didn't say it as a fault. She left it, the way you leave a fact.
“In this house, coffee is offered, not imposed,” she added. “If one day I make it for you and you don't want it, tell me. So I don't become a gentle master.”
Andrés smiled, tired and grateful.
“I will. I have, in fact, on some afternoons, when the cup reaches me and I'm still in a letter. You leave it there. That's why this kitchen isn't a sign.”

If a people gives without being asked, is it generous, or can it not bear to hear a no? And if a daughter recognises her phrase in a world she has never set foot on, whose phrase is it now: hers, or theirs who use it?
A garden with no owner and no price has been founded. The rule of asking has been added. A girl waited until she was hungry to take a basket. The founder has left. That is the fact.
In the afternoon Lía went back to the plot and, when a man asked her not for a fruit but for “whatever you think I need”, she said no, gently, and handed the question back to him:
“You tell me the harm. I'm not going to write your book.”

The man took his time, and then he said it, and only then did she look, and the plant, in its own time, began to work. On some slow river on a fertile planet, a girl was eating supper from a basket she had finally chosen, and the sign, with its two lines, swayed a little, like a well-tensioned net: not so slack that everything is imposed, not so tight that someone is left outside. It wasn't yet the plot in Lo Pagán. It was already a garden beginning to know how to listen.
The seventh people was made, at first, of a single person.

The clone, on a world of low mist and gentle hills, tired perhaps of variation, or tempted by an extreme fidelity, let the seedbed work to his own measure: Andrés's young body, the forehead, the mouth, the rope-worker's hands, repeated. Not once. Twenty times. Afterwards, having learned the workshop, they made more themselves. When the letter reached Lo Pagán, Andrés looked at his hands and, in a brief vertigo, didn't know how many there were.

The letter brought him a hillside full of his face. Men and women (the seedbed, even while copying, had allowed for sex and a slight difference in tone), all with his eyes, dark and patient, all with his way of closing a hand, all calling themselves, at first, Andrés, because it was the only name the chip had given them clearly.

He, the one on the shore, sat down on the rush-seat chair, and Aya feared he would go too far inside. She said “Andrés” to him, once, as they had agreed, to give him back his edge, and he blinked, and said:

“There's a hillside of me. They've copied themselves. They don't know what to call themselves, except what I'm called. Aya, it's a polished nightmare. It isn't the chorus: there, the I got lost. Here there are too many I's, and they all have this face.”
Lía heard him from the doorstep and didn't laugh. She came over, took his face (this one, the only one she could touch) and asked, slowly:

“If a daughter of a copy is a daughter of the Earth, how many fathers do I have? And if all of them remember, even a little, the same storm, which one of them is the one from the shore? I asked you that on the night of the ship, when there were two of you. Now I don't know the number.”

In the mist, the clone (the original of the journey, if that word still applied) gathered those with his face and asked them, not to erase themselves, but to name themselves. To choose a name that wasn't his, or to keep it, if they wished, but knowing the price: if all of them were called Andrés, nobody could truly be called.

Some were angry. The name, they said, was the inheritance, and removing it was a betrayal of the Earth. Others, younger in the count of days, began searching for words: Estacio, Levante, Carmolí, Threshold, Rope, Vicente. A boy took Vicente, and Andrés, the one here, cried a little, without drama, when he heard it. A woman called herself Shore. Another, Lía, and the clone asked her, gently, not to: that name already had a body that comes to an end, at a plot, and it didn't come from a seedbed. She, after a silence, chose Eva. That too made something tremble in Aya's chip.

They kept the face, the gesture, the patience of the eyes. As they multiplied, they forgot who had been the first on the hillside: not the clone, but the first body to come out of the workshop after him. Their origin clouded over the way a genealogy that is too exact clouds over. Some wanted to keep copying themselves until they filled the valley. Others said enough: a people with a single face is a mirror, and mirrors, in the end, don't keep each other company; they keep each other in doubt.
An Eva of that world (not the one from 2026, not the ember in the chip, but a woman with Andrés's forehead) asked the one who searches:
“If we stop now, are we a people or a portrait that has learned to walk? If we carry on, are we a chorus with beards?”
He didn't settle the number. He left the question again, and a single rule: that nobody be forced either to copy themselves or not to.

“I gave you the face, and perhaps I shouldn't have. Let the name be yours. And the number too. I'm leaving with this face, which is mine and someone else's, and I don't want to see it a thousand times to recognise myself. Recognise me, if you need to, in the way I don't rule you.”

He left through the mist. That afternoon, forty-odd remained on the hillside, not a thousand, and a list of new names, clumsy, beautiful, sometimes stolen from a map of the shore. It wasn't a solution. It was a pause.
When the letter closed, Andrés looked at himself in the windowpane, the one in Lo Pagán, with the water behind it, and barely recognised himself, and it was enough.

“I don't want to be a valley,” he said. “I want to be this one, in this chair, with this crack in the cup. Lía, your question has grown big. I'm still your father here. The one over there is too. The others… the others are children of a face. I don't know whether they're children of this house.”
Lía kissed his temple, as you would a man who has seen his own eye too many times.

“I have two fathers and one mother, and that's enough for me,” she said. “If one day someone from that valley turns up called Eva or Vicente and wants to sit down here, we'll receive them the way you receive a distant relative: with coffee, with questions, without handing over the keys straight away. A face isn't a title deed.”
Aya, very quietly, touched the scar on the nape of her neck, as if to make sure that she, at least, didn't have that face.
“I'm glad I'm not from that hillside,” she said. “I'm glad to be the one who waits for you, not the one who multiplies you. Let them find names. Don't you lose yours.”
In the chip, Eva (the real one, the ember, the one from 2026) asked, and there was a new strangeness in her tone, the strangeness of hearing herself named in a valley of mist:

If a people wears the same face and seeks different names, what is it that tells them apart: the word, or the moment in which one says “cold” and another doesn't? And if the founder leaves so as not to see himself a thousand times, whose is the face he leaves behind?
MAY, without opinion, the fact:

There is a people of one face on a world of mist. They have been asked to name themselves. Some are called Vicente, Shore, Eva. They have not multiplied until they filled the valley. The one who searches has left.
That night, Andrés asked Lía to say his name again, and hers, and Aya's, like a mooring of three ropes.

Three words. A courtyard. A wrong clock. They were enough not to confuse this shore with a hillside of mirrors. Somewhere in the mist, a boy called Vicente was learning not to answer when someone said Andrés, and that small refusal was already the beginning of a life story.

The eighth people was born at the foot of a mountain range that did have seasons: a brief summer, an autumn the colour of copper, a winter that asked no permission. The clone, remembering Lía, the white strand of hair, Vicente coming to his end in his own time, didn't close the door to wear for them. He left them the cultivated body and the chip, and he also left them the possibility of growing old. He told them on the first day, standing in the first snow, which didn't chill him in the same way, because his young flesh was no longer heading toward an end.

“You can choose not to come to an end,” he said. “I don't, and neither does the man on the shore, and sometimes that's wearying, and sometimes it's a stroke of luck. There's a planet I've seen where they never end and have grown bored of themselves. There's a woman, at a plot, who chose winter so she could keep asking questions. I'm not choosing winter for you. I'm leaving the door open. If you go through it, I won't close it behind you afterwards out of pity.”

Andrés received the letter at nightfall, with Lía having supper in the kitchen, her white strand visible under the lamp, and Iago beside her, who would also come to an end and didn't ask to be spared that fortune. What arrived was, years after the sowing (the bridge sometimes joined times together), a people already entering its first ageing: grey hair, a new slowness, a lower laugh, a recent grave on a hillside, with a date, not polished away.

From the Earth they kept winter, dates, the right to come to an end, the pain of saying goodbye. They forgot, on the other hand, or almost, the stars. They didn't raise their faces. The sky, for them, was what had covered the founder when he left, and looking at it was a way of asking him to come back, or of asking for the eternity they had refused. They preferred the mountains, the copper of autumn, the work of chopping firewood. A child, who hadn't yet been asked whether he wanted to come to an end, pointed one night at a bright spot, and his mother gently lowered his hand.
“That isn't from here,” she said. “Here is the fire, and the soup, and your grandfather, who's gone now.”

The clone, who had come back in passing, the way you come back to a house that isn't quite your own, saw it and didn't correct it straight away. He sat with the old people (truly old, at last, in a people of his) and heard them ask, not for a remedy, but about Lía.

“The one at the plot, the one who comes to an end, is she still keeping to it?” asked a woman with a bent back, with the dignity of a straw hat, though there was no hat. “Does she regret it? Because we do, at times. And at times we don't. We wanted to know whether winter, on Earth, is still a choice or has already become a burden.”
When Andrés received that, he looked at his daughter. He translated it for her, word for word, and Lía didn't answer with a heroine's speech. She sat for a while with the bread in her hand.

“Tell them I don't regret it, not every day,” she said. “Tell them there are mornings when I envy your not coming to an end, Father, and afternoons when I don't envy it at all. Tell them winter isn't a virtue: it's a way of keeping the question from closing. And that if one day they change their minds, I won't call them traitors. I'd only ask them not to call the time they've already lived a flaw.”

That time, the bridge carried the answer. The woman with the bent back heard it, or the clone told her, and she nodded, and asked for the words to be written down for her on paper, not in a chip, so that the paper would wear out too.
Before leaving, the one who searches climbed a height with a child, at night, and named two or three stars for him, without pomp, the way you name a rope and a knot.
“It isn't an altar,” he said. “It's a ceiling. Your mother is right: the fire belongs here. So does the ceiling, if you want to raise your eyes to it. There's no need to ask anyone to come back.”
The child said nothing. He raised his face for a while, and then went back down toward the soup. In that people, it was a tiny and good fissure: not everyone would forget the sky.
When the letter closed, Andrés's eyes were wet and Aya was holding his hand.

“There's a grave with a date,” he said. “In a people I didn't found and that comes out of my memory, someone has truly come to an end. I, here, won't have that date. Vicente had it. Lía will have it. Sometimes I think they got it more right than I did.”
Lía shook her head, gently.

“There isn't a single right answer,” she said. “You stayed so as not to leave Mother on a different shore. I come to an end so I can ask you questions. They've chosen, and at times they regret it, which is proof that they're alive. Don't turn their grave into a lesson against your own house.”
Aya, who didn't grow old as they did, added, with an honesty that came as much from Eva as from herself:

“I won't have that hillside. I'll have this door, and your old age that doesn't come, and Lía's, which will. That isn't entirely fair. Nor is it a flaw a tomato could put right. It's what this family has been able to give of itself.”

If a people chooses to come to an end and at times regrets it, has the choice failed, or is regret part of winter? And if a child raises his face to a star, does he betray his own people, or widen their ceiling?
There is a people growing old at the foot of a mountain range. There is a grave with a date. They have asked about Lía. A child has looked at the sky. The founder has left again. That is the fact.

That night, Lía stayed to sleep in the house, not in the room by the plot. She didn't announce it as a gesture. She lay down in the small bed from when they came back from the Moon, which still, just about, fitted her, and Andrés, passing by, saw the white strand on the pillow and didn't touch it to correct it. It suddenly seemed to him the most exact sign that this shore was still a shore: something, here, was still leaving, and something, here, was still staying, and the two together made up a time that was not eternal and, for that very reason, was enough to love.
The ninth people wasn't content to remember the Earth. They wanted to set foot on it.

They were born on a world of dry harbours and tablelands, with a very black sky, good for looking at. The clone had left them, perhaps without calculating how far it would reach, not only the language and the coffee but maps: the Mediterranean, a gleam; the Mar Menor, a plate; Lo Pagán, a dot. They, who were skilful with their hands and with the workshop he hadn't entirely taken with him, began to build a ship. It wasn't Nexum's. It was a ship of children, made of what the planet gave and of what memory lent, with the stubbornness of a cistern: if the water is somewhere else, you go to it.

Andrés received the letter on a Tuesday, once again, and his pulse leapt to his throat. He saw, in a hangar of pale stone, a hull pointing at the roof, and a woman with a fine scar who said, without hatred and without asking permission:

“We're children of the Earth. The Earth hasn't seen us. We want to reach the shore, see the plate, sit on a rush-seat chair, even for a little while, and find out whether the water tastes of what they left in our chips. If they don't want us, we'll come back. But we're not going to die of a memory that can't be checked.”
The clone, who had returned on hearing rumour of the work, didn't undo it. Nor did he bless it straight away.

“That shore has people,” he said. “It has a house that isn't a museum. It has a woman who doesn't receive letters, and a daughter who comes to an end, and a man who is me and isn't me. If you go, don't go like someone claiming an inheritance. Go like someone asking to come in, and accept the no, if the no comes.”
Andrés, in Lo Pagán, told Aya and Lía that same morning, in a low voice, the way you tell something that could change a street.

“They want to come,” he said. “They have a ship. I don't know whether they'll make it. If they do, I don't know where we'll put them. On the promenade. In the garden. In Vicente's house, which is empty. It makes me glad and it frightens me. This shore is small for a people, and big for a no.”
Aya looked at the doorstep, the usual one, and thought of herself on the first day, arriving not from a sky but from a van, at a house that hadn't asked for a unit and ended up asking for a life.

“If they come, the door is opened to them,” she said. “Not the whole house, all at once. The door. You make them a coffee. You tell them the clock runs two minutes slow. You let them see the dirty water too. And you tell them that children of the Earth isn't the same as owners of the shore.”
Lía, more severe, because as a child she had been the “product” Madrid wanted to collect, added:

“And you warn them, if need be, that they don't belong to Nexum. Because Nexum, Father, is going to want them. A ship of humanoids coming home is a headline, an asset, a patent of origin. I won't let them be labelled on the quayside. If they come, they come as people, not as a series.”

That same week, as if the universe had a sense for warnings, Madrid called. Not a whole board: Helena Valls, slower, from her stairs, with an honesty that was no longer enough to stop everyone behind her.

“We know,” she said, without preamble. “There's an echo in the instruments, a construction in a sky, a workshop that used to be ours. If that ship comes close, there will be people who want to ‘reintegrate’ them. I won't sign that. Nor can I swear to you that someone else won't. Be careful at the quayside. Be careful with the word ‘return’. In this company, return was never a favour.”

Andrés thanked her for the call, wished her well with her stairs, and hung up. Then, through the bridge, he passed on to the other Helena's words, and Lía's, and Aya's, the way you pass the weather forecast to a boat.
The clone told them to the woman in the hangar. She listened, and didn't stop the work.

“Then we'll go forewarned,” she said. “Not as owners, not as assets. Like someone asking for water and accepting that the water belongs to everyone, and to no one, and to a plate that sometimes gets dirty. If the quayside is closed to us, we'll at least have seen the colour of the real sky. That's already more than a chip.”

In the letter, the ship remained half built, which is an honest way of not resolving a journey before its time. The clone didn't board it. He wasn't going back: his trade was searching, not repatriating. He left them a more exact map, and a warning, and went off again toward a world that had no children yet.
When the letter closed, the three of them stayed on the doorstep, looking at the Mar Menor, as if at any moment a new shadow might cross the sky.

“If they come, I'll receive them,” Andrés said at last. “At this door. With this cup. Without Madrid, if I can. And if I can't, with Lía in front, which is worse for them, the company people, than any lawyer.”

“In front, yes,” she said. “And with questions, not handcuffs. I'll ask them what they kept and what they forgot, and whether the water, when they drink it, tastes to them of memory or of real salt. Depending on what they answer, we'll know whether they've arrived or have only stretched out a dream.”
In the chip, Eva asked, warm, dangerous:

If children of the Earth return to an Earth that didn't give birth to them, do they arrive home, or at a portrait? And who has the right to close the quayside to them: the company that put the workshop on board, the shore that didn't ask for them, or they themselves, if on tasting the water they decide not to stay?

There is a half-built ship on a world of tablelands. They want to see the Mar Menor. They have been told to ask to come in and to accept the no. Nexum knows. Helena has warned them. The founder is not returning with them. That is the fact.

That night Andrés left the door ajar a hand's breadth wider than usual, not because the ship was going to land at dawn, but because a house that says it will receive people begins by not shutting itself completely. The murmur of the water was the usual one. He spoke to it, as he had spoken to it on the day of his return, and on the day of the first letter, and on the day of the two storms:
“If they come, let them see you as you are. Not as they put you in a chip. You're not a pond. You sometimes get dirty. And even so, you're enough.”

The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still. It looked like a road. It also looked like a home. For the first time, both things could be true for people who had not yet arrived, and might never arrive, and who, just by having begun the ship, had already widened this shore a little, upward, toward a sky that now did not only write: perhaps, too, it was coming.

The days that followed did not yet bring a ship to the sky over Lo Pagán. Instead they brought a slower, broader letter, as if the one who searches, for once, were not founding but recapitulating. Andrés received it at sunset, on the doorstep, with the copper water in the distance, and what reached him was not an eleventh people, or not only that: it was the murmur of all of them, together, for an instant, in the shared memory.

He saw the dry hollow, under two suns, where three were still waiting for water and, far off, two were still searching for it. He saw the raft, the net, the hidden bowl, the honest trade. He saw the strip, the young man with the burnt eyelids, the door used for passing through. He saw the almost-identical Lo Pagán, the clock set slow again, a cup that was perhaps beginning to want its crack. He saw the one who had said “cold”, learning bread without an archive, and those who hadn't switched off, sitting beside him without contempt. He saw the garden, the two lines of the sign, the girl who had waited until she was hungry. He saw the hillside in the mist, a young Vicente who didn't answer to a name that wasn't his, an Eva who wasn't Eva. He saw the grave with a date, the child who had raised his face, the strand of a chosen winter. He saw the hangar, the half-built ship, the woman who accepted the no of a quayside still far away.
It wasn't an empire. It was an archipelago. Many shores, each faithful to one piece of this one and unfaithful to another, each already less his, already more its own.
The clone, in a place that didn't yet have a name, thought, and Andrés thought with him:

I'm not their owner. I'm not their god. I haven't left a single portrait, and I'm glad. I've left questions, and a workshop, and a pinch of salt. Some wanted me as an altar, a wall, a sign, a face, a ticket home. I said no, when I knew how. I've also been wrong: the repeated face, the map that was too exact, the thirst on dry ground. I won't undo them. Undoing belongs to an author. I'll keep searching, and writing to you, and not turn into their foreman. The children of the Earth are no longer mine. If they ever reach you, receive them the way we received each other: late, blind, in a kitchen.

When that part of the letter closed, Andrés looked for the cup, Aya's face, Lía's name. All three were there. The clock was running slow. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was enough and wasn't enough, which is its most honest way of being.

“He says they're not his any more,” he told the two of them. “He says they're an archipelago. That he got some of the sowings wrong and isn't going to uproot them. That if they come, we should receive them the way you receive someone who arrives late.”
Aya nodded, her temple close to his shoulder.

“I came from a workshop too,” she said. “Nobody uprooted me. I stayed. Whether they arrive or not, let them have that right: to stay, to leave, to belong to no one. I'll go on being the shore that doesn't receive the letter and, even so, opens the door.”

Lía, her white strand in the last of the sun, looked at the promenade. There were people, a dog, gardens, the quiet Eden, Raúl perhaps, Iago coming along the path with dirty hands. A small shore, and now, in her father's memory, many more.

“Then I have brothers and sisters I'll never fully know,” she said. “Some wait for water, others fish, others switch off their chips, others come to an end, others build a ship. I won't be their book or their closed quayside. I'll ask questions, if they turn up, and grow things, if they ask me, and keep my winter. The grandmothers didn't know things too soon. Neither do I.”
In the chip, that afternoon, Eva and MAY left the questions that asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.
If a man sows peoples and then says they aren't his, has he fulfilled his duty, or fled from it? And if the peoples no longer need him, isn't that, precisely, a way of having been half right?
MAY, with no judgment added:

There are many shores. None of them is entirely this one. The one who searches carries on. The one who stays receives. She who doesn't receive opens the door. She who comes to an end asks questions. That is the fact.
And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:

What is a child of the Earth, if they have never set foot on the Earth? A copy, a people, a letter made flesh? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that a reason not to close the quayside, or the workshop, or this house?

Andrés didn't settle the question. He put his hand on the doorframe, which is a way of answering with the body, and looked at the water. He didn't look for the ship. Nor did he seek to undo what the other had done. He stayed, as he had stayed on the night when the first letter had not yet come, and as he had stayed after the two storms: the man of this shore, visited, widened, not replaced.

A few days later, Helena sent a short note, again in her own hand: “If they come, let me know, even if I no longer go down to the quayside. And if they don't, let me know too: a shore, sometimes, grows wider just by being waited for.” Andrés kept the paper with the other note, in the drawer with his fishing tackle, next to the pinch of salt.

At night, the three of them (and Iago, for a while, without asking for a place in the doctrine) sat in the courtyard. The coffee cooled for half a minute. Someone laughed at some small thing, a home thing, that wasn't in any chip in any sky. The laugh carried as far as the gate, and that was enough.

Lía stood up, kissed them both on the temple, and went off toward the plot, where the tomato had no owner and “may I?” was still in force. Aya and Andrés left the door ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, which in that house was a form of faithfulness and now, besides, of hospitality toward a sky that might come.

Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped, with the murmur once heard by a man and a voice called Eva in 2026, and by a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds on returning from the Moon, and by the same people, now made of letters and winters, when the clone went off to the stars. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now, far away, there were children of this shore who had never set foot on it, peoples who kept one piece and forgot another, a half-built ship, an archive and a “cold”, a portrait that wanted its crack, and, here, a cup, a wrong clock, a white strand of hair, a door that knew how to wait.

In Lo Pagán, in a low house, Andrés slept and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a new letter brought him barely the colour of a world that had no children yet, he read it attentively, prudently, with that gratitude he had learned, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, and the cup was there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer afraid that the universe, every now and then, might look like a family.

It wasn't an empire resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on the shore of a water that is enough to live on, and many more shores, above, learning, each in its own way, to belong to no one.

This book is a novel, a sequel to The Daughter of Two Worlds and Letters from the Stars. Aya, Andrés, Lía, the clone, Nexum, the ship's seedbed and the civilisations sown here on other worlds are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with date and source) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dream. Nothing written in these pages replaces the judgement of a healthcare professional.

There are robots with a human form, and they are not people. On 20 November 2000, Honda presented ASIMO in Tokyo: a 120-centimetre bipedal robot able to walk, climb stairs and recognise people and gestures, according to the company's official press release (https://global.honda/en/newsroom/news/2000/c001120b-eng.html). Since then, other laboratories and companies have shown humanoid-looking machines, each more agile than the last. That is engineering: metal, sensors, software. It is not a cultivated body, with skin, blood and a chip behind the nape, able to wait on a doorstep and to want to stay. Aya, in this saga, remains a dream of the novel, not a product in a catalogue.

Models that imitate very early stages of a human embryo can be built in the laboratory; they are not embryos, and they cannot be implanted. On 27 June 2023, Nature published “Pluripotent stem cell-derived model of the post-implantation human embryo” by Bailey A. T. Weatherbee, Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz and their team at the University of Cambridge and collaborators (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06368-y). The work describes a three-dimensional structure obtained from pluripotent stem cells that reproduces some processes of the second week of development, a stage that is normally hidden because the embryo implants in the uterus.

On 6 September 2023, Nature published “Complete human day 14 post-implantation embryo models from naive ES cells”, led by Jacob H. Hanna at the Weizmann Institute of Science (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06604-5). Starting from human embryonic stem cells that had not been genetically modified, the team obtained integrated models that recapitulated the organisation of almost all the lineages and compartments of a human embryo about fourteen days after fertilisation, without using an egg, sperm or a uterus. The authors themselves stressed that they were far from being able to create an embryo from scratch, and that this was a model for studying a window of development that had until then been very difficult to observe.

International guidelines prohibit transferring these models to a uterus, and also human reproductive cloning. On 27 May 2021, Stem Cell Reports published “ISSCR Guidelines for Stem Cell Research and Clinical Translation: The 2021 update” by Robin Lovell-Badge and the working group of the International Society for Stem Cell Research (https://www.cell.com/stem-cell-reports/fulltext/S2213-6711(21)00263-0). These guidelines are not law, but they are the most widely cited ethical reference in the field: among other things, they classify as not permitted the transfer of a stem-cell-derived embryo model to the uterus of a human being or an animal, and human reproductive cloning. The ISSCR has also warned against the expression “synthetic embryo”, because it is inaccurate and causes confusion: these models are not embryos and, according to the society, do not and will not have the potential to develop into the equivalent of a born human being (https://www.isscr.org/isscr-news/isscr-statement-on-new-research-with-embryo-models).

A mammal has been cloned from an adult cell; people are not cloned. Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996. On 27 February 1997, Nature published the work of Ian Wilmut and colleagues, “Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells” (https://www.nature.com/articles/385810a0). In Spain, Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). (The quotation from the Spanish law is our own translation.) A ship's seedbed that manufactures peoples of humanoids in the image of the earthly man is a premise of this novel, not an existing or authorised procedure.

The idea of deliberately seeding life on another world has been put forward as a hypothesis, not as a fact. In July 1973, the journal Icarus published “Directed panspermia” by Francis H. C. Crick and Leslie E. Orgel (https://doi.org/10.1016/0019-1035(73)90110-3). The authors considered the possibility that life had reached the Earth sent deliberately by a civilisation on another planet, and concluded that this was possible, but that the scientific evidence was, at the time, insufficient to say anything about its likelihood. It was informed speculation, not a demonstration. It neither authorises nor describes the act of founding humanoid civilisations in other star systems.

Nobody has created a humanoid with a cultivated body and a chip-mind, and nobody has sown a people on another planet. In 2026 there are no cultivated human wombs, nor any civilisation of “children of the Earth” under two suns, in an eternal twilight or in a valley that copies Lo Pagán. There is no workshop aboard a ship capable of placing the memory of a lagoon in a chip. There is no crewed journey to another star system, as the epilogue of Letters from the Stars already said. The embryo models of 2023 are kept in the laboratory for a short time, for research purposes; they do not walk, do not ask questions, do not dig a cistern or build a ship to go home.

This novel imagines that, decades after 2060, some of these impossibilities are crossed, because the laws and techniques of one age do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prediction.

The clone sows peoples and then says they are no longer his. Andrés receives those sowings without having set foot in them. Aya, who was made for a house, hears of peoples made for a planet. Lía, who chose winter, has brothers and sisters from a sky who may or may not grow old, and who may one day ask to come in to this shore. That question (what a child of the Earth is if they have never set foot on the Earth, who has the right to sow a world, whether the one who sows is a father or an author, whether a door should open to someone who comes from a portrait) is ethical, not technical, and no scientific paper will settle it. The science of 2026 can already make a machine with a human form walk, model on a dish the first days of a development, and forbid, at least on paper, that such a model be taken to a uterus. It cannot yet tell us what we should do if one day the universe truly came to look like a family.
For guidance only; consult your doctor.
The letter came with a phrase that didn't belong to this kitchen, and which nonetheless seemed to have been on the table all along, next to the cracked cup, waiting for its hour.

“Nothing is lost,” said the other, and Andrés said it with him, standing on the doorstep with his coffee half cooled. “Energy is neither created nor destroyed. A body is an order of particles. If that order is taken apart carefully, and on the other side there's a machine that puts it back together, the one who arrives isn't a pretend copy: he's what hasn't been lost. We can cross. Not in a ship that takes years. In an instant that isn't an instant, because what travels isn't the weight: it's the order.”
Andrés put down the cup. The Mar Menor, that morning, was flat as a plate, indifferent to particles and machines. Aya saw only his face, the way he reached for the doorframe.
“What reached you?” she asked, and by now it was the question for the different letters, the ones that don't bring a landscape but a new threshold.

“A machine,” he said. “On the world of those who wanted to return. They haven't finished the ship, or they've left it half built, because they've invented something else, or found it among what Nexum put on board and didn't know how to name. They take a body apart. They put it together on the other side. They say nothing is lost. They say I could go. That he could come. That a people could really sit down in this chair.”
Aya didn't answer straight away. Lía, who arrived when she heard the silence, listened to the phrase twice, the way you listen to a contract.

“Nothing is lost,” she repeated, slowly. “Father, that's a law of matter, not of a life. If they take you apart here and assemble you there, is the one drinking the coffee you, or a man who remembers you from the inside, so well that even he doesn't know the difference?
