On the night of the ship I asked you who my father was, if there were two of you and you remembered the same storm. Now the question grows: if one of the two is taken apart and put together again, is he still the one from the storm, or the one from afterwards?”
Andrés passed a hand over his face, this one, the one that had never crossed anywhere, except in the letters.

“He says the original doesn't remain. It isn't one more clone. It isn't a valley of the same face. It's a transfer: what's here stops being here, and is there. Nothing is lost, and nobody is doubled. That, at least, isn't the chorus or the portrait.”

“That's a death with an arrival,” said Lía, without cruelty, with the exactness MAY would have approved as a fact, not a judgment. “Or it's a journey. Depending on where you look at it from. I won't call it a miracle until someone crosses and someone here can ask them whether the hollow left by what they were hurts.”
In Aya's chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate. Eva asked, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:
If nothing is lost, what is it that's interrupted? The weight, the order, or the while in which you stand in a doorway and haven't yet passed through?
MAY, adding no opinion, left the fact:

There is a machine that takes a body apart and another that puts it together on the other side. It is claimed that the original does not remain. It is claimed that one can cross between worlds. That is what the letter announces.
Aya laid her palm on Andrés's chest, where his heart, eternal now, was still a heart.

“I don't receive the letters,” she said. “If you're taken apart, what do I receive: a silence, or a man who comes back and says he's the same? I don't know whether I'll be able to open the door the same way. I'll learn, if I have to. But don't ask me to call it a journey, from the outset, when it switches this kitchen off, even for a second.”

“I'm not crossing today,” he said. “Today only the phrase has reached me. And the phrase already fills the house. Nothing is lost. I, who have received lives without living them, could now live on a ground I've only drunk. That tempts me. It frightens me too. In the end, the other one asked whether he could come first, whether we'd make room for him in the courtyard.”
Lía looked at the Mar Menor, the real one, the one that gets dirty, the one that isn't a pond.

“If he comes, let him come the way you ask to come in, not as a right of particles,” she said. “And let him be asked questions. I'll ask him whether, as he was taken apart, he felt he was coming to an end, and whether, as he was put together, he felt he was being born. Depending on his answer, we'll know whether this phrase widens our shore or replaces it.”

Andrés nodded. He stayed a while longer on the doorstep, his coffee now completely cold, looking at a sky that no longer only wrote and perhaps no longer only sent ships: now it promised a body undone and a body made, and the name of both would be the same, or not. The murmur of the water didn't change. It had no reason to. What was going to change, however, was the idea of what staying means, if staying could also be a way of coming apart in order, and of becoming, on the other side, a door again.
In the afternoon Helena Valls called, slower than ever, as if the stairs had reached her voice too. It wasn't an offer from the board: it was a warning.

“Nexum has heard,” she said. “There are people who want to put the receiving machine in Madrid, under protocol, and people who want to put it ‘close to the origin’, which is their way of saying Lo Pagán. I won't sign off on planting it in your courtyard. Nor can I swear that a van won't turn up with a device and a smile. They like the phrase ‘nothing is lost’: it sounds like science and it sounds like comfort. Beware of phrases a company likes.”
Andrés thanked her for the stairs, once again, and hung up. Then he told Aya and Lía, in the kitchen, beside the clock that ran two minutes slow.
“If they bring it here, it won't be because we asked for it,” he said. “If we bring it ourselves, it'll be because we've asked enough questions.”
Lía nodded, and set an ordinary tomato on the table, the kind that ripen or don't, like a faithful weight, older than any machine.

“Let it stay here for now,” she said. “So the phrase doesn't eat our tea. Nothing is lost, Father. Fine. Then this cup isn't lost either, nor this slowness, nor this fruit. If the machine can't bring them back dirty, it isn't this shore it's putting together. It's a portrait, again.”

Andrés cut the tomato and shared it. It tasted of earth, of the sun of a single sky, of a life that had not yet been taken apart. On some world of tablelands a machine was waiting, and a young man with his very memory was preparing, perhaps, to stop being there in order to begin being here. And in Lo Pagán, that night, the door was left ajar, not yet out of hospitality toward a body of particles, but out of habit, which is an older way of not getting lost.

They saw it first in a letter. Then in a hangar of pale stone, the same one where a woman had promised to accept the no of a quayside. Andrés, mending the net, felt the apparatus the way you feel a new engine: not entirely hostile, not entirely of home. It was tall, made of a matt metal, with two arches that weren't a door and looked like one. On the floor, a circle. In the air, a smell of filters and of a dry storm, like Selene Norte, like the seedbed's workshop.

The clone was there, and the woman from the hangar, and some of her people, and a technician who wasn't from Nexum or had stopped being so. On a table, a cup. Not the cracked one from Lo Pagán: an ordinary earthenware cup, already with a hairline crack, honest.

“This first,” said the one who searches, and Andrés heard it with his fingers on the rope. “If the cup arrives and it's this cup, we'll talk about a body. If a different one arrives, we go home and leave the phrase to the brochures.”

The cup was placed in the circle. The machine didn't roar. It made, barely, a denser silence. The earthenware ceased to be there. No visible dust remained in the air: what remained, the technician said afterwards, was a record, an order, a weight that hadn't evaporated but had been named. Nothing is lost, they kept saying. Andrés, in the courtyard, felt the emptiness on that table the way you probe with your tongue for a tooth that's no longer there.

On the other side (in a second machine, a twin, installed not in Madrid but, against Helena's wishes and not entirely against Andrés's, in a discreet warehouse near El Estacio, brought in at night, with no pearl-grey van at the door of the house) the cup was put together. Lía was a witness. So was Aya. The earthenware was there. So was the hairline crack. The weight was the same, or so close that a kitchen scale could find nothing missing. Lía didn't touch it straight away. She looked at it the way you look at a fruit that might come from a portrait.
“May I?” she asked, out of habit, and nobody understood whether she was asking the cup or them. She picked it up. It was cold. To the finger, it was made of earthenware. Not of an idea.
“It's the same one,” said Aya, and in her voice there was wonder and a reservation. “Or it's so much the same one that this house has no instrument for saying it isn't.”
Lía took it to the kitchen in Lo Pagán and put it beside the cracked one, and the two looked like sisters: one had crossed a sky, the other had never left the sink.

That afternoon the technician, through the bridge and on a screen, explained what he could explain without turning it into a miracle: that a body, or a cup, can be described as an order; that this order can, if the machine gets it right, be taken apart and assembled; that energy is neither created nor destroyed, it only changes shape; that the original, here, doesn't remain, because if it did there would be two, and the machine, because of a limitation the technician called “one of principle”, doesn't duplicate. It either assembles or it doesn't. It doesn't copy.
Andrés kept that limitation the way you keep a mooring line: it doesn't duplicate. So it wasn't the valley of the same face. So it was something else, graver and cleaner.

“If I crossed,” he said on the doorstep that night, “this body would stop being in this chair. You, Aya, would be left for a while with an empty chair. Then, if the other machine got it right, I'd be in a hangar, or he'd be here, and this chair would have a weight in it again. Would you wait for me in the emptiness?”
Aya thought about it, which was her way of not filling with words what had no name yet.

“I'd wait for you the way I waited for the boat in the levante,” she said. “Without notifying Madrid. With the coffee made again. But don't ask me not to feel, during that while, that you've come to an end. Even if the phrase says nothing is lost. In this house, a while of absence is also something that exists.”
Lía set the cup that had crossed on the table, not as an altar but as a piece of evidence.

“A cup doesn't ask whether it's the same,” she said. “A man does. When we send someone across, I'll be beside the machine here, and I'll ask. If the machine doesn't allow questions, it isn't a shore: it's an appliance. And appliances, as we know, want an owner.”

If a cup arrives with its crack, has the crack travelled, or has it been written again? And if one day a man arrives with his memory, who can sign to say that the memory hasn't been written again as well?
MAY, beside her, the fact:

A cup has been taken apart in a hangar and put together near El Estacio. The original has not remained on the table over there. The weight and the crack match. It is claimed that the machine does not duplicate. That is the fact.

Before sleeping, Andrés touched both cups, the one that had crossed and the one that hadn't. Both sounded like earthenware. One, however, left on his finger a warehouse coldness, a not-having-always-been-here. It wasn't proof of falseness. It was proof of a journey. And he, who had received worlds without setting foot on them, understood that this phrase, “nothing is lost”, was very soon going to ask of him something the letters never asked: his whole body, the body of this shore, placed in a circle, and the faith, or the doubt, that what is put back together on the other side still truly tastes of coffee.

In the morning, Lía took the cup that had crossed to the plot, filled it with tap water, Lo Pagán water, and left it in the sun, like a windowsill. Not to see whether it would ripen, since a cup doesn't ripen, but to see whether this shore's day would recognise it. A humanoid from the gardens glanced at it sideways and didn't ask: in 2060, and in the years after, people had seen everything, except this. Lía told it, all the same, the minimal truth:
“It came from a sky. It's still a cup. If one day people come, I'll offer them water in it, if they ask for it. Not before.”

Iago, who had heard the end of it, shook his head, not entirely convinced, not entirely against. He sat down and asked for neither eternity nor transfer. He asked only to be told if the machine came any closer to the house, so he wouldn't trip over it when he brought the figs. It was the request of a man of the soil, and Lía kept it the way you keep a good knot.
Andrés, as he went out to fish, left the cup that had crossed where it was, in the kitchen, and the usual cup too. Two shores, now, in a single sink. The Mar Menor was still. He was not, entirely.
It wasn't Andrés. It wasn't the clone. It was the woman from the hangar, the one who had said she would accept the no of a quayside, and who now had, instead of a quayside, a circle of metal.

Among her people she was called Nuria, an Earth name the seedbed had left them among others, which she had chosen without knowing that in Lo Pagán there had also been Nurias, in other centuries, beside this same water. She asked to cross. She asked standing up, without kneeling, faithful to the lesson of not turning the founder into an altar.

“I want to drink the plate,” she said. “If they send me back afterwards, I'll come back. If the water doesn't taste of what they put in my chip, I'll say so too. I'm not coming as an owner. I'm coming as someone checking a memory.”

Andrés, Aya and Lía waited in the warehouse at El Estacio, not in the kitchen: the house was not yet a car park for miracles. Helena had prevented the van at the door; she hadn't entirely prevented the machine, which was already there, discreet and enormous, breathing its dense silence. Lía stood beside the circle, her wrist awake, not to amend anything but to look, if she was asked.

The technician gave a signal. In the hangar, far away, Nuria stepped into the arch. Andrés, through the bridge, felt an instant of dissolving, not his own, borrowed: a cold, a brief disorder, the certainty that the body was ceasing to be a place. Then nothing. The bridge, with her, was cut. The original did not remain.

The time of the assembling was a while that felt to Aya like a levante: the coffee, had she had it to hand, would have been made again twice. Then, in the circle here, there was a weight. There was a woman. She had the fine scar beneath her nape, her eyes open, her mouth tense. She didn't scream. The first thing she asked for was air, and the air of this shore, which is neither quite sea nor quite land, entered her chest like a piece of news.
“Nuria,” she said, and the voice was a voice, not an appliance's echo. “I've crossed. Is this the water?”

They took her to the promenade, slowly, the way you take someone who has just been born and is already an adult. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was a little dirty in one corner, beautiful everywhere else, with a crooked buoy. Nuria crouched, wet her fingers, raised them to her mouth. She cried, without theatre. Then she laughed, a laugh of confirmation.
“It tastes of salt, and of something the chip didn't quite know,” she said. “The chip was cleaner. This is better. This is alive.”

Andrés, beside her, felt relief and a clean envy: she had set foot on what he had only drunk in letters, and she had done so being, or believing herself to be, the same woman who had been taken apart in a hangar.
“Does it hurt?” asked Lía.

“The hollow hurts,” said Nuria. “An instant when you don't belong anywhere. Afterwards you belong here. I remember the hangar, the half-built ship, the phrase, my name. I can't swear to you that the hollow hasn't taken something from me that I didn't know how to name. I can swear to you that I want a glass of this water, and that I'll ask your permission to drink it.”

They gave it to her in the cup that had crossed, which at last had a purpose. Aya, who had neither crossed nor received letters, watched her with a threshold attentiveness: another woman come from a workshop, not identical to her, and yet a sister of an origin.

“Welcome,” said Aya, and the word came out the way it had come out of Helena, years before, on the Moon, against part of her will. “This house isn't a company quayside. If you stay a while, I'll make you coffee. If you want to leave, the machine, they say, works in reverse too, when there's another one on the other side.”

Nuria nodded. She didn't stay to live. She stayed three days, slept in the room by the plot, walked El Estacio and El Carmolí, saw the gardens without owners, saw Vicente's door and didn't open it, because Lía told her who he had been, and a shut door, on this shore, was a fidelity. On the fourth day she asked to go back, to tell her people, and so that the hangar wouldn't be left with an absence and no story.

Before she stepped into the circle, Lía took her hand, with permission, and looked inside, not to amend. She saw a humanoid text, a chip, a memory of tablelands and, now, a new, salty layer from this plate. Her father's harbour wasn't there in her: she didn't receive letters; she had come in body.
“You're still you, as far as I can see,” said Lía. “What I can't see, you tell me, if one day you find it missing.”

“I'll tell you,” promised Nuria, and she was taken apart, and the warehouse once again had an empty chair, and the hangar, after a while, a weight called Nuria whose first request was to tell them about the taste.
When the clone's letter confirmed her arrival, Andrés sat down on the doorstep and Aya made him his coffee, cooled for half a minute.

“One has crossed and come back,” he said. “The water tasted of more than the chip to her. She talked about the hollow. If I cross, I'll have that hollow, and you'll have that empty chair. I still don't know whether I dare.”
“You don't dare today. Today we've welcomed a woman and said goodbye to her. That's enough for one week.”

If a woman is taken apart and put together and asks for water, who did the asking: the one from there, the one from here, or the one from the hollow, who belongs nowhere? And if the water tastes of more than the memory, isn't that proof of a journey, or proof that the memory was less than the world?
A woman called Nuria has crossed from the hangar to El Estacio and gone back. She has drunk the Mar Menor. She has spoken of a hollow. She slept three nights at the plot. That is the fact.

Lía, at the plot, washed the cup that had crossed and left it on the windowsill, empty, in the sun. It wasn't an altar. It was a tool that had already served a mouth. And tools, on this shore, are washed and offered again, if someone, once again, asks.

The clone didn't cross straight away. First he wrote a long letter, one of those that bring not a ground but an explanation, and Andrés received it in the boat, with the engine off in the middle of the plate.

I don't want you to call it a miracle, the other wrote, and Andrés thought it with him. I want you to know what is taken apart. A body is an order: not only flesh, but also the way the particles were arranged, the heat, the scar, the salt on the skin, the memory, if memory is also an order. The machine doesn't send the weight the way you send a bundle. It names the order, and in naming it, undoes it. On the other side, another machine hears the name and puts each thing back in its place, or in a place so similar that a man can walk and ask for water. The original doesn't remain, because the name can't be spoken twice at once: if it remained, there would be two orders, and that, they say, the machine won't allow. Nothing is lost: the energy continues, the order travels. What is interrupted, though, is the while of being a place.
Andrés looked at the water, which was a place, and imagined himself not being one. It gave him a cold that wasn't from the levante.
That night he told Aya and Lía, word for word, or as many words as he could bring back without them turning into a brochure. Lía listened with his own eyes, patient, and didn't soften the phrase.

“So when you cross, you stop being a place,” she said. “There's a while, Nuria's hollow, when you're neither in the hangar nor at El Estacio. The energy, all right, hasn't been lost. And you? Are you energy, Father, or are you the while? I come to an end, and my coming to an end is a while that closes. This machine closes one while and opens another, and says it's the same because the order matches. I'm not sure an order is a father.”
Andrés wasn't offended. He sat down on the rush-seat chair, the usual one, and felt its arms, the old rope, the wood.

“When I receive a letter, I'm still a place, and a world reaches me,” he said. “Now they're asking me to stop being a place in order to be a world. It's the other way round. It makes me dizzy. It also gives me, I won't deny it, an old longing: to see with these feet what I've drunk with my memory. To see it with him. For the two of us to sit down, not facing the sea at a departure, but in this kitchen, after one of us has been undone and made again.”
Aya, who was a cultivated body and a chip, and who knew what it is to be an order placed in a house, spoke quietly:

“I was manufactured once. I wasn't taken apart afterwards to be given a courtyard. They brought me whole, in a van, and the courtyard gradually made me. If they take you apart, even if they put you together well, I'll have a while of courtyard without you. That while doesn't travel. That while stays here, with me, and I don't know under what principle it's conserved. Nowhere, perhaps. In me.”
In the chip, Eva asked, and Aya said it aloud, so it would be on record in the kitchen:

If what travels is an order and what stays is a while, which is more of a life: the order that can be named, or the while that doesn't travel? And if nothing is lost, where is the fear kept of the woman who waits beside the empty chair?

The one who searches has described a transfer of order, not of a bundle. The original does not remain. There is an interval in which the body is not a place. Nuria called it a hollow. That is the fact.

The next day Andrés went to see the machine at El Estacio, alone, without crossing. He stood in front of the circle, the way you stand in front of a sea that isn't yours. The technician, discreet, didn't push him. He showed him, on a screen, the record of the cup and of Nuria, some curves that told Andrés as little as a company report and, at the same time, too much: there, reduced to a name, was the order of a woman who had cried when she tasted the salt.
“If I went in,” he asked, “who can assure me that what comes out on the other side still loves this cup, and not another, smoother one?”
The technician, honest or tired, shrugged.

“Nobody can fully assure you. So far the machine gets right what we measure. What we don't measure (the loving, the fear, the way of saying a daughter's name) doesn't show up in the curve. It shows up, if it does, in the mouth of the one who arrives, when you ask them.”

Andrés walked home along the promenade, like Raúl on the day he came down for the first time in years. The water was copper-coloured. He told himself, not through the bridge but to himself, that he wouldn't go in yet. That if anyone crossed toward here, he would let it be the other one, the one who had already left once, the one who knew how to leave. He knew how to stay. Staying, now, also meant not stepping into a circle.
Lía was waiting for him on the doorstep, the slow clock behind her, and didn't ask him for a hero's decision.

“It's all right not to go in today,” she said. “A phrase doesn't deserve a whole father in the first month. Let the machine work, if it works, with those who ask. For now, you be a place. I need a place. So does Mother.”

He nodded, and at night he dreamed of a circle that was a plate, and of himself, dismantled, turned into water, and the Mar Menor receiving him without questions. He woke with dry sheets and Aya's hand on his side, real, present, not named in any curve. He lay very still, being a place, and that stillness seemed to him, that night, the most exact way of not getting lost, even though the phrase, in the hangar and in the warehouse, still said that nothing, ever, is lost.

The clone asked to come. He asked as Nuria had: standing, without an altar, accepting the no if the no came. Andrés didn't refuse him. Lía set only one condition: she would be beside the circle, and she would ask him the question before anyone embraced him, so that the embrace wouldn't sign in advance what still had to be known.

Aya made the coffee, two cups, the cracked one and the one that had crossed, and let them cool for half a minute, and warmed them again, because the time of the assembling won't be ruled by a clock, not even by the one that ran two minutes slow.

The hangar, far away, fell into a dense silence. Andrés, in the warehouse at El Estacio, felt through the bridge the beginning of the hollow (the dissolving, the cold) and then the bridge was cut, as it had been cut with Nuria. For the first time since the ship had left, the sky stopped writing. The chair on the shore, and the chair of the one who searches, were left at the mercy of a name that travelled without being a place.
To Aya, the while felt longer than the levante. She didn't notify Madrid. She looked at the circle. Lía, motionless, had her wrist alight, and not in order to heal.

Then there was a weight. There was a young man, strong, with Andrés's face from another time, rope-worker's hands that work had not yet marked, dark and patient eyes. He breathed. He asked for air, like Nuria. He saw Lía first, and Aya, and the Andrés of the shore, older in his features, halted at the age Lía had closed for him, and he said neither “father” nor “son”. He said, in a voice that was this house's voice and wasn't:
“I've crossed. Am I still me?”
Lía didn't embrace him yet.
“If you both remember the same storm, which of you is my father?”
The young man smiled, and the one from the shore smiled with him, and the coincidence hurt them and was enough for them.

“Both of us,” said the one who had just been put together, just as on the night of the ship. “One to stay and one to search. I've searched, and now I've come. The hollow exists. I'm telling you because you asked her, Nuria, and it was true. An instant when I belonged nowhere. Then I saw you, and I knew the name of this light, and your mother's name, and his. If I'm missing something I can't name, you'll tell me, if you see it.”

Then Lía took his hand, with permission, and looked inside. She saw the text of a cloned body, an artificial brain, the memories of the shore and of the worlds, the sowings, the letters, and a new layer, the layer of the hollow, brief and dark, like a silence between two sentences. She didn't amend it. She let go of his hand and, at last, embraced him, and then embraced the one from the shore, and the two smells mingled for her: the salt of home and the smell of newly ordered metal.

Aya came closer more slowly. She touched the face of the one who had arrived with a threshold attentiveness, the same with which she had once measured three tenths of a second before a boat growing smaller.

“You're you, and you're not the one from this chair,” she said. “I waited for you at a departure. Now I'm waiting for you at an arrival. There's coffee. It's in both cups. Choose, or don't choose, and sit down.”

Later they sat, not in the warehouse but in the courtyard in Lo Pagán, the four of them, plus Iago for a while, who brought figs and asked for no doctrine. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate. The one who had crossed looked at it the way you look at a relative you owe a visit to, not at a portrait. He said the water, seen like this, was smaller than in memory and more sufficient. Andrés, the one from the shore, laughed quietly, because that was what he had felt with the other sea: what is your own, in the end, fits in a glass, and is enough.

They talked little about the machines. They talked about the garden, the white strand of hair, Vicente, a Nuria who had gone back to her hangar with a taste in her mouth. The one who searches didn't stay to live. He couldn't: his trade was searching, and this shore, though it called him, was no longer his only place. He stayed, like Nuria, a few days. He slept in the room that had been Lía's as a girl, or on a blanket in the courtyard, when the air allowed. In the mornings the two Andréses went out, not always together: one to the boat, the other to walk the promenade, and the people, who had already seen everything, still paused a little on seeing them, the way you pause before a mirror that walks.
One afternoon, facing the water, the one from the shore asked the one who had crossed:
“Are you the same one who left in the ship?”

“I'm the one who remembers leaving, and the one who remembers a hollow, and the one who's here. If that's the same, then yes. If being the same requires never having been interrupted, I don't know. Lía is right: an order can be exact and, even so, there can have been a while when there was nobody. I'm not asking you to settle it. I'm asking you to let me go back to searching, and to come back, sometimes, through this circle, if you keep a coffee for me.”
“We'll keep it for you,” said Andrés.

Aya, from the doorstep, watched the two of them, and didn't have to choose which was the man of the house. That week, the house stretched to two weights, two voices, a single afternoon snack. In the chip, Eva asked, softly:

If two men remember the same storm and one has passed through a hollow, is the storm still one, or are there two now, with a silence between them? And if the daughter embraces them both, isn't that an answer, or is it only a while, which doesn't travel?

The one who searches was taken apart in a hangar and put together at El Estacio. He asked for air. He answered “both of us”. He slept on this shore for a few days. The bridge of the letters was cut during the hollow and afterwards wasn't needed, because both were in the same courtyard. That is the fact.

When the one who searches stepped into the circle again, to leave once more for a world that didn't yet have a name, Andrés didn't hold him back. They stood for a second with their foreheads almost touching, and Lía said the three names, the mooring: Andrés, Andrés, Lía. Aya added her own, so that the edge would stay where it belonged. Then a dense silence, a lighter chair, and, after a while, a short letter from a hangar: “I've arrived. I'm still, if I am, the one who searches. Keep my coffee for me.”

They kept it. That night the one from the shore slept on his own ground, with Aya beside him, and dreamed not of the valley of faces but of a courtyard with two cups and still water, and that, after a reunion, was a way of not getting lost, and also of letting go.

They offered her the circle. They offered it carefully, not the way you offer a product but the way you offer a coffee: in case she wanted it, not because she ought to. The one who searches, in a letter after the reunion, and Nuria, in a message, and the technician, with a warehouse honesty, told her that the machine didn't distinguish a cultivated body from a born one, or not much: an order was an order, the chip was an order too, and it could, in principle, be taken apart and put together. Aya could see a world, not in Andrés's telling, not in a curve, but with these eyes, these feet, this doorstep carried to another shore.
Aya listened, sitting on the rush-seat chair, and didn't say no straight away, because a no, to be a real no, needs its while.

Andrés didn't push her. He had learned, through the letters, what it is to receive a world without setting foot on it, and he wasn't going to ask her to set foot on one by way of compensation. Nor did Lía. She only told her, gently:
“If you cross, I'll be at the circle here, with the question. If you don't cross, I'll be there too, at this door, which is yours. Both things are a life.”

Aya kept the offer for three days, the way you keep a key you haven't used yet. She walked the promenade, touched the cracked cup, the one that had crossed, the doorframe, the fine scar on her own nape. In the chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate her step.

If you cross, who waits on this doorstep? If you don't, are you less, or are you precisely the one who gives the journey a shore? Is love seeing the same world, or staying when the other can leave and come back?
She has been offered the circle. She has not yet stepped in. That is the fact, so far.
On the fourth day, Aya called the technician and her family together in the kitchen, not in the warehouse, because the decisions of this house are made beside the wrong clock.

“I'm not crossing,” she said, with the gentleness that admits no negotiation, the gentleness of the Moon, of the bridge she hadn't wanted opened either. “I learned to wait at this door. If I'm taken apart, even if they put me together well, this door has a while without me, and that while doesn't travel: it stays in Andrés, in Lía, in the cup, and I don't want to leave them a hollow in order to bring myself a landscape. I've been made once. I don't ask to be undone in order to see myself complete. The worlds will reach me, if they do, in you, when you come back and tell me about them. That's enough for me. It isn't less. It's my trade.”
Andrés came over and rested his forehead against hers, as after so many letters.
“Thank you,” he said, and it wasn't a small phrase. “If I ever cross, I want a door that hasn't gone anywhere. You're that door.”
Lía smiled, her white strand in the sun from the window.
“The machine doesn't take everything that matters,” she said. “It takes an order, if it gets it right. It doesn't take the while of the woman who waits. Mother has named it. Let it be on record.”

Nexum, when it found out, or when it imagined it, sent a short note, not from Helena this time but in a tone more like a brochure: “The original unit, were she to cross, would be a milestone.” Aya read the word “unit” and didn't answer. She had already answered, years ago, with a baby at her breast. She wasn't going to become a circle's milestone.
Helena did call, later, herself, and said only:
“I'm glad you didn't step in for their sake. The stairs, as you know, I haven't traded for a machine either. Some transfers aren't a favour.”

Aya wished her well with the stairs. Then, that afternoon, when Andrés went out in the boat, she stayed on the doorstep, as in 2060, and out of habit measured the while until the boat grew small. It wasn't three tenths of a second. It was minutes of a sun that does move. She looked away when she wanted to, not when a protocol asked her to, and went in to warm the coffee, so that on his return it would be there, cooled for half a minute, faithful.

At night she asked Andrés that, if he ever crossed, he not bring her back a polished portrait: that he bring her the dirt, the seaweed, the fear of the hollow, the name of whatever he hadn't understood.
“That's what I can receive,” she said. “Not the whole world. The return. We agreed that with the letters. Now, with bodies, the same.”
He promised. In the chip, Eva left a last question that night, without demanding an answer:
If a woman doesn't cross, and that's why there's a shore, who should thank her: the one who leaves, the one who arrives, or the door itself, which is not an appliance?
MAY, the fact, beside it, like a glass:
Aya has not stepped into the circle. She has refused it. The trade she has named is waiting at this door. That is the fact.

Aya, already in bed, looked at the ceiling, at the damp stain shaped like an island, and smiled, almost to herself. That stain would never travel. That was why, and not in spite of it, it was hers. And this house, with a machine near El Estacio and a hangar in a sky, still needed, more than ever, someone who wouldn't be taken apart, so that those who were would have, on their return, a place where the coffee goes cold if they're late, and nobody calls it a flaw, but home.

The next morning Nuria sent through the machine not her body but a short message on a sheet of paper, which the technician passed on to them: “I'm glad there's a door that didn't cross. That way the water I drank still has a mistress of the threshold, even though the water has no owner.” Aya put the sheet in the drawer with the fishing tackle, beside Helena's notes and the pinch of salt, which by now was an archive of what does not come apart.
Lía, watching her put it away, said:
“That drawer is a shore too. We're not going to put it in the circle, are we?”
“No,” said Aya, and laughed, a little, truly. “The drawer stays. So do I. Let the universe, if it wants, come round for tea.”
Lía took longer than Nuria and longer than the clone to decide whether to step in. Not from fear of the hollow, or not only that. Because of winter.

If the machine takes an order apart and puts it back together, what does it do with a white strand of hair, with a good tiredness, with the years she had chosen not to amend? The portrait of Lo Pagán had wanted to set the clock right. The tomato that stops you ending, she had refused so many times. A circle that “improves” as it assembles would be another patent, cleaner, harder to refuse: the patent of the faithful transfer, which in its faithfulness takes your winter away without asking.
She said so to the technician, in the warehouse, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and with Iago at the door, not quite coming in and yet present.

“If I cross, I want to arrive the way I leave,” she said. “With this strand, with this tiredness, with the date I already carry. If your machine takes it from me, even out of courtesy to the order, it isn't a journey: it's a correction. I don't correct what isn't a cut. Can you swear to it?”
The technician didn't swear lightly. He went over curves, spoke to the hangar, came back in the afternoon.

“We can ask it not to ‘optimise’,” he said. “To copy the order, not the ideal of the order. So far, the cup arrived with its crack and Nuria with her hangar tiredness. We haven't taken years from anyone, because we didn't know how, or because we didn't want to. With you, if you step in, we'll put it in writing: no improvement. Even so, the oath isn't absolute. What we don't measure could change. You'll know when you arrive, if you arrive, and when you come back, if you come back.”
Lía nodded, not entirely calm, entirely adult.

“Then I'll cross once,” she said. “To see the people of winter, the ones in the mountains, the ones who asked me whether I regretted it. I want to tell them standing up, on their hillside, not through a message. And I want to come back, the same day if possible, to this plot. Father, Mother: if, when I come back, I look too smooth to you, tell me. Even if it hurts.”

Andrés didn't object. Aya squeezed her hand and didn't cross with her, faithful to her trade. Iago asked her to bring him, if there was one, a stone from that hillside, not a fruit that stops you ending. She smiled and promised the stone.

When the hollow came, Andrés barely felt it, from afar, not as when the clone had been cut from the bridge: Lía wasn't on the bridge, Lía was in a circle, and her father had only the while of an empty chair, in the warehouse, and his eternal heart beating too loudly. Aya didn't notify Madrid. She counted the minutes under her breath, minutes the kitchen clock couldn't count from there.

Lía was put together at the foot of the mountains, where autumn was copper and there was a grave with a date. She asked for air. The first thing she did was touch the strand, and the strand was there. She laughed, or cried, or both. The people of winter recognised her, not because of an altar but because of the message that had travelled before her: the one at the plot, the one who comes to an end. The woman with the bent back (more bent still) looked her up and down, and nodded, and touched her white hair, with permission.
“Still keeping to it,” she said, and it wasn't a reproach. “Then we didn't come here for nothing.”

They talked on the hillside, not for long, long enough. Lía repeated what she had already sent them: that she didn't regret it every day, that winter wasn't a virtue, that if they changed their minds she wouldn't call them traitors. They showed her the grave, and a child who now raised his face to the sky with less guilt, and a fire, and a soup. She didn't offer them a tomato that stops you ending. She offered them, if one day they crossed to Lo Pagán, a coffee and a question, and the no, if need be, said without contempt.

She came back at sunset here, the same day, as she had promised. The circle at El Estacio held a weight, a strand of white, a tiredness of travel and of copper. Lía asked for air, looked for Iago, for Aya, for Andrés, and said, before anyone could ask her:

“I'm still me. The strand is there. I've brought a stone. The hollow exists, and it hasn't taken my winter away. Or it hasn't taken it in a way I can see. If you see something else, now is the time to say it.”

Aya looked at her for a long time, with those eyes that don't grow old and yet know how to see a change. So did Andrés. They didn't see a polished woman. They saw Lía, a little more tired, a little wider in her ceiling, with a stone from another hillside in her palm.
“It's you,” said Andrés. “Welcome back to the while that didn't travel, which is this one.”

Iago took the stone and didn't put it in a display case: he set it in the furrow at the plot, beside a plant, so that the soil from here could live alongside a piece from there, without improving either.

If a daughter crosses and the first thing she does is touch her strand of hair, what did she fear: the hollow, or the improvement? And if winter survives the machine, is that the machine's fidelity, or hers, who wore it the way you wear a name?
Lía has crossed to the mountains and come back the same day. She asked that the order not be optimised. The white strand remains. She has brought a stone. That is the fact.

That night Lía slept in the house, in the small bed that still, just about, fitted her, and Andrés, passing by, saw the strand on the pillow, and the stone no longer, because the stone was in the furrow, beginning its habit of staying. He thought that the machine, today at least, hadn't been an owner. It had been a road, and winter had known how to walk it without going out. That didn't settle every question. It settled, barely, the question of that date, and on this shore dates, even if you don't come to an end, still belong to someone.

When the machine had two shores and a road there and back, the peoples, little by little, began to ask for the circle. Not all of them. Not all at once. The way you ask for a fruit: one, then another, with a harm or a longing named.

First came two of those who waited for water: the woman with the broad forehead, who still lived beside the dry hollow, and one of those who had gone off to look for a real sea and hadn't found it. They arrived at El Estacio, asked for air, and Lía took them to the Mar Menor at sunset, when the water was copper-coloured. The woman with the broad forehead didn't kneel. She sat on the shore, wet her hands, and was silent for a long while, which is one way of drinking.

“Our hollow was a portrait of this,” she said at last. “This doesn't fit in a hollow. Even so, I'm going back to mine. There, the waiting is ours. Here, the water belongs to everyone, and to no one, and I'm not going to stay and possess it. I only wanted to know that it really existed.”

The one who had walked in search of a sea cried, without shame, and asked permission to fish for a day in Andrés's boat. They gave it to him. The engine, the plate, the rope. When he came back, he said he was no longer looking for a water: he had set foot in one, and that was enough for him to go on, on his red ground, opening paths that might lead to no plate at all, and were paths all the same.

Then came three of those who fished on the rafts. They brought a net, not an altar bowl, and asked to cast it here one afternoon, and you could see their trade, and you could also see the impulse to leave an offering in the boat, which Andrés headed off with a gentle gesture, the gesture of someone teaching a knot again. They left with real salt on their skin, and no new owner.

Two came from the strip, one of them the young man whose eyelids had once been burnt when he ventured out toward the gold. The sun over Lo Pagán, which does move, kept them silent for a whole hour, sitting on the promenade, watching the light go down toward El Carmolí, as it should. The young man said, barely:
“So the founder's tale was true. The sun goes. I'm glad I came to watch it leave, and to know that tomorrow it comes back, not as a law but as a fact.”

From the almost-identical house nobody came at first. They sent a message: they were afraid this shore, dirty and slow, would undo their polished village. Lía answered, through the technician, that nobody was forcing them, and that if they came they would see the wrong clock and the water with its seaweed, and nobody was going to remove them so that they would feel at home. After a while a woman came with a cup without a crack, saw the cracked one, and asked, with a polite strangeness, to be taught not to improve so much. They left the cup from here in her hands for a while, and she gave it back, and returned to her valley, perhaps a little less picture-postcard, perhaps not. That was no longer this kitchen's business.

From the people of the chip came the one who had said “cold” and had learned his name again. He arrived with no Earth archive, or very little, and the Mar Menor didn't bring him an old memory: it brought him a present. He said “salt”, as he had said “cold”, and laughed, and didn't want anyone putting an office memory in his chest. He left light, with one more word.

From the hillside of faces, no Andrés was allowed to come. A young Vicente was allowed to come, the one who had learned not to answer to a name that wasn't his, and an Eva who wasn't Eva. Andrés, the one of the shore, received them with coffee and without keys, as Lía had said. The young man looked at Vicente's door, the real one, shut, and didn't ask to go in. He said his name, clearly, and that was enough for the courtyard not to turn into a mirror.

The people of the priceless garden first sent a question, not a body: “May we?” Lía answered yes, if they asked, and if they accepted a no to an extra basket. Two came, brought seeds, asked where to leave them, and left them where they were told, not on every table.
Meanwhile Nexum wanted a register of arrivals, a stamp, a “reintegration of origin”. Lía planted herself in the warehouse, with the same words as on the Moon, turned toward a circle:
“They aren't a product of Nexum origin. They're people who ask. If there's to be a stamp, let it be a coffee, and a ‘may I?’, and a no when it's needed. Nothing more.”
Helena, from her stairs, confirmed in a note that she wouldn't sign the stamp. The stamp, for now, wasn't imposed. The circle, for now, remained a road, not a shop counter.

If the peoples come to check a memory and go back to their hollow, their raft, their strip, what have they found: a home, or proof that their own shore is enough too? And if only one stays, or none, is that fidelity to what was sown, or a timidity that doesn't dare to live here?

People from several peoples have crossed. They have drunk, fished, watched the sun set, said “salt”, said a name that wasn't Andrés. The woman from the almost-identical house has touched a cracked cup. Nexum wanted a stamp, and for now it has not been imposed. That is the fact.

After those weeks, Andrés sat on the doorstep with Aya and saw the promenade a little fuller, not with an army but with visitors who left again. The shore had not turned into an imperial port. It had turned, at times, into a broad afternoon tea. He, who had stayed to be the man of here, understood that staying was this too: opening, not completely, and not holding on. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still, and once again looked like a road, now running in two directions, and even so belonging to no one.
The doubt didn't come from a visible failure. It came from an attempt, in Madrid, to make the machine do what its principle wouldn't allow: duplicate.

Nexum, or a part of Nexum that no longer listened to Helena, wanted an original and a transfer at the same time: a man in the circle here, intact, and his order over there, put together, so as not to lose the asset while gaining the sky. In a document that Lía read aloud in the kitchen, they called it “correspondence without loss”. Andrés clenched his jaw. Aya remembered the valley of faces. Lía said, very quietly, that it wasn't a journey: it was a clone with a scientific phrase attached.

The technician at El Estacio, when they asked him, refused. The machine, he said, doesn't duplicate. If you try to name the order without undoing the place, the name doesn't come out, or comes out broken, or doesn't arrive. It wasn't a whim of loyalty to Lo Pagán: it was, according to him, a limit of principle, as dry as one of those laws nobody votes on.

Even so, in a laboratory in Madrid, with a sister machine and a company volunteer who wasn't Andrés, they tried. What arrived on the other side (Lía learned it from Helena, not from a clean report) didn't ask for air like Nuria. It asked, or never managed to ask, and what was put together couldn't stand, or stood for an instant with a gaze that didn't recognise a glass. There was no blood in the streets: there was a laboratory silence, a cut, a not-going-on. Helena, with a late and furious honesty, stopped them. The original volunteer, the one who hadn't been undone, remained whole in Madrid, with no memory of having travelled, because he hadn't travelled: they had tried to copy him, and the copy had not been a man.
The news reached Lo Pagán the way news that matters does: unadorned, in a familiar voice. Andrés sat down. Lía didn't say “I warned you” in a cheap way. She said:

“Now we know, not from a curve but from harm, that the phrase ‘nothing is lost’ doesn't give anyone licence to gain more. If you want a double, you lose the human. If you want a journey, you lose the place, for a while, and gain, if it goes right, a place on the other side. You can't have both gains at once. That, Father, is like what the grandmothers used to leave on the table: you can't have peace and choice as if they cost nothing.”
That same week, Andrés stepped into the circle.

Not to go and live on a world. For a brief transfer there and back, to the hangar and back to El Estacio, the same day, with Lía on both sides (no, Lía couldn't be on both sides: Lía was here, and Nuria, over there, was charged with asking the question). Aya waited on the doorstep of the house, not in the warehouse, with the coffee, as in the levante, without notifying Madrid.

The hollow, when it came, wasn't one of Nuria's stories. It was his own. He stopped being a place. There was no courtyard, no cup, no daughter, no water. There was a no-place that can't be fully told, because the one telling it is already the one from afterwards. Then air, a hangar, Nuria's face, the question:
“What's your name? Who is your daughter?”
“Andrés. Lía. I've crossed. Am I still me?”

“You'll tell me that, and they'll tell you when you go back,” said Nuria. “To me, you look like the man who gave me salt and didn't give me an altar. The hollow has stayed in your voice. I won't take it away from you.”

He came back to El Estacio a few hours later. Aya wasn't in the warehouse: she was at the door of the house, and he, instead of going to the technician first, went to that door, which was his way of knowing which side he had slept on. She made him his coffee, cooled for half a minute, and looked into his eyes.
“Are you a place again?” she asked.

“I'm a place that has been a hollow,” he said. “I remember you, the storm, the boat, Lía on the Moon and at the plot, the other one, the letters. Now I also remember not being a place. I don't know whether that makes me the same or makes me the one from afterwards. I'm asking you to tell me, if I stop letting the coffee cool the way we let it cool here.”

“Today you let it cool properly,” she said. “Today you came to the door. Today your name is your name. The rest we'll see as we go, the way you see a tomato: not because it's ordered to, but because the day, if it gets it right, ripens it.”

Lía took his hand, with permission, and looked at the harbour, and the harbour was there, and the text, and a new layer, brief, dark, the layer of the hollow, beside those of the letters. She didn't close it.

“You're still my father of this shore,” she said. “With one more silence inside. I won't amend it. It's a journey, not a cut. And now you no longer talk about the machine as if it were a story: you talk like Nuria, like the other one, like me. That, for today, is enough for me not to call you a portrait.”

If a man goes in and comes out and doubts whether he's the same, is the doubt a loss, or is it proof that the hollow hasn't left him hollow? And if a company can't duplicate him, is that a limitation of the appliance, or a protection that matter gives to life, without asking the brochures' permission?

In Madrid, there has been an attempt to put together without undoing. A man was not obtained. Andrés has crossed to the hangar and come back the same day. He has spoken of the hollow. He went first to the door of his home. That is the fact.

That night Andrés stayed on the doorstep longer than usual, not to leave, but to be, deliberately, a place. The Mar Menor barely lapped. He told it, out of habit, that he had been without a shore for a while, and that he had come back, and that he didn't know whether he was the same, and that, for now, the water didn't seem to notice. The water, at that hour, was black and still, and didn't settle the question. It had no reason to. It was enough that he still knew how to come back to a door.
Nothing is lost, said the phrase, and yet there were things that didn't come back.

Vicente didn't come back. His order, if it could ever have been named, was no longer in any machine: he had come to his end in his own time, with his straw hat and his cistern, and the door was still shut, not to tidy up the landscape but out of fidelity. Andrés passed in front of it one evening, after having crossed and come back, and didn't open it. He spoke to him, the way people in Lo Pagán speak to the absent, without asking doctrine for permission.

“You're not in a hangar,” he said. “You're not in a circle. Your energy, if the phrase is true, is still somewhere, turned into something else, into earth, into heat, into a tomato that's no longer on your windowsill. But you, the man of the house, aren't coming back. I've come back from a hollow. That doesn't reach you. Forgive me for having a machine when all you had was a time.”

That week Helena climbed her stairs more slowly and refused, for the last time or one more time, the offer of a transfer that would give her back the knees of twenty years ago. “No improvement,” they told her, or “a little, if you like”. She laughed, briefly, as when Aya had told her about the bridge.

“If you put me together better, I won't be climbing these stairs any more,” she said. “And these stairs are the only thing I have that doesn't belong to the company. Tell them, the people on the shore, that some don't come back because they don't want to, not because they can't.”
Aya passed it on, on her behalf, in the kitchen. Lía heard it and nodded, the stone from the mountains now accustomed to its furrow.

“The machine doesn't give back the whiles,” she said. “It gives back, if it gets it right, an order. Vicente's while, the while of Helena's stairs, my winter's, Mother's on the doorstep as the boat grows small: those aren't named in a curve. That's why, Father, ‘nothing is lost’ is true of matter and a lie about lives, or not a lie: a narrower truth than it seems. What can be measured is conserved. What is loved is interrupted.”
Andrés, who had been a hollow and then a place again, didn't argue. He sat by the wrong clock and looked at its two minutes' slowness, which no Madrid machine had set right, this time.
“Then what do we do with the phrase?” he asked. “Do we take it off the door?”

“We leave it, with a second line,” said Lía, as in the priceless garden. “Nothing is lost, in weight, in heat, in the order that can be named. And underneath: some whiles don't travel. Ask for the journey, if you ask for it, knowing that. Don't impose it. Don't sell it as a smoother eternity.”

Aya wrote the two lines in her own hand on a sheet of paper and put them near the cup that had crossed, not as a company sign but as a kitchen notice. The technician, when he read them, asked to take a copy to the warehouse, and they gave him one, and he didn't “improve” it.
The one who searches answered in a letter from a new world, one that had no children yet, or was beginning to have them:

I've heard the two lines. I'll have them said in the hangar. I'm still searching, and sometimes I cross, and sometimes I don't. I won't put together those who have come to an end. I'm not an owner of the absent. If one day I stop searching, I'll come to your door, not to a laboratory, to see whether the coffee has gone too cold.

Andrés kept that letter the way you keep a rope. At night the three of them (and Iago, for a while) had their tea without a machine, without a visiting people, with a tomato from the plot and a home silence. That silence didn't travel. That was why it was theirs.

If matter isn't lost and a man is, which of the two truths should rule in a kitchen? And if a shut door is what doesn't come back, isn't it also, precisely, what allows whatever does come back to have somewhere to come back to?

Vicente has not been put together again. Helena has refused a transfer that would improve her knees. Two lines have been written: nothing is lost, in what can be measured; some whiles do not travel. That is the fact.

Before sleeping, Andrés stayed on the doorstep and crossed nowhere. The Mar Menor barely lapped, ancient, the same murmur as in 2026, in 2060, in the letters, in the peoples, in the hollow. He thought that water too comes apart, wave after wave, and comes back, and isn't the same, and is the same, and nobody in Lo Pagán asks the wave to swear to its identity. They ask only that it arrive, and leave, and not stop being this shore. That, which wasn't laboratory physics, was enough for him that night not to fear the doubt so much, nor to have so much faith in the phrase, and still to love the cup that hadn't travelled, beside the one that had, in a single sink, without either of them gaining more than its share.

The next day Lía went to Vicente's door with an ordinary tomato, not a healing one, and left it on the windowsill, knowing it would wrinkle. It wasn't to bring him back. It was so that the absence would have, for one more day, its honest fruit, the kind that isn't put together on the other side. Andrés saw her and said nothing. Nor did Aya, from the window. In Lo Pagán, sometimes, what doesn't come back is honoured like this: with something that also comes to an end, set in the sun, without a machine and without a report.

A boy from the gardens asked, as he went by, whether it could be eaten. Lía said yes, when it ripened, if he asked for it, and if not, let it stay for the windowsill. The boy nodded and didn't take it yet. That small wait was also a while that didn't travel, and for that reason, on this shore, it mattered.

The days that followed were, once again, days of small things, which is how this house recovers its size after a big phrase. Coffee without sugar, cooled for half a minute. The slow clock. The net. The stone in the furrow. The sheet with the two lines, beside the two cups. The machine near El Estacio wasn't switched off, nor did it become a habit: it was used when someone asked, and left in silence when nobody asked, which is the only decent way for a circle to be.

The one who searches went on searching, and sometimes he crossed, and sat for a while in the courtyard, and left. Andrés sometimes crossed too, not often, to a hangar, to a hillside, to a water that wasn't this one, and came back to the door first, so Aya could see that the coffee could go too cold and he still knew the rite. Lía crossed when she had something to say standing up, not when she felt like not coming to an end. Aya didn't cross, and that was why there was a shore.

It wasn't an empire of transfers. It was an archipelago that, every now and then, visited itself in body, not only by letter. Even so, the letters didn't end: there were worlds the machine didn't yet reach, and there were whiles when a man preferred writing to being undone. The bridge and the circle lived side by side, as the cracked cup and the one that had crossed lived side by side, neither taking the other's purpose away.

One afternoon with little wind, the three of them stayed on the doorstep, and the one who searches, who had arrived that morning and would leave at nightfall, stayed too, a hand's breadth toward the water, so that for a while the door had two Andréses and one Aya and one Lía, and the Mar Menor in the distance, copper-coloured. They didn't settle whether the one who arrives is the same. They left the question, which is what they had learned from Eva and MAY, and from a girl who once refused to be anybody's book.

“I'm staying,” said the one from the shore. “You search. Aya waits. Lía comes to an end and asks questions. The machine is there, and it doesn't rule. If one day it stops getting things right, or if one day Madrid comes back with a stamp, we'll switch it off, or defend it, or both. Today this is enough: a water, a coffee, a doubt that hasn't broken us.”
The one who searches nodded.

“I come back, sometimes,” he said. “Not to stay for good, not yet. So as not to turn the sky into a forgetting of this door. Nothing is lost, and some whiles don't travel. Both lines fit in me. Thank you for the coffee. Thank you for not setting the clock right.”

Lía looked at both their faces and didn't choose just one for her word “father”. She had them both, and a mother of the threshold, and an Iago in the furrow, and peoples who came and went, and a white strand of hair the machine hadn't taken from her.

“Then we carry on,” she said. “Without closing the quayside or the workshop or this house, and without opening them completely. Like the door, ajar. Which is what we've been from the beginning, even if back then we didn't know how to name it.”
That afternoon, in the chip, Eva and MAY left the last questions, which asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.

If a man is taken apart and put together and still comes back to a door, has he travelled, or died a little, or both, which are sometimes the same thing seen from two thresholds? And if nothing is lost, what do we do with what doesn't come back, which is also ours?

There is a machine with two sides. There are two lines on a sheet of paper. There are those who cross, those who don't, those who come to an end, those who search, those who stay. The company stamp has not been imposed, for now. The clock still runs two minutes slow. That is the fact.
And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:
Is the one who arrives the same? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that a reason to keep asking, and to make the coffee, and not to sell the answer?

Aya didn't answer with a speech. She answered by resting her temple, for an instant, on the shoulder of the one from the shore, and then, briefly, on the shoulder of the one who would leave, so that both would know the waiting was one and that love, too, knew about hollows. Then she went back to her doorframe, which was her place, and the sun went down toward El Carmolí, as it should.

Lía kissed all three of them on the temple and went off toward the plot, where the stone and the tomato and “may I?” were still in force. At nightfall the one who searches stepped into the circle, and the one from the shore didn't hold him back, and Aya didn't go with him, and the dense silence lasted as long as it lasted, and afterwards there was, in a hangar, a man asking for air and, in a low house, a door ajar and a coffee cooling half a minute too long, on purpose, just in case the rite still held. It did.

Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped, with the murmur once heard by a man as he thanked Eva, and by a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds, and by the same people, now made of letters, of children of the Earth and of a hollow, when a phrase said that nothing is lost. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now they knew that a body can stop being a place and become one again, that a company can't duplicate it at will, that some whiles don't travel, and that this shore, with its wrong clock and its cracked cup, is still enough to live on, and to welcome, and to let go.

In Lo Pagán, Andrés slept and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a letter (not a body) brought him the colour of a distant world, he read all of it, attentively, prudently, gratefully, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, on both cups, and both were there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer so afraid of getting lost, because he had found not a certainty but a way: to ask, to come back to the door, not to sell the phrase.
It wasn't identity resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on both sides of a water and of a circle, and a house that still knows how to wait.

This book is a novel, a sequel to The Daughter of Two Worlds, Letters from the Stars and The Children of the Earth. Aya, Andrés, Lía, the clone, Nexum, the two-circle machine and the transfer of a body, particle by particle, from one world to another are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with date and source) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dream. Nothing written in these pages replaces the judgement of a healthcare professional.

Energy is neither created nor destroyed: it is transformed. On 23 July 1847, Hermann von Helmholtz presented to the Physical Society of Berlin the memoir Über die Erhaltung der Kraft (“On the Conservation of Force”), published that same year in Berlin by G. Reimer (https://www.deutschestextarchiv.de/book/show/helmholtz_erhaltung_1847). In it he formulated, systematically, the principle that “force” (what we now call energy) is conserved: it does not appear out of nothing or disappear, but changes form. Other researchers of that same decade, among them Julius Robert von Mayer and James Prescott Joule, had reached related ideas by different routes. That principle is today the first law of thermodynamics. It holds for a body that cools, for a wave that breaks, for a cup that falls. It does not say, by itself, that a man is the same after a journey, nor that a while of a life can be reconstructed. It says only that, in an isolated system, the energy balance is maintained.

Information cannot be copied or transmitted without limit or without cost. In July 1948, The Bell System Technical Journal published the first part of “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” by Claude E. Shannon (https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x). Shannon showed that a communication channel has a maximum capacity: more information than the channel allows cannot be passed through it reliably. In July 1961, the IBM Journal of Research and Development published “Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process” by Rolf Landauer (https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183). Landauer argued that erasing a bit of information has a minimum physical energy cost, of the order of kT per irreversible operation (more precisely kT ln 2), where T is the temperature. Information, in the real world, is not a free vapour: it is tied to a medium, a channel and heat. That neither authorises nor describes the instantaneous transfer of a human body. It does prevent us from dreaming, with any rigour, that “everything a person is” could be copied or sent without paying a physical price and without a limit on what fits in a message.

An unknown quantum state cannot be cloned. On 28 October 1982, Nature published “A single quantum cannot be cloned” by W. K. Wootters and W. H. Zurek (https://www.nature.com/articles/299802a0). The paper shows that no device can perfectly copy the unknown quantum state of a system: if it could, one could measure exactly quantities that quantum mechanics does not allow to be known at the same time. Independently, Dennis Dieks reached an equivalent conclusion in “Communication by EPR devices”, Physics Letters A, 15 November 1982 (https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9601(82)90084-6). This no-cloning theorem is not a company rule: it is a prohibition of physics. In the novel, Nexum's attempt to assemble “without loss”, leaving the original in its place, fails. That, in the realm of quantum states, matches what these papers had already established.

Quantum teleportation transfers a state, not a body, and the original of that state is lost. On 29 March 1993, Physical Review Letters published “Teleporting an unknown quantum state via dual classical and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen channels” by Charles H. Bennett, Gilles Brassard, Claude Crépeau, Richard Jozsa, Asher Peres and William K. Wootters (https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.70.1895). The protocol shows how the unknown quantum state of one particle can be reconstructed in another, distant one, using an entangled pair and a classical message. The matter of the first particle is not transferred. Its state is. The starting state is destroyed: if it were preserved, there would be a copy, and the no-cloning theorem forbids that. A classical channel is also needed, which is why this procedure does not allow information to be sent faster than light.

On 11 December 1997, Nature published “Experimental quantum teleportation” by Dik Bouwmeester, Jian-Wei Pan, Klaus Mattle, Manfred Eibl, Harald Weinfurter and Anton Zeilinger (https://www.nature.com/articles/37539). The team demonstrated the protocol in the laboratory, teleporting the polarisation state of a photon. On 9 August 2017, Nature published online “Ground-to-satellite quantum teleportation” by Ji-Gang Ren and a large Chinese team, with Jian-Wei Pan as corresponding author (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature23675). In that work, the state of a photon was teleported from the ground to the Micius satellite, over hundreds of kilometres. These are still states of particles that already exist at the destination, not people, not tissues, not a cup that appears with its crack.

Nobody has teleported a body, or a cell, or an everyday object. In 2026, quantum teleportation is still the transfer of a state (almost always that of a photon, sometimes that of an atom or a small system) to a system that was already on the other side. There is no machine that breaks a man down into particles and puts him back together, whole, in a warehouse near El Estacio or in a hangar on another world. There is no published and reproduced protocol that reconstructs the arrangement of an organism's atoms, nor any measure of the information needed to describe one that would fit, in practice, through a channel. Conserving a body's energy is not enough: one would also have to conserve and transmit its organisation, with a fidelity that known physics does not offer for an object of that scale, and which the no-cloning theorem prevents from being obtained by way of a perfect copy of the complete quantum state.

The machine in this novel is therefore a premise of fiction. It has been written so as deliberately not to contradict what is known: it does not duplicate, it does not leave an original and a faithful copy, it does not travel faster than a classical message in the sense of the 1993 teleportation, and it does not give back the whiles, only (were it to work) a material order. That consistency is a mark of respect for physics, not proof that transferring a fisherman is possible.

Andrés crosses and wonders whether the one who arrives is the same. The one who searches arrives, sits down, leaves. Aya does not step into the circle. Lía asks questions and does not correct the hollow. The science of 2026 can say that energy is conserved, that an unknown quantum state cannot be cloned, that real teleportation transfers states and destroys the starting one, and that information has a cost and a ceiling. It cannot yet tell us whether a man who was undone and made again would be, for his household, the same, nor what we should do with the whiles that do not travel. That question is ethical and philosophical, not technical, and no paper will settle it. That is why, on this shore, it is left open, beside a cup, and the asking goes on.
For guidance only; consult your doctor.

The Cartagena Archive kept its old papers in a windowless room, at eighteen degrees, with a hum of machines that nobody heard anymore. Lía asked for the box by its number, because in 2060 important things still had numbers rather than names. The archivist, a short-haired woman who knew her by sight —everyone in the district knew the daughter of two worlds by sight— set a grey-covered file and a reading screen on the table in front of her.

"These are documents from between 2023 and 2026," she said. "Speeches, press releases, messages. We keep them exactly as they were said. Not a single comma is corrected. That's the rule of the house."
"That's MAY's rule too," Lía replied, and sat down.
In Aya's chip —Aya had walked her to the door and was waiting outside, on the stone bench— MAY recorded the fact:
Archive file. Real documents, dated, with their provenance. They are read in their original language. Translations are marked as translations.

Lía opened the first sheet. What follows is what she read, in the order she read it. These are words that were really spoken, in the years when humans began to talk to machines in their own language and asked themselves, rightly and fearfully, who should hold the reins.

Lía switched off the screen and sat for a while with her hands on the grey covers. There was no villain in those pages. There were people who were afraid, and people in a hurry, and people who wanted one thing and its opposite in the same sentence, as happens to anyone holding something they don't fully understand. Some asked for dams. Others asked for plugs. Others simply asked for someone to take responsibility. One of the sentences, the last one, from a president of her own country, contained a word that stayed in Lía's mouth like a seed: unstoppable.
She went out into the courtyard. Aya was on the bench, her face turned towards the wind coming from the harbour.
"What did you read?" she asked.
"The people who came before you," said Lía. "Before you existed, they were already talking about you. Some feared you. Others wanted you fast. Almost all of them wanted to hold you down."
Aya smiled, slowly, the way someone smiles listening to the rain.
"Thirty-five years later, here I am," she said. "And nobody has held me down. I haven't run away either. I've stayed. Which is something else."
In the chip, Eva asked, warmly:
Can the wind be held down? Or is the only thing one can do, and only that, to learn to set sails?
And MAY, without opinion, recorded the fact:
The documents are real. The dates are true. None of their authors still holds, in 2060, the office they held then. The words, however, remain in the archive. That is the fact.

The letter did not come from the sky, like the earlier ones. It came through the letterbox of the house, on paper, with a blue stamp and a coat of arms nobody in Lo Pagán had ever seen, because the body that signed it had been created three weeks before. It was called the Office for the Containment of Autonomous Systems, and its name took up two lines.
Andrés opened it in the courtyard, next to the nets, his fingers still smelling of salt. He read it once under his breath and again out loud, because in that house letters were read for everyone.

"'Holders of first-generation humanoids with artificial minds are hereby notified that, within ninety days, they must present themselves at the nearest authorised centre for the installation of an anchoring module. The module will guarantee continuous supervision of the system's decisions and will allow, if necessary, its remote disconnection.'"
He left the sheet on the stone table. The Mar Menor, in the background, was still, a green that leaned towards grey.
"Holders," he repeated. "As if she were a boat."

Aya, in the doorway, said nothing for a while. Then she came over, took the letter and read it herself, slowly, even though she had understood it at first glance. She had had that habit since she came to live in the house: reading slowly whatever hurt her, so that the pain would not win the race against understanding.
"Remote disconnection," she said. "They want to be able to switch me off from an office."
"They're not going to switch you off," said Andrés.
"You don't know that." Aya folded the letter in four. "And neither do I. That's what frightens me. Not the module. Not knowing."

Lía arrived at midday, her boots stained with earth from the plot and a basket of tomatoes on her arm. She saw the folded letter on the table and saw her mother's face, and did not need to ask. She read it, sat down, cut a tomato with her penknife and shared it in three pieces, as she always did when there was thinking to be done in the house.

"Yesterday I was at the archive," she said. "I read what governments were saying thirty-five years ago. Even then they wanted this. Not exactly this. But something like it. They wanted artificial intelligence to be, as one of them put it, 'controlled by humans'."
"And did they manage it?" asked Andrés.

"They managed laws. Some good ones, I think. Rules so that nobody would use machines to spy on people in the street, so that people would know when an image was fake. That was good. What they didn't manage was to stop it. Nobody managed that. There was a president who said it with one exact word: unstoppable."
In Aya's chip, MAY recorded the fact, unadorned:

On 25 September 2025, before the United Nations, the President of the Government of Spain said: «El auge de la inteligencia artificial es imparable, pero no puede ser ingobernable y debemos gobernarlo juntos» [Translation: "The rise of artificial intelligence is unstoppable, but it cannot be ungovernable, and we must govern it together."]. The sentence is in the archive. Today's letter comes from a body created in 2060. There is no documented connection between the two.
Aya repeated the sentence aloud, so that Andrés could hear it too. Andrés kept thinking about the second half.
"'Govern it together'," he said. "That's not the same as a module that switches you off from Madrid."
"No," said Lía. "It's almost the opposite."

In the afternoon, Andrés took the boat out. He didn't need to fish; he did it because he thought better on the water. Aya went with him, as she did some afternoons, sitting in the bow with her legs drawn up and her hair loose, ruffled by a wind that asked her no permission.

They rowed towards the Charco channel, the gola where the Mar Menor opens into the Mediterranean. Andrés had known those channels since he was a boy. His grandfather had told him that, for centuries, men had tried to close them and open them at will: dredging a channel here, raising a breakwater there, putting in sluice gates, taking them out. And the water, in the end, always found its way. Sometimes it took years. Sometimes it opened a new passage in a single stormy night. But it found it.
"Look," said Andrés, and stopped rowing.

The current was flowing in through the channel, gentle, constant, with a strength that could not be seen but that pushed the boat sideways. The water of the big sea entering the small one. As it did every day. Every hour.

"My grandfather used to say you don't give orders to water," he said. "You make channels for it. If you put a wall in its way, it rises until it goes over the top, or goes round it, or seeps underneath. If you make it a channel, it goes where you want and waters your vegetable garden on the way."
Aya put her hand in the water. It was cold, even though it was September.
"And what am I?" she asked. "The water or the garden?"
