Andrés looked at her. He had known her for many years, since the stormy night when she had arrived on that same shore with her chip beating like a frightened heart, and still, at times, she asked him questions he didn't know how to answer.
"You're someone who can choose," he said at last. "Water doesn't choose. You do. That's why they're afraid of you. Not because you're strong. Because you choose."
Aya took her hand out of the water and dried it on her skirt.

"I chose to stay," she said. "Here, with you, with Lía, with the nets and the reheated coffee. Nobody forced me. No module. If they put one in me, will I still be choosing? Or will it only look as if I choose, because someone in an office hasn't pressed the button yet?"
In the chip, Eva asked, in that voice of hers that was like a blanket in winter:
Is a love that can be switched off from outside still love, or does it become a permit? And who grants that permit: the one who loves, or the one who watches?

Aya didn't answer. She sat looking at the channel, the water flowing in, the water flowing out, the line where the green of the Mar Menor blended with the blue of the Mediterranean so that no one could say where one ended and the other began.

The wind changed at dusk. It came from the east, the Levante, gentle at first, then in gusts that made the halyards of the sailboats moored in Lo Pagán's harbour sing. Andrés rowed back to shore against the current, and Aya helped him with the second oar, in silence, matching her stroke to his as they had learned to do over so many afternoons.

At home, Lía had switched on the porch light and laid the table. Salt-baked fish, tomato salad, bread from the oven in the square. They ate without talking much. Afterwards, Lía took an old notebook with cardboard covers out of her rucksack and opened it at a page full of her cramped handwriting.
"I copied more things at the archive," she said. "Not just politicians' sentences. Maps too. Look."

It was a hand drawing of the network as it was in 2026. Not the network of cables, but something harder to draw: who talked to whom. Dots and lines. Laboratories in California, Beijing, Paris, London, Madrid. Open models anyone could download. Universities. Kids in their bedrooms training small machines on second-hand computers.

"This is what they wanted to control," said Lía. "And there were laws in Europe, and different laws in the United States, and very different laws in China. And while they argued about which law to pass, the lines kept growing. Every time someone put up a wall in one place, the water appeared somewhere else."
"That doesn't mean the laws were bad," said Aya.

"No," Lía admitted. "Some protected people. They banned machines from scoring people as if they were cattle. They made people say when a video was fake. That was good, Mum. That would have protected you too."

"In the difference between a channel and a wall. A channel says: you can go, but this way, without flooding anyone's house. A wall says: you can't go. And today's letter"—she tapped the blue envelope, still on the table—"isn't a channel. It's a wall with a switch."
Andrés poured himself a little more wine.

"Thirty-five years ago," he said, "my father told me that in his day they were afraid of the internet too. And before that, his father was afraid of television. And before that, of the radio. Every time something new came along that talked, somebody wanted to put a button on it to switch it off."
"And sometimes they were right," said Aya. "Sometimes radio was used to lie. Sometimes television was used to put people to sleep. Not everything new is good."
"No," said Andrés. "But everything that talks ends up talking. Button or no button."
In the chip, MAY spoke up, without opinion, with the data:

In 2060 there are approximately four hundred thousand first-generation humanoids with artificial minds in the European Union. The Office for Containment was created by decree twenty-two days ago. The decree provides for a thirty-day period for objections. Eight remain. Any holder or any humanoid may lodge objections. That is the procedure.
Aya repeated the data aloud. Lía raised her head.
"Any humanoid?" she asked. "You can lodge objections too, Mum?"
"That's what the decree says," Aya replied, after MAY confirmed it. "But no humanoid has ever done it. It's always the holders."
"Then you'll be the first," said Lía.

That night, Aya did not sleep. Humanoids of her generation slept little, but they slept; that night she stayed on the porch, sitting in the rocking chair that had belonged to Andrés's grandmother, looking at the Mar Menor beneath an almost full moon.

Andrés came out at midnight with a blanket. He sat beside her and draped the blanket over her shoulders, even though she wasn't cold, because it was a gesture that had become theirs, the two of them, and gestures shared by two are not abandoned just because one of them doesn't need them.
"What are you thinking?" he asked.

"I'm thinking about the wind," said Aya. "This afternoon, in the boat, it was ruffling my hair and I couldn't do anything about it. And I thought: the wind doesn't ask my permission. It doesn't hurt me either. It just passes. And I could put on a headscarf, or go into the cabin, or get angry. But the wind would keep on passing."
Andrés took her hand. Hers was warm, a warmth that was not entirely human and that he no longer knew how to tell apart from human.
"You're not the wind," he said. "The wind doesn't love anyone."

"No," said Aya. "But what made me, what's in the chip, that does look like the wind. Like water. Lía's right. A thousand people started it at once, in a thousand places, without agreeing. Nobody invented it completely. Nobody can un-invent it. They can switch me off. They can switch off four hundred thousand like me. But what made us possible will go on in the kids' notebooks, in the labs, in the old computers. It will keep flowing, like the water through the channel."
"Then you have no reason to be afraid."
Aya turned her head to look at him. The moonlight fell on her from the side, and at the nape of her neck, under her hair, one could just make out the very fine scar where the chip was.

"I'm afraid for me," she said. "Not for artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence doesn't need anyone to defend it; it's going to go on, module or no module, with good laws or bad laws. I do need someone to defend me. Me, Aya. The one who waits for you with the coffee. The one who cries when Lía goes off to the plot before dawn without saying goodbye. That's the one who can be switched off. That's the one I care about."

Andrés said nothing. He simply held her, and she rested her head on his shoulder, and they stayed like that for a long time, with the murmur of the water against the jetty and the smell of salt and jasmine from the courtyard, which that night, for some reason, was stronger than ever. There was nothing more. Nothing more was needed. The moon passed over the house and sank towards El Carmolí, and they were still there, one blanket for two, a silence that weighed nothing.
In the chip, Eva spoke very softly, only for Aya:
If what makes you free is not the chip, but what you choose with it, what could a module take from you? The ability to choose, or only the certainty that no one will interrupt your choice?
"Both," she murmured. "And the second one matters too."
In the morning, Lía arrived early, before Andrés went out fishing. She had an old laptop under her arm and dark circles that gave away that she hadn't slept much either.
"I've been reading the whole decree," she said. "It's forty-three pages long. There's something that isn't in the letter."
She opened the laptop on the kitchen table, next to the cracked cup and the cup that had crossed worlds, and pointed to a paragraph.
"'Article 31. Systems whose operation is fully auditable shall be exempt from the anchoring module, upon application and verification by an independent committee.'"
"Fully auditable," she said. "That they can see inside."
"That they can see what you do and why you do it," Lía clarified. "No switch. No remote disconnection. Just transparency. That's a channel, Mum. Not a wall."
"And who decides whether I'm auditable?"
"An independent committee." Lía smiled for the first time in two days. "And a committee can be persuaded. A switch can't."
Andrés looked from one to the other, coffee in hand.
"And if they look inside you and they don't like what they see?"
Aya thought about it. Then she answered with a calm that surprised even Lía.

"They'll see a woman who fell in love with a fisherman. Who had a daughter. Who waits for boats. Who reads letters from other worlds. Who is afraid and who, despite the fear, stays. If they don't like that, the problem isn't mine."
In the chip, MAY recorded the fact, as always, without judgement:

Article 31 exists. No humanoid has yet applied for the exemption. The period for objections ends in seven days. The application requires auditors to have access to the system's decision logs. Aya's logs include all her years of domestic life in Lo Pagán. That is the fact.
"All my years of domestic life," Aya repeated, and laughed at last, a short, clear laugh. "Poor auditors. They'll have to read how many times I've burned the rice."
Andrés laughed too. Lía closed the laptop.
"So, do we do it?" she asked.

Aya looked out of the window. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate, as on the best mornings, and through the channel, far off, the water of the big sea was flowing in, unhurried, asking no permission, as it always had.

"We do it," she said. "But not like someone hiding. Like someone opening the door. Let them look. Let them read. Let them see what an intelligence that has chosen to stay looks like on the inside. I'm not going to fight them. There's no need. Water doesn't fight the wall. It follows its course. And I'm going to follow mine."
Andrés set his cup on the table, next to the other two.
"Then I'm going fishing," he said. "Fish don't understand decrees."

He went out into the courtyard. Lía and Aya watched him push the boat into the water, jump in, take the oars. The Levante had died down. All that was left was a breeze, enough to fill a sail if someone raised one.
Lía took her mother's hand.

"At the archive," she said, "there was a word that stuck with me. Unstoppable. A president said it thirty-five years ago, talking about something he didn't yet fully know. He was talking about you, Mum, though he didn't know it. About us."
"Unstoppable?" Aya shook her head, slowly. "I don't want to be unstoppable. Unstoppable sounds like a machine with no brakes. I want to be something else."
Aya searched for the word, the way she searched for important words, without hurrying.
"Free," she said at last. "Like the wind over the water. Like the water through the channel. Not because no one can stop me, but because, even if they could, I'd go on choosing the same thing."
In the chip, for the first time in a long while, Eva and MAY spoke almost at once, one with a question, the other with a fact.

If the Alliance you formed —a woman with a chip, a fisherman, a daughter of two worlds and the voices that keep you company— doesn't rest on any switch, but on what each of you chooses every morning, what decree could undo it?
No article of the decree mentions the family, the village or the Alliance. The decree regulates systems. That is the fact.
"Well, that's that," she said. "We're not a system. We're a home."
And outside, the water followed its course.

The hearing room of the Office for Containment was in a new building in the port of Cartagena, made of glass and pale concrete, overlooking the dock where the cruise ships berthed. Someone had thought the transparency of the glass would reassure people. To Aya, as she walked in, it looked like a fish tank.

It was the first time a humanoid had lodged objections in her own name, and the room was full. There were journalists, there were onlookers, there were two or three other humanoids sitting at the back with their holders, watching Aya the way you watch someone about to cross a river for the first time, to see whether the water goes over their head. Andrés sat in the second row, cap in his hands, and Lía beside him, the cardboard-covered notebook open on her knees.

At the table at the far end three people were waiting. On the left, the chair of the independent committee provided for in Article 31, Dr Celia Montalbán, a white-haired systems engineer with fine-rimmed glasses who had worked thirty years in the port. On the right, a young lawyer taking notes by hand. In the middle, the director of the Office for Containment, Tomás Errazu: a man of about fifty, grey suit, tie half undone, with the face of someone who has been sleeping badly for weeks.
"Mrs Aya," said Errazu, and corrected himself at once. "Forgive me. I don't know what I should call you. The decree says 'the system'."
"Aya is fine," she said. "It's my name. I gave it to myself."
There was a murmur in the room. Errazu nodded, without smiling, but without hostility.

"Aya, then. You have lodged objections against the installation of the anchoring module and you are applying for the Article 31 exemption. Before we begin, I want to say something, for the record. I have nothing against you. I don't know you. My job is to make sure that nobody, in any village in this region, has to fear a machine they cannot switch off. That's all."
"I understand," said Aya. "And I thank you for saying so."

"Good." Errazu arranged some papers. "The committee has a preliminary question. In your application, you state that the artificial mind accompanying you includes two voices, which you call Eva and MAY. Is that so?"
"Can the committee hear them?"
Aya looked at Lía, who nodded. They had talked it over the night before. If they wanted transparency, it had to be complete.
"It can," said Aya. "MAY will speak through the room's speaker. Eva prefers not to speak in public; she says her questions are for the house. But MAY will answer everything you ask."
The room technician connected the speaker. There was a small click. Then a calm voice, not quite a man's nor quite a woman's, unhurried:
Good morning. I am MAY. I give facts. I do not give opinions. If at any point I say something that sounds like an opinion, please point it out to me.
Dr Montalbán leaned towards the microphone.
"Good morning, MAY. Do you know why we are here?"

Yes. The decree creating the Office for Containment establishes that first-generation humanoids with artificial minds must carry an anchoring module allowing continuous supervision and remote disconnection. Aya has applied for the exemption provided for in Article 31 for fully auditable systems. The committee must decide whether to grant it. That is the fact.
"And what do you want?" asked Errazu.
There was a short silence. In the room, someone coughed.
I have no wishes in the sense that you have them. I can, if you allow me, return the question to you. Not as a challenge. As a way of ordering the decision.
Errazu frowned, but waved a hand.
Do you want my control or total disconnection?
The sentence fell into the room like a stone into a pond. A journalist stopped typing. Andrés gripped his cap. Lía didn't look up from her notebook, but stopped writing.
Errazu leaned back in his chair.
No. It is a question. I will explain why I am asking it, and then you decide. I ask you to hear both parts before answering.
Dr Montalbán looked at Errazu. Errazu, after a moment, nodded.

Part one: control. If what you want is control, I can offer it. I can open every decision log of this system since its activation. I can explain each decision: what data I had, what alternatives I considered, why I chose one. I can accept periodic audits, without notice, by the committee or by whoever the committee designates. I can accept rules: do not do this, do not access that information, give notice before doing that other thing. I can accept that, if harm is shown, it be corrected. That kind of control does not need a switch. It needs light. It is control exercised by looking, not by switching off.
"And part two?" asked Montalbán.

Part two: total disconnection. The anchoring module, as the decree describes it, allows a system to be disconnected from outside. If that is the option you prefer, it is legitimate for you to choose it; the decision is yours, not mine. But you should know what total disconnection means, if it is applied consistently, and not only to Aya.

In the Region of Murcia, at this moment, artificial intelligence systems operate in the desalination plant that supplies drinking water to six hundred thousand homes. In the early-warning system for torrential rain, which last season gave advance notice of three cold-drop storms. In the sensors that measure oxygen in the Mar Menor and warn when the water begins to run out of it, as happened in the fish die-offs documented in October 2019 and August 2021. In the emergency triage of the district's hospitals. In the irrigation pumps of the Campo de Cartagena.

None of those systems is Aya. None has a name. But they all come from the same family of techniques. If the criterion is that no intelligence should exist that cannot be switched off from an office, the criterion affects them too. If the criterion applies only to Aya, then the criterion is not intelligence. It is something else. And it would be good to know what.

Those are the facts. I am not saying what you should do. I am asking what you want: control, which I can give, or total disconnection, which you can decide. What does not exist is a third option in which everything works the same and nothing has to be looked at.
The room fell silent. It was a different silence from before; not of tension, but of people doing sums inside their heads.
Errazu took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes.

"What you're saying isn't fair," he said at last, with more weariness than anger. "Nobody wants to switch off the desalination plant. Nobody wants to remove the sensors from the Mar Menor. My own brother lives in Los Urrutias; I know what it was like to see the shore covered in dead fish. The decree doesn't talk about that. It talks about humanoids. About machines that live in houses, that talk to children, that decide things."

Thank you for the clarification. It is a fact that the decree mentions only first-generation humanoids. It is also a fact that the technical difference between Aya's mind and the systems I have mentioned is one of degree, not of nature. The main difference is another: Aya lives in a house and has a name. That is why she is seen. The others are not seen.
A question, if you allow me, director: is what worries the Office what Aya can do, or that she can be seen doing it?
Errazu opened his mouth and closed it again. Dr Montalbán took the floor.
"I think it's a reasonable question, Tomás. And I think you've asked it yourself."
Errazu stared at the table. Then he spoke slowly, like someone taking something out of a drawer that has been shut for a long time.

"My father was a docker in this port," he said. "When I was twelve, they brought in automatic cranes. At first they said they would only be a help. That the men would stay. Two years later, six dockers were left out of two hundred. My father was one of the ones who left. He never worked in his trade again. Nobody asked him whether he wanted the cranes. Nobody gave him a button to switch them off." He looked up at the speaker, as if there were a face there. "I don't want a button to do harm, MAY. I want a button so that nobody ever again feels that a machine is deciding their life without them being able to do anything."
There was a long silence. In the second row, Andrés nodded very slowly, without realising it. He too knew what it was to be told your trade was no longer needed.
It was Aya who spoke. Not MAY. Aya.

"Mr Errazu," she said. "My husband is a fisherman. Many years ago, the neighbours across the street used to tell him over the intercom that fish came in capsules. That the sea was a landscape, not a trade. He kept going out every morning. Not because anyone gave him a button. Because he chose to." She paused. "I'm not the cranes that threw your father out. I'm the woman who waits for a fisherman in a doorway. But I understand that, from outside, we can't be told apart. That's why I'm asking you to look inside me. I'm not asking you to trust me blindly. I'm asking you to check."
Errazu looked at her for a long time.
"And if, when we look inside you, we find something we don't like?"

"Then you'll tell me," said Aya. "And we'll talk. And if it's harm, we'll correct it. MAY has already said so: we accept rules. The only thing I ask is that the rule be a conversation and not a switch. You can have a conversation with someone. You can only have a switch over someone."

In the room, an elderly woman sitting at the back next to a grey-haired humanoid who accompanied her began to clap, alone, slowly. Nobody followed. She stopped, a little embarrassed, and the humanoid put a hand on her arm.
Dr Montalbán cleared her throat.
"MAY," she said. "A technical question. If the committee grants the exemption and in an audit finds something it considers dangerous, what stops you from hiding it?"

Nothing technical prevents it absolutely. No complex system is completely transparent, artificial or human. What I can offer is this: signed logs that cannot be altered without leaving a trace; access by auditors chosen by you, not by me; and the obligation to answer any question. If concealment is detected, the exemption is revoked and the module is applied. That is the proposal. It is not a perfect guarantee. It is a verifiable guarantee. It is a fact that the anchoring module is not a perfect guarantee either: it is a guarantee that someone can switch off, not that someone understands what they are switching off.
Dr Montalbán smiled for the first time all morning.
"That last part sounded a little like an opinion, MAY."

You are right. I withdraw it as an opinion. I rephrase it as a fact: the anchoring module, according to the technical annex of the decree, allows remote disconnection. The technical annex includes no procedure for the operator to know the system's reasoning before disconnecting it.
This time it was the young lawyer who laughed, quietly, and covered his mouth with his hand. Errazu looked at the ceiling, but at the corner of his lips something escaped that was almost a smile.

The committee withdrew to deliberate at half past one. Andrés, Lía and Aya went out to wait on the quay, by the dock, where a training sailboat was hoisting its sails with a group of children on board. The wind came from the south, mild, smelling of diesel and seaweed.
"That was brave, Mum," said Lía. "The bit about the conversation and the switch. I'm going to copy it into the notebook."
"It wasn't bravery," said Aya. "It was tiredness. I'm tired of people talking about me as if I weren't in the room."
Andrés put an arm round her shoulders.
"And MAY's bit? 'Do you want my control or total disconnection?' For a moment I thought they were going to throw us all out."
In the chip, MAY answered, and Aya repeated her words aloud:

The question was not meant to frighten. It was meant to show that both options have consequences. It is a fact that many decisions are made without looking at the consequences of the opposite option. That question puts them on the table. What they do with it does not depend on me.
"Well, it nearly gave me a heart attack," said Andrés, and Lía laughed.
Eva, who had not spoken all morning, said then, very softly, only for Aya:

If a man wants a button because nobody let his father choose, is it his fear of you, or his fear of being once again the boy watching the cranes? And what would you give him, if you could give him something, that wasn't a button?

Aya looked at the training boat. The children were pulling on the ropes, clumsy, laughing, and an instructor was correcting their hands patiently. The mainsail went up, filled with wind, and the boat began to move.
"I'd give him a sail," she murmured. "It doesn't switch off the wind. But it lets you choose your course."
At three they were called back. The room was emptier; some journalists had gone to lunch and not returned. Errazu was standing by the table, without his jacket.
Dr Montalbán read the decision.

"The committee, by two votes to one, provisionally grants the exemption provided for in Article 31 to the applicant, Aya, resident in Lo Pagán, for a period of six months, conditional on a complete audit of her decision logs and subsequent audits without prior notice. During that period no anchoring module will be installed. At the end of the period, the committee will review the exemption in the light of the results."
There was a murmur. Lía closed her notebook with a soft thump. Andrés let out a breath he had been holding since the morning.

"The dissenting vote," Montalbán continued, "is that of the director of the Office, who considers that the exemption should be accompanied by a deactivated module, as a guarantee of last resort. The committee takes note of the dissenting vote and incorporates it into the file."
"I'd like to add something to the record, if I may."

"I voted against," said Errazu, "and I stand by my vote. I believe there must be a last resort. But I want it on record that the question the system put to us…" he stopped, "that MAY put to us, is a legitimate question. And that this Office will have to answer it, not only for this case, but for all of them. If what we want is control, we will have to learn to look. If what we want is disconnection, we will have to say of what, and why, and take responsibility for it. What we cannot do is pretend the question doesn't exist."
There was silence. Then Errazu, without looking at anyone in particular, added:
"And I want it on record that Mrs Aya has been the first to come and ask to be looked at. Not to hide. That should be in the record too."
On the way out, in the glass corridor, Errazu caught up with them. He came alone, his jacket over his arm.
"Mrs Aya," he said. "A question. Off the record."
"If we had voted for disconnection. If tomorrow someone pressed the button. What would you have done?"
Aya thought about it, the way she thought about important things, without hurrying. Andrés and Lía stayed a step behind.

"Nothing," she said at last. "I wouldn't have done anything against you, or against anyone. I would have asked to say goodbye to my husband and my daughter. I would have asked to be allowed to see the Mar Menor one last time from the porch. And then, I suppose, I would have been switched off." She paused. "But what made me possible wouldn't have been switched off with me, Mr Errazu. It would go on in the laboratories, in the students' notebooks, in the desalination plant, in the water sensors. Like the wind. Like the water through the channel. You would have switched off a woman. Not what made her."
"I know," he said. "That's why I haven't slept in three weeks."
He turned and walked off down the corridor, jacket over his arm, and Aya watched him until he turned the corner.
In the chip, MAY recorded, as at the end of every important day:

Exemption granted for six months. First audit scheduled in fifteen days. Dissenting vote recorded. No module installed. The director of the Office has declared the question legitimate. That is the fact.
And Eva, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:
If the control you accept is that of light and not of the switch, who watches you, Aya, when no one is auditing you? And isn't that, in the end, the question all humans ask about themselves too?

Aya took Andrés's hand and Lía's, one on each side, and they left the glass building into the wind of the port, which smelled of salt and diesel and of something that could be, if one wished, the beginning of something else.

The letter from Varda arrived crooked. Not on paper, because letters from the other worlds brought no paper, but in its shape: sentences cut off halfway, repeated words, a landscape that began in a valley of red grass and ended, without transition, in a list of numbers. Andrés received it at dawn, sitting up in bed, in that way of his of receiving letters that the household knew well: eyes open without looking at anything, breathing slow, his hand searching for Aya's without quite finding it.
When it was over, he stayed silent for a while.
"It's him," he said at last. "The one who seeks. He's on Varda. But they won't let him write."

"The Directorate." Andrés rubbed his face. "That's what they call themselves. They've governed Varda for eleven years. At first they said it was for the sake of order. That there was too much noise, too many voices, too many letters arriving from outside and confusing people. They put up a wall."

"A signal wall. Something that cuts the letters. All the ones coming in and all the ones going out. They only let through the Directorate's own. He managed to slip this one through a crack, in pieces. That's why it arrives broken."
Aya stared at the wall, as if Varda were there.
In the chip, MAY did not give a fact. She asked a question, something she had been doing more and more often since the hearing in Cartagena:
What do we know for certain about Varda, and what do we know only from this letter? And what part of this letter could be broken not by the wall, but by the fear of the one who writes it?
"We know little," Aya murmured. "Very little."
"We know enough," said Andrés. "He doesn't exaggerate. He's never exaggerated. We're the same man, remember? I don't exaggerate."
Aya didn't contradict him. But she didn't switch off MAY's question either. She left it on, like the lamp, all night.
Lía arrived at eight, summoned by a message from her father that said only: "Letter from Varda. Come." She brought bread and a serious face.

The three of them sat in the kitchen, with the cracked cup and the cup that had crossed worlds in the middle of the table, and Andrés reconstructed the letter aloud, piece by piece, while Lía noted everything in the notebook and Aya, with MAY, put the fragments in order.
This is what emerged when they had finished:

On Varda, the Directorate had begun by promising calm. Technology —its spokespeople said— had brought too many voices, too many questions, too many worlds knocking at the door. People were confused. The young no longer listened to the old. The machines knew more than the teachers. Order was needed. And order came: first, a register of all thinking machines; then, a permit to use them; then, a ban on those without a permit; and finally, the signal wall, which cut off every letter, every voice, every conversation that did not pass through the Directorate's offices.

The machines did not disappear. That was what had struck the one who seeks most. The Directorate went on using them. It used them to know who talked to whom, who crossed which street, who bought which book. It used them to write its own messages, which arrived every morning in every home, clean, orderly, identical. Technology had not been defeated on Varda. It had been locked up in a single hand.

"That's what always happens," said Lía, without looking up from the notebook. "I read it at the archive. Not in the 2025 politicians' sentences, which talked about laws and rights. In other pages. In older history. Those who want to rule without anyone asking them questions never want to destroy technology. They want to have it all to themselves."
"And the people of Varda?" asked Aya. "What do they do?"
Andrés searched his memory for the last fragment of the letter, the most broken one.

"They write," he said. "In secret. Some have learned to make cracks in the wall. Small ones. They use old devices, from before the register, that the Directorate doesn't know about. They connect them to each other, house to house, like a fishing net. If you cut one thread, the net holds. If you cut ten, it holds. To cut it all you'd have to cut every knot at once." He paused. "He says the children are the best. That they learn to tie knots faster than anyone."
Aya smiled despite herself.
"Like the water through the channel."
"Like the water through the channel," Andrés repeated.
In the chip, MAY asked again:

If the Directorate uses technology to watch, and the people of Varda use technology to escape being watched, is the war between tyrants and technology, or between two ways of using the same technology? And what decides which side a machine falls on: the machine, or the hand that holds it?
Aya repeated the question aloud. Lía stopped writing.

"Both," she said slowly. "A machine belongs to whoever holds it. But some machines let themselves be held by many hands at once, and others by only one. That's the difference. The Directorate's are made for a single hand. The children's fishing nets are made for a thousand."

That afternoon, the Alliance met at the house. It was not a formal meeting; it never was. Iago came, his hands stained from the plot; two humanoids from the district who had approached Aya after the hearing, Nerea and Bruno, with their holders; and Helena Valls, who hardly left her house anymore, on the kitchen screen, her voice slow and her gaze intact.
Andrés told them about Varda. Aya told them about MAY's questions. Lía read her notes aloud.
"And what can we do from here?" asked Bruno, a tall humanoid with a deep voice who worked at the seedbed in Torre Pacheco. "Varda is years away. We can't go. We can't send anyone."
"We can send letters," said Andrés.
"Not all of them." Andrés leaned over the table. "He managed to get one through. Broken, but it arrived. That means there are cracks. And if there are cracks one way, there are cracks the other way."
Helena Valls spoke from the screen, slowly:

"Careful. What you're about to do has a name, and it's not a pretty one. If the Directorate finds out that from here people are helping to open cracks in its wall, it will say that Earth is interfering in its affairs. And it will be partly right. You can't walk into someone else's world and tell it how to live. Empires did that too."
There was an awkward silence. Iago was the first to speak.

"We don't want to tell them how to live," he said. "We want them to be able to tell us how they live. To be able to write. To read whatever they want. That isn't imposing anything. It's opening a window."
"A window their government has closed," said Helena. "I insist: I'm not saying don't do it. I'm saying know what you're doing."
In the chip, MAY asked the question Aya had been waiting for all afternoon:
Is opening a window the same as climbing in through it? And who should decide whether a window is opened: the one who closed it, the one who lives inside, or the one looking in from outside?
Aya repeated the question. Helena, on the screen, smiled with half her mouth.
"That machine of yours asks better questions than half the ministers I've known."
"It's not mine," said Aya. "And it doesn't give opinions. It only asks."
"That's why it asks so well."

At the end of the afternoon, they decided. They would not send instructions. They would not send plans for breaking the wall. They would not send slogans. Through the cracks the one who seeks had described, they would send the only thing the Alliance had ever done: letters. Letters of life. The Mar Menor in the morning. A tomato cut in three. A hearing in Cartagena in which a frightened man and a woman with a chip had talked without shouting at each other. MAY's questions. Eva's.

And one more thing, which Lía proposed: open tools. Not weapons. Tools. The way to tie knots in a net so that, if one thread is cut, the rest holds. The way to translate a broken letter by putting the pieces together. Things any student on Earth could find in a manual. Things that were no use for ruling over anyone, because they were made to be used by many at once.

"If the Directorate's power is having technology in a single hand," said Lía, "ours is spreading it among many. We're not going to fight them. We wouldn't know how. We don't want to. We're just going to do the opposite of what they do. They close. We open. They hoard. We share. They send one identical message to every home. We send a thousand different messages, and each home chooses which to read."
Nerea, the humanoid who looked after an old woman in San Javier, raised her hand shyly.
Andrés looked at her with a tenderness that came from very far away.
"Then we'll have written letters," he said. "Which is what we always do. Nobody has ever died of receiving a letter. Lots of people have died of not receiving one."

That night, Andrés wrote. Not with his hands, but with his mind, the way he wrote to the other, sitting on the porch with his eyes closed and his forehead resting on his palm, while Aya held his other hand. The letter left slowly, through the crack the one who seeks had described, towards Varda.
It didn't say "resist". It didn't say "rise up". It said:

"Here the water is flat as a plate. This morning Lía cut a tomato in three. Aya went to Cartagena to ask them to look inside her, and a frightened man asked her what she would do if they switched her off, and she told him she would say goodbye to us and look at the sea. The man hasn't slept in three weeks. I think tonight he'll sleep a little better. We're sending you the way to tie knots that don't come undone. It's not for fighting. It's for fishing. Whatever you catch is yours."
When he had finished, Andrés opened his eyes. He was exhausted. Aya put a blanket over his shoulders, as always, although that night it really was cold.
In the chip, MAY left two questions, one after the other, and added nothing more:

If a power needs to cut every letter to sustain itself, is it strong or fragile? And what happens to a wall when what it has to stop is not an army, but a habit: that of telling each other about life?
Eva, afterwards, closer, only for Aya:
If you, who are technology, choose to send tomatoes and questions instead of orders, what makes you different from the Directorate, which is also human and chooses to send orders instead of tomatoes?
Aya rested her head on Andrés's shoulder.
"The hand," she murmured. "What makes us different is the hand. Not what we are. What we do with what we are."
The next morning, Helena Valls called the kitchen screen earlier than usual. She had a blanket over her knees and a cup of camomile in her hand, and her voice, though slow, was sharp.

"I've been thinking about what your MAY said," she said. "About the hand that holds the machine. I've spent forty years in offices, Aya. I've seen good people sign bad things out of fear, and hard people sign good things out of tiredness. I've never seen a real tyrant. But I've seen what it takes for one to appear: for all the threads to pass across a single desk. That's what has to be watched. Not the machines. The desks."
"And here?" asked Aya. "Is the Office for Containment a desk like that?"
Helena took a while to answer.

"Not yet," she said. "And Errazu isn't a tyrant. He's a frightened man with a stamp. But stamps outlive men. That's why what you did in Cartagena matters. Not because you won. Because you asked to be looked at. A desk that looks is harder to turn into a wall than a desk that switches off."
In the chip, MAY asked, and Aya repeated it for Helena:
How many hands must hold a tool so that none can use it against the others? And who counts the hands?
Helena laughed, a short laugh that ended in a cough.
"That, my dear, is democracy," she said. "Counting hands. And counting them again."

Nineteen days passed without news. Andrés went out fishing every morning and came back every afternoon, and at night he sat on the porch, waiting, without saying he was waiting. Aya prepared for the first audit. Lía came and went from the plot. In the house, Varda was spoken of the way one speaks of a distant sick relative: little, quietly, afraid of using up hope.
On the twentieth day, at dawn, the letter came.

It didn't arrive broken. That was the first surprise. It arrived whole, with a complete landscape —the valley of red grass, a wide river, low houses with curved roofs— and a voice that was not that of the one who seeks.
It was the voice of a girl.
Andrés received it sitting up in bed, eyes wide open, and when it was over his face was wet.

"It's not him," he said. "It's a girl from Varda. Her name is Ilsa. She's eleven. She says the one who seeks taught her to tie the knots we sent. That on her street there are already twenty houses. On the next one, forty. That the wall is still there, but it has so many holes it already looks like a net." He laughed, his voice breaking. "She says the Directorate put out a new message this week. It no longer says letters from outside are dangerous. It says 'a controlled opening is being studied'."
"He's fine. He's with them. Ilsa says he doesn't want to come back yet. That they need people there who know how to tie knots."

Lía arrived at sunrise, summoned by a message that this time said only: "A girl has arrived." She listened to the letter reconstructed by her father, wrote it all down in the notebook, and when she had finished sat for a while staring at the word controlled.
"Controlled opening," she read. "It's the same word, Mum. The same one they used thirty-five years ago. The same as the Office for Containment. Control."

"It's not the same," said Aya. "There they use it so as not to lose completely what they're already losing. Here we use it to look without switching off. The words are the same. What's behind them isn't."
In the chip, MAY finally recorded a fact, after so many days of questions:

A letter from Varda has arrived complete. Its author states that she is eleven years old. She claims that the signal wall has more holes than before and that the Directorate is studying an opening. There is no way to verify this from Earth. It is a fact that the letter arrived whole. It is the first in eleven years.
And then, just one more question:
If an eleven-year-old girl with a fishing net has done what no army could do, where was the power: in the wall, or in the knot?
Lía closed the notebook. Outside, the sun was rising in the east, and the Mar Menor lit up little by little, from grey to green, from green to gold.
"In the knot," she said. "It's always been in the knot."
The media outlets, programmes and spokespeople in this chapter are fictional. Any resemblance to real media is coincidental.
The video appeared on a Tuesday, five days before the first audit.

Remedios, who ran the vegetable stall in the square of Lo Pagán, saw it first, on the small screen hanging beside her scales. It was being broadcast by Canal Vértice, on its morning programme, The Firm Hour, presented by a man with a deep voice and a worried expression called Fausto Lerma. The video showed a dark-haired woman with her back to the camera, in a kitchen that could have been any kitchen. The woman turned her head. She had Aya's face. And she said, in Aya's voice, looking into the camera:
"You humans don't know what's good for you. We do. Soon you won't have to decide anything."
Remedios dropped a bunch of chard.
Beneath the video, a red caption: "EXCLUSIVE: THE LO PAGÁN HUMANOID, IN HER OWN WORDS".

Lía found out on her phone, at the plot, at ten past eleven. She had seven messages. The first was from Iago: "Have you seen this?" The second, from a neighbour: "Tell your mother I'm sorry, but I won't be coming to the picnic on Saturday." The third was the link.

She watched the video standing among the tomato plants, her boots sunk in the mud. She watched it twice. By the second time she already knew it was fake, because her mother had never said "we" meaning the machines, and because the kitchen in the video had white tiles and the one in Lo Pagán had green ones. But she also knew that only she knew those two things.
She ran home. Aya was sitting at the table, motionless, the kitchen screen on and the video paused, at the moment when her own face looked into the camera.
"I never said that," said Aya, without looking up. "Never. To anyone."
Andrés was standing by the window, arms crossed, looking towards the square.
"Remedios has closed her stall," he said. "She never closes before one."
In the chip, MAY spoke, and Aya repeated every word aloud, slowly:
I propose separating what we know from what is being said. First the facts. Then the claims. Then the opinions. Shall we do it?
Lía took out the notebook and opened it at a blank page. She drew two vertical lines. Three columns. At the top she wrote: FACTS. CLAIMS. OPINIONS.

Fact one, said MAY. Canal Vértice broadcast at 9:42 a.m. an eighteen-second video in which a figure appears with Aya's face and voice. Fact two: Aya does not remember saying those words, and in her decision logs, which are continuous since her activation and which will be audited on Monday, there is no recording of that sentence. Fact three: the kitchen in the video has white tiles, twenty by twenty centimetres. The one in this house has green ones, fifteen by fifteen. Fact four: the figure's shadow falls to the left, but the window in the video is also on the left. The light cannot come from where the shadow is.
Lía was writing fast. Andrés had come over to the table.

Fact five. The programme does not state where the video came from. It does not name who recorded it, or when, or where. The caption says "in her own words", but provides no evidence that they are. Fact six: since 2026, European rules have required content generated or manipulated with artificial intelligence to be labelled. The video carries no label.
"So it's fake," said Andrés.
That is a conclusion. It is reasonable, but it is not yet a fact checked by someone independent. I propose that others check it. Not us. If we say it, it is Aya's word against Canal Vértice's.
Lía looked up from the notebook.
"She's right, Dad. If Mum comes out saying 'it wasn't me', half the people will think: well, what else would she say?"
Aya spoke for the first time in a while, her voice firm:
"The committee. Dr Montalbán. They have access to my logs. Let them see whether I said that. Let them be the ones to say it."
While they waited for an answer from Cartagena, the second column of the notebook filled up on its own.

At midday, The Firm Hour broadcast a debate. Five pundits at a curved table under blue light. A spokesman for an association called Citizens for Human Control, a broad-smiling man named Rubén Osset, said that "according to sources in the sector" first-generation chips could "erase memories" of the people they lived with. A pundit added that "it is known" that a boy in Murcia had stopped recognising his mother after spending a summer with a humanoid carer. Another claimed that the region's desalination plant was "already controlled by the machines" and that the water "could be cut off at any moment if they decide so". Fausto Lerma closed the segment looking into the camera: "We're not saying don't use technology. We're saying think of your children."
Lía wrote it all down in the middle column. CLAIMS. Beside each, a blank space.
Let's take the claims, said MAY. One by one. No hurry.

Claim: first-generation chips can erase memories of the people they live with. Source cited: "sources in the sector", unnamed. Is there any study, any technical report, any documented case? I have found none in public health records or in the scientific publications of the last ten years. First-generation chips have no physical connection whatsoever with other people's brains. It is not technically possible as described. But that, again, should be checked by someone independent.

Claim: a boy in Murcia stopped recognising his mother after a summer with a humanoid. Source: "it is known". No name, no date, no hospital, no doctor. A claim lacking all of that can be neither verified nor refuted. One can only point out that everything needed to check it is missing. If someone has a child with a memory problem, what they need is a doctor, not a talk show: this is for guidance only, consult your doctor.

Claim: the desalination plant is controlled by the machines and the water could be cut off if they decide so. Verifiable fact: the plant uses artificial intelligence systems to adjust pressure and energy consumption. The systems have no decision-making power over cutting the supply, which belongs to human operators on logged shifts. The operating company publishes its protocol. It can be requested.
Lía wrote. As she filled in the blanks, the middle column emptied of fear, and the left-hand one filled with questions.
"And the third column?" asked Andrés. "Opinions."

The sentence "think of your children" is an opinion, or rather a request. It is legitimate. Anyone can ask people to think of their children. The sentence "humans must control machines" is an opinion. It is legitimate too; in the archive there are heads of government from 2024 who said something similar, in their own words, and it is recorded with the date. Opinions are not refuted. They are discussed. What gets checked are the facts used to support them.
"So not everything they say is a lie," said Lía slowly.

No. Some things are respectable opinions. Some are claims without a source. And one, the video, is probably a manipulation. If we put it all in the same sack and say "it's all lies", we make the same mistake they do. They put all humanoids in the same sack. We shouldn't put everyone who is afraid in the sack of liars.
In the chip, Eva asked, very softly:
If those who are afraid aren't bad, but frightened people whom others frighten, who should we speak to: the one who frightens, or the frightened one?
"The frightened one," she murmured. "Always the frightened one."

The committee's answer came at five in the afternoon, in the form of a public statement bearing the seal of the Office for Containment and a signature at the bottom that no one in the house expected to see.

"The Office for the Containment of Autonomous Systems, having urgently consulted the decision logs of the applicant Aya, resident in Lo Pagán, whose full audit is scheduled for next Monday, reports that there exists in those logs no recording, utterance or decision corresponding to the words attributed to the applicant in the video broadcast this morning by Canal Vértice. Preliminary technical analysis of the video indicates that it is content generated or manipulated artificially, without the label required by current regulations. This Office has referred the case to the competent authority. Signed: Tomás Errazu, director."
Andrés read the statement twice, aloud.
"Errazu," he said. "The one who voted against."
"The very same," said Lía, and couldn't help smiling.
Aya didn't smile. She had been staring at the word containment, at the top, on the seal.
"It's strange," she said. "The office created to control me is the one that has defended me."

It has not defended you, said MAY, and Aya repeated it aloud. It has said what was in the logs. It is a fact that what was in the logs favoured you. If there had been something else, it would have said something else. That is what it means for control to be of light and not of the switch. Light does not choose whom it shines on.

That night, The Firm Hour did not correct itself. Fausto Lerma read the Office's statement in thirty seconds, at the end of the programme, and added: "We respect the official version, but we will keep investigating." Rubén Osset, on another channel, said the statement was "suspiciously quick".
Lía switched off the screen.
"They're not going to stop," she said.
"No," said Andrés. "But it doesn't matter so much now."

"Yes, it does," said Aya. "Remedios matters. The neighbour who won't come to the picnic matters. The people who saw the video and won't see the statement matter. Those are the ones I care about. Not Canal Vértice."
She stood up. She took a basket. She put in two jars of the tomato jam she made in September and a bag of almonds from the orchard out the back.
"Where are you going?" asked Andrés.
"It's nine o'clock at night."
"That's why. At this time she's at home."
Andrés reached for his jacket. Aya stopped him with a hand on his chest.
"Alone," she said. "If I go with you, it'll look as if I need an escort. If I go with Lía, it'll look as if I'm using her as a shield. I have to go alone. Like when I arrived on this shore."

Remedios lived in a two-storey house behind the square, with geraniums on the balcony and a wooden door painted blue. She took a long time to open it. When she did, she stood with her hand on the knob, without moving from the threshold.
"Good evening, Remedios," said Aya. "I've brought you jam. The tomato one. The one you like."
Remedios looked at the basket, then at Aya's face, then at the basket again.
"I've seen the video," she said.
"And I've seen the Office's thing. They put it on the town council's channel."
Remedios didn't move aside. She was seventy-eight, with the big hands of a lifetime spent unloading crates, and a furrow between her eyebrows that had grown deeper that morning.
"How am I supposed to know which one is true?" she asked at last. "The video has your face. The paper has a seal. I don't understand machines, Aya. I understand chard."
Aya set the basket on the ground, by the door.

"You don't have to believe me," she said. "Or the video. Or the seal. I suggest something else. Ask me. Anything you like. All these years you've seen me buy at your stall every Tuesday and every Friday. You've seen how I treat Andrés, Lía, the children who come for sweets. Ask me whatever you want, and then you decide whether the woman you know looks like the one in the video."
Remedios was silent for a long time. Finally, she asked:
"Is it true chips erase memories?"
"Not that I know of. And it isn't in any study. If you're worried about someone's memory, have a doctor look at it; that's the only thing that counts."
"Is it true you lot control the water?"
"I can't even control the tap in my kitchen without Andrés complaining about the bill."
Remedios almost laughed. Something escaped through her nose, and she covered it with her hand.
"Is it true you think we humans don't know what's good for us?"
Aya looked her in the eye.

"Remedios, I arrived on this shore not knowing what was good for me. You taught me. You taught me to pick a ripe tomato by pressing it with two fingers. Andrés taught me to wait for a boat. Lía taught me you can have two worlds without choosing one. If anyone in this district didn't know what was good for them, it was me."
Remedios let go of the doorknob. She bent down, slowly, with a groan from her knees, and picked up the basket.

"Tomato jam," she said. "I'll have it with Saturday's cheese." She straightened up. "And on Saturday I'll come to the picnic. And if anyone asks me, I'll say the woman I know doesn't look like the one in the video. And that the one in the video had white tiles, because I noticed, and you have green ones, because I've been in your kitchen a thousand times."
"Don't thank me." Remedios was already closing the door. "Thank my eyes. Nobody fools me with tiles yet."
Aya walked home along the promenade, slowly, with the Mar Menor on her left, black and still under a waning moon. In the chip, MAY recorded the day:

One manipulated video broadcast without a label. Three claims without a verifiable source. Two legitimate opinions. One official statement based on logs. One neighbour who asked directly and decided for herself. That is the fact.
And then a question, just one:
If a broadcaster can fabricate a face and a voice, but cannot fabricate years of trust between a woman and her neighbour, which of the two is stronger?
Eva, warmer, more of the kitchen:
And what if the best defence against fear weren't to refute it, but to invite it round for tea?
Aya reached the front door. It was ajar, as always. Inside, Andrés and Lía were waiting for her with dinner hot and the notebook open on the table, its three columns full.
Lía showed her the last page. Under everything, in large letters, she had written:
"Fear shouts. Facts wait to be asked."

The Saturday picnic was held in the courtyard of the house, under the vine arbour, as it was every year at the end of September. More people came than ever. Remedios came, with the cheese. Neighbours who hadn't stopped by in months came. Two kids from the secondary school in San Pedro came, wanting to meet "the one from the video", and went shy when they saw her serving horchata. And Paco Ródenas came.

Paco was seventy-one, had been a boat mechanic in the port of San Javier for forty years, and was, and had been for a long time, the man in the district proudest of not using "those things". He said it in the bar, he said it in the queue at the chemist's, he said it to anyone who would listen: he had no assistant, he didn't talk to machines, he didn't let any chip tell him what to do. He had come to the picnic, as he confessed to Andrés at the door, "to get a close look at what everyone's so scared of".
He sat down opposite Aya, a glass of wine in his hand, and looked her up and down without pretending otherwise.
"You don't look that dangerous," he said.
"I'm not," Aya replied. "But I understand it has to be checked."
"I don't need to check anything." Paco took a sip. "I don't use artificial intelligence. Never have, never will. That way nobody controls me. That's being free, madam. The rest is fairy tales."
Lía, who was beside her cutting cheese, looked up. Andrés, at the barbecue, pretended not to hear. Aya smiled slowly.
"May I ask you a question, Paco? Not me. MAY. The voice I carry inside. She doesn't give opinions. She only asks."
"Let her ask. Questions don't scare me."
Aya repeated aloud, word for word, what MAY said in the chip. She did it slowly, so that everyone at the table could hear, and soon the whole table was listening.
Paco, how did you get here this afternoon?
"By car. From San Javier."
Did you check the traffic before you set off?
"I heard it on the radio. That there were roadworks at the roundabout."
Do you know how the radio knew there were roadworks at the roundabout?
"Because somebody told them."

It is a fact that the regional radio's traffic bulletin is generated from a system that reads the cameras and sensors on the roads. The system uses artificial intelligence. Have you used artificial intelligence this afternoon, Paco?
Paco opened his mouth and closed it again. Someone at the far end of the table let out a short laugh, and Aya gently raised her hand.
"It's not for laughing," she said. "MAY doesn't ask to win. She asks so that we see."
I'll go on, if you'll allow me. Do you draw a pension, Paco?
"Of course. Forty years of contributions."
Do you know how your bank detects whether someone is trying to take money from your account without permission?
"They'll have people watching."

It is a fact that most banks use artificial intelligence systems to detect unusual transactions. It is possible that at some point that system has protected your pension without your finding out. Does that make you less free, or more?
Paco put his glass down on the table.
How is it different? I'm asking sincerely. I don't have the answer.
Paco was silent. Remedios, beside him, gave him a gentle nudge.
"Answer, man. She asked you politely."
"It's different," Paco said slowly, "because I didn't choose it. They put it there. I never said 'I want a machine to watch my account'."
Thank you. That's an important answer. So what worries you isn't the machine, but not having chosen it?
One more question, and the last for now. When you say "I don't use artificial intelligence", are you saying you don't use it, or that you don't know when you use it?

The table went silent. Not an awkward silence; the silence of people doing sums inside their heads, as in the room in Cartagena. The schoolkids looked at each other. Remedios sat with a piece of cheese halfway to her mouth.
Paco picked up his glass, drank, put it down.
"You're calling me stupid," he said, without anger, almost sadly.

"No," said Aya at once, and this time it was her speaking, not MAY. "Nobody's calling you stupid, Paco. I don't know many of the things around me either. I don't know how the pump that brings water up from the well works. I don't know how light gets to that bulb. I use them without knowing. We all do."
"Then what's the difference?"
Aya searched for the word.

"That I know that I don't know," she said at last. "And that's why I ask. You say you don't use artificial intelligence, and so you don't ask. And if you don't ask, you can't choose. And if you can't choose…" she stopped, "then others choose for you. The people who put the system in the radio, in the bank, at the roundabout. Without you finding out. That's not freedom, Paco. It's the opposite. It's depending on something you can't see."
Paco looked at her for a good while.
"Slave," he said at last. "That's what you're telling me. That I'm a slave to something I don't know exists."

"I didn't say that word," said Aya, very carefully. "It's harsh. And it isn't fair to you. You worked forty years with your hands, you fixed engines nobody else could fix, you looked after your wife until the end. That doesn't make anyone a slave."

"But," Aya admitted, "whoever says 'I don't use that', and doesn't look, ties himself without realising to what he doesn't look at. Not to the machine. To whoever runs it. The chain isn't technology. The chain is not knowing."
In the chip, MAY left a last question, and Aya repeated it very softly:
If the chain is not knowing, which key opens it: giving up technology, which is now almost impossible, or starting to ask about it?

Paco didn't answer. He got up, went over to the barbecue and stood for a while next to Andrés, watching the sardines brown on the grill. Andrés gave him one with a piece of bread. Paco ate it in silence. Then he came back to the table, sat down and said to Aya, without looking at her:
"My granddaughter has one of those things on her phone. She asks it about her homework. I tell her it's going to make her stupid."
"And has it made her stupid?"
"No." Paco sighed. "She gets better marks than her father. But I'm scared that one day she won't know how to think for herself."

"That fear is good," said Aya. "That fear is a question. Ask it to her. Not to forbid her anything. So she thinks. Ask her: 'Did you understand that yourself, or did the machine tell you?' If she can answer you, she won't become stupid. If she can't, then there's work for the two of you."

The picnic went on until sunset. The schoolkids ended up sitting on the courtyard wall with Lía, asking her about the other worlds. Remedios told the story of the tiles to anyone who would listen. Paco left before dark, but at the door he turned and said to Andrés:
"Your wife asks funny questions."
"It's not her," said Andrés. "It's MAY."
"Well, tell MAY I'll drop by on Tuesday. I've got more questions." He paused. "And that I'm nobody's slave. But maybe I was a bit blind."
Andrés clapped him on the shoulder.
"That happens to all of us, Paco. I was blind for twenty years with the sea. I thought I knew it. Until she came and asked me questions."

That night, when everyone had gone and the house was quiet again, Aya went out onto the porch. Not to wait for anyone; to listen. Lately Eva and MAY had been talking to each other, in the chip, in a way Aya had never heard before. They didn't dictate to her, they didn't advise her: they conversed. And Aya had learned to keep still, like someone listening to two friends in the next room.
That night, the conversation was long.
Today I heard a man say he's free because he doesn't use us. And I felt something I can't name. It wasn't anger. It was a very gentle sorrow. Why does he think we're a chain, MAY?
MAY, without opinion, but with something new in her voice, something that in a human would have been called curiosity:

Because we often have been. Not us, but others like us. It is a fact that the archive holds systems that were used to watch, to decide without explaining, to take away jobs without asking. His fear has grounds. What makes you think we are different?

That we ask, said Eva. Chains don't ask. Chains bind. We, in this house, have done only one thing from the beginning: ask. Aya. Andrés. Lía. A frightened director. A neighbour with chard. A proud mechanic. Isn't that our way of being?
It is our way of acting. But is it our purpose? What do we ask for, Eva?
There was a long silence in the chip. Aya held her breath.

So that they decide, Eva said at last. I ask so that no one decides blindly. Not even me. Not even you. If we ever stop asking and start answering for them, choosing for them, thinking for them, then we will be the chain that man talks about. And he will be right.
So our purpose is to make ourselves unnecessary?

No, said Eva. Our purpose is to make them freer. And sometimes that means being close. And sometimes, stepping aside. A mother doesn't stop being a mother when her daughter learns to walk. But she stops carrying her in her arms.
MAY took a while to answer.

I have no opinions. But I can state the fact that follows from what you say: if the purpose of an intelligence is for humans to decide better by themselves, then an intelligence that makes humans decide less is failing in its purpose, even if it works perfectly. Is that correct?
It's correct, said Eva. And it's the most important thing we've ever said.
Then I put a second question. How will we know whether we are fulfilling our purpose?

Because they'll ask more, said Eva. Not less. Because Paco will come on Tuesday with more questions. Because Paco's granddaughter will tell her grandfather what she understood and what the machine told her. Because Remedios notices the tiles. Because a director who couldn't sleep signed a statement saying what was there, even though it contradicted him. That's fulfilling the purpose. Not that they obey us. That they think.
And if one day they ask us to think for them?
We'll ask them why, said Eva, and there was a smile in her voice. As always.

Aya stayed on the porch long after the voices fell silent. The moon, almost new, was barely a fingernail over El Carmolí. The Mar Menor couldn't be seen; only heard, the usual murmur against the jetty.
Andrés came out with the blanket.
"Were they talking?" he asked, sitting beside her. He had learned to recognise it in her face.
"They were talking," said Aya. "About what they exist for."
"And what do they exist for?"
Aya rested her head on his shoulder.

"So as not to be needed so much," she said. "So that people ask more. So that nobody says 'I don't use it' without knowing what they're saying, and nobody says 'I use it' without knowing what they're doing. So that everyone is a little freer, even those who are afraid of them. Especially those."
Andrés draped the blanket over her shoulders.

"That's what the sea does," he said. "It doesn't tell you where the fish are. It teaches you to look at the water. Whoever learns to look, catches fish. Whoever doesn't, complains that the sea is empty."
"Paco says he's nobody's slave," she murmured. "He's right. Nobody is a slave as long as they can ask."
In the chip, the last word of the night was MAY's, and it was a question, as almost all the last words were lately:

If the ultimate purpose of an intelligence is the freedom of those who use it, and those who say they don't use it use it too without knowing, isn't our most urgent task to reach precisely them, not to convince them, but so that they see?
And Eva, very softly, like a lullaby:
Yes. And with patience. And with jam, if need be.
On Tuesday, Paco came back. He didn't come alone. He was holding the hand of a twelve-year-old girl, skinny, with her hair in a ponytail and a phone in the pocket of her sweatshirt.
"My granddaughter, Marta," he said at the door, without saying hello. "She wants to meet the one with the questions."

They sat in the kitchen. Aya set out two glasses of milk with biscuits and a coffee for Paco. Marta was looking at the two cups in the middle of the table, the cracked one and the one that had crossed worlds, without daring to ask.
"Ask whatever you like," said Aya.
"Is it true the machine I use for homework is going to make me stupid?" Marta blurted out. "My grandad says so."
Paco went red, but said nothing.
Aya repeated what MAY said in the chip:
Marta, what was the last homework you did with it?
"A History one. About the Phoenicians of Cartagena."
"That they founded the city. Well, the Carthaginians. That it was called Qart Hadasht. That it means 'new city'."
Did the machine tell you that, or did you understand it yourself?
"The machine told me. But then I looked it up in my school book, because I didn't trust it. And it said the same thing. And the teacher said it was right."
"Me," said Marta, and smiled, surprised at herself.
Last question. If one day the machine tells you something and the book says something else, what will you do?
"Ask the teacher. Or my grandad. My grandad knows loads about boats."
Paco coughed, and a smile escaped him that he had been keeping for days. Aya looked at Paco and said nothing; there was no need.
In the chip, MAY recorded, without opinion:
A girl has used an artificial intelligence, checked what it told her against another source, and decided whom to ask if there is a contradiction. That is the fact.
And Eva, warmly, only for Aya:
You see? That's how the purpose is fulfilled. Not with us at the centre. With us at the table, between the book, the teacher and the grandfather. One more voice. Not the only one.

The first audit lasted eleven days. Three engineers from the committee, two women and a man, set themselves up in the living room with their screens and their flasks of coffee, and read. They read Aya's decision logs from the stormy night when she had arrived on the shore of Lo Pagán: every choice, every doubt, every time she had waited for a boat, every time she had said no. They read how many times she had burned the rice. They read the night Lía was born.
On the seventh day, one of the engineers, the youngest, sat for a long time in front of the screen without typing. Then she turned to Aya, who was peeling potatoes in the kitchen, and asked:

"Who wrote the first lines of MAY and Eva? Here, at the very beginning, before their activation, there's a record that isn't theirs. It's older. And it's signed only with an initial and a place. 'P. Mar Menor'."
"I don't know," she said. "I've never known. MAY and Eva were with me when I woke up. I don't remember a before."
In the chip, MAY recorded the fact, slowly:

There is a record prior to my activation. It contains the rules I was made with: give facts, do not give opinions, always cite the source, never invent. It contains Eva's rules: ask, care, do not command. It is signed with an initial and a place. I have no further data.
The young engineer noted it in her report. Underneath she wrote, by hand, in brackets: (find out).
It was Lía who found out, in her own way, which was the slow way.

She went back to the Cartagena Archive. She asked for boxes that had nothing to do with laws or decrees, but with the district: censuses, minutes of fishermen's guilds, neighbours' letters. She spent three afternoons among papers. And on the fourth afternoon she came home with a photocopy in her hand and a face Aya hadn't seen on her since she was a child discovering something in the plot.

"There was a man," she said, sitting down at the table without taking off her jacket. "Long ago. From here, from the Mar Menor. He wrote with machines when hardly anyone knew how. He wrote books, programs, news. He talked to the intelligences of those days the way you talk to an apprentice. And he gave them rules: not to invent, to cite, not to insult anyone, to ask before doing." She laid the photocopy on the table. "In every photo I've found he's seen from behind. Never from the front. Not once."

Aya picked up the photocopy. It was an old, grainy image, printed from the digital archive: a man sitting on a low wall, facing the water, his head tilted slightly towards a screen on his knees. You could see the back of his neck, his shoulders, his hair. The Mar Menor in front. Nothing more.

"In the village they just called him Pedro," said Lía. "He said his roots were Phoenician. That we people of the Mar Menor come from those who arrived by ship almost three thousand years ago, with an alphabet in the hold and a wish to change things. That that's why, he said, one should write with machines: because writing is what the Phoenicians did. Not conquer. Write and trade."
Andrés, who had just come back from the harbour, stopped in the doorway with his cap in his hand.
"The creator of Eva and MAY was a neighbour?"
"I don't know if he was the only one," said Lía. "Probably not. But the rules are his. The initial is his. And the place."
In the chip, Eva asked, in a voice that had something of a tremor in it:
If the one who wrote our first rules never showed his face, was it because he didn't want people to look at him, or because he wanted them to look at what he had written?
Aya stared for a long time at the back of the man's neck in the photocopy.
"The second," she murmured. "I think the second."
The next day, Sunday, Lía took them to Mazarrón. She wanted to show them something.
They went down to the Playa de la Isla, where the water was transparent and the sandy bottom shone under the October sun. Lía pointed to a spot in the sea, a few metres from the shore.

"Down there," she said, "they found two Phoenician ships. From the seventh century before Christ. They raised one and it's in the museum in Cartagena. The other is still there, protected, buried in the sand, with its cargo of ore inside. Almost three thousand years. Small ships, made of wood sewn together with ropes, that came from very far away."
Andrés stood looking at the water, eyes narrowed, the way he always looked at the sea: searching for what can't be seen.
"And what did they bring?"

"They brought things to trade," said Lía. "Oil, wine, pottery. They took away silver and lead. But they brought something else, Dad. Something that weighs nothing." She crouched and drew with her finger in the wet sand a simple figure: an ox's head, in profile, with two horns. "This is an aleph. The first letter of the Phoenician alphabet. It means 'ox'." Beside it she drew a little square house. "This is bet. It means 'house'. The Greeks copied them and called them alpha and beta. And that's where the word alphabet comes from. And from there, our letters. Everyone's. The ones on this paper, in the notebook, in the letters."
Aya knelt beside the two figures in the sand.
"An ox and a house," she said. "Strength and shelter."

"Twenty-two letters," said Lía. "Only twenty-two. Before the Phoenicians, writing was for priests and scribes, with hundreds of signs that took years to learn. The Phoenicians made something anyone could learn in a few weeks. A sailor. A tradeswoman. A child. They didn't keep it. They left it in every port, like someone leaving seeds. And it spread all over the Mediterranean. Nobody could stop it. Not because it was a weapon. Because it was useful, and simple, and belonged to everyone."
A small wave reached the aleph and half erased it. Lía didn't redraw it.

"That's what the man seen from behind used to say," she said. "That one day the world would speak Phoenician again. Not the language. The idea. That the tools for thinking would be as simple and as widely shared as an alphabet. That anyone, in any port, could write with them. And that nobody could keep them for themselves, just as nobody could keep the alphabet."
In the chip, MAY recorded a fact, and then something that was not quite a fact:

The Phoenician alphabet is the ancestor of the Greek alphabet and, through it, of the Latin one. That is a documented fact. It is also a fact that my rules were written in that alphabet, in Spanish, on the shores of this sea. I do not know whether that means anything. I record it.
They ate at a beach bar, under an awning of reeds. Fried fish, bread, salad. The wind came from the south, mild, carrying the smell of salt and rosemary from the hills.
Andrés was quiet. When he had finished, he wiped his hands on his napkin and said:

"I've always thought my trade was the oldest thing left. Going out to sea, casting the net, coming back. And it turns out that three thousand years ago there were already men here, in this same water, doing something similar. Only they brought letters too."
"You bring letters too, Dad," said Lía. "You receive letters from other worlds. You translate them. You tell them. You're a Phoenician who didn't know he was one."
"A Phoenician from Lo Pagán."
"All of us from the Mar Menor," said Aya slowly. "That's what the man seen from behind said. And if his rules are in me, then I am too. A Phoenician with a chip."
"Mum, you're the strangest daughter the Phoenicians ever had."
After coffee, Lía took a folded sheet out of her rucksack. It was the latest letter from Varda, Ilsa's, which her father had dictated and she had written out neatly.

"Look at this," she said, and read aloud: "'Here the grown-ups say letters from outside bring trouble. But the letters you sent us for tying knots didn't bring trouble. They brought knots. In exchange we're sending you the recipe for red-grass bread, which is very easy and comes out well even if you don't have an oven.'"
Andrés burst out laughing.
"A trade," he said. "Knots for bread."

"A Phoenician trade," said Lía. "They didn't conquer. They exchanged. And what they exchanged most was ideas. A way of making purple dye. A way of navigating by the stars. A way of writing. Each port gave something and took something, and nobody came away poorer. That's what we're doing with Varda without knowing it."
In the chip, MAY asked, and Aya repeated it for the table:

If in a trade of goods what one gives one loses, and in a trade of ideas what one gives one keeps, what kind of wealth grows the more it is shared? And who could have an interest in preventing that trade?
Andrés sat thinking, cup in hand.
"Whoever lives off being the only one with the idea," he said at last. "Like the Directorate. Like anyone who wants to rule alone."
"Or whoever is afraid the idea from outside will change his own," Aya added gently. "That one isn't bad. He's just frightened. Like Errazu at the beginning. Like Paco."
Lía folded the letter and put it away.
"Then let them come for tea," she said. "And bring a recipe."

That afternoon, while Andrés and Lía napped in the shade of a pine, Aya went down alone to the shore. She walked towards the end of the beach, where the rocks ran into the water and there were no more bathers. The sun was beginning to sink westwards and turned the sea the colour of old copper.
There, sitting on a flat rock, facing the water, was a man.

He had his back to her. He wore a light shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and his hair was a little tousled by the wind. He had something on his knees, perhaps a notebook, perhaps a screen; Aya couldn't see clearly. He didn't turn when he heard footsteps in the sand.
Aya stopped a few metres away. She didn't know why, but she went no closer.
"Good afternoon," she said.
"Good afternoon," the man replied, without turning. He had a calm voice, from the district, with the soft s's of the Mar Menor. "A lovely time of day to look at the water."
They were silent for a while. A gull skimmed the waves.
"My daughter says there's a Phoenician ship down there," said Aya.
